en: Chapter One: The Chapter on Inquiry Susiddhikara Sūtra, Volume One, Part One At that time, the Bodhisattva Krodha-Mañjuśrī joined his palms in reverence, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Vajradhara, and addressed him with this question:
"In the past, I heard from the Venerable One..."
I have heard the rituals for the maṇḍalas of all the Vidyārājas and their sequential procedures;

furthermore, I have heard of the spiritual efficacy and majestic power of the various retinues of these Vidyārājas. For the sake of all sentient beings in the future, I pray that the Honored One will deign to provide a detailed explanation.
How may one obtain the sequence of rules for the recitation of mantras so as to swiftly attain accomplishment?
Although all mantra methods are of a single essence, the number of dharmas to be accomplished through them is immeasurable.
What are the characteristics of mantras? What is an ācārya?
And what is a disciple who has attained accomplishment?
What are the locations that constitute the most excellent places?
How are mantras swiftly accomplished?
What are the signs of subjugation?
What is the sequence of the skillful means for reciting mantras?
What is the offering of flowers?
What are the incense and unguents?
What is incense and burnt incense?
What are the characteristics of lamps and oil?
What is the offering of food?
What is śāntika? What are the characteristics of pauṣṭika?
What are the characteristics of vaśīkaraṇa?
Among these three types, what specific functions does each accomplish?
What are the characteristics of their accomplishment in the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior?
And how is the ritual invocation of the Dharma performed?
How does one practice making offerings?
How does one protect and maintain the body?
How does one extensively uphold the Dharma?
Which verses and mantras should be recited?
How is the consecration performed?
And how is the mantra tested?
How should one receive the entrustment?
How are the syllables made perfect?
How does one obtain increase?
What are the various sequential ritual applications for performing homa?
By what substances can one achieve swift accomplishment?
And what are the characteristics of the perfected medicinal elixir?
What are the characteristics of taking medicine?
How is medicine purified and prepared?
What is the proper dosage of medicine?
What are the characteristics of the various medicines?
How does one protect the articles for accomplishment?
How are they distinguished and categorized by number?
How does one enjoy accomplished substances?
How does one recover lost objects?
And how does one, having been defeated, cause others to be defeated?
How is the characteristic of creating obstacles known?
How is the maṇḍala accomplished?
What is the maṇḍala of ritual matters?
What is the consecration maṇḍala?

Regarding the questions asked above, according to their essential points, I pray only that the Venerable One, endowed with great compassion, will analyze each one in detail and explain them extensively for me.
At that time, the Great Vajradhara, the Worthy One of All Mantra-Holders, Adorned with Auspiciousness, addressed that Great Wrathful One of Great Resolve, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
O Great Wrathful One!
Since you have been able to pose such a question to me, you should listen with a single-minded focus to this supreme and subtle dharma-vidhi, the Susiddhikara Five Adornments.
What are the five?
First is diligence;
second is the vidyārāja.
Third, it refers to the removal of hindrances;
fourth, it refers to the accomplishment of all heroic deeds;
fifth, it refers to the accomplishment of all mantras.

"If there are those who practice other mantra methods within this *Susiddhikara Sūtra* and do not achieve success, they should also maintain the root mantra of this sūtra, and they shall quickly attain accomplishment."
Among the three families (*trikula*), this sūtra is the king; it is also capable of accomplishing all such matters as:

protecting the body, summoning, binding the boundary (*sīmābandha*), making offerings, providing assistance, adjudicating punishments, and giving instructions. It brings about the accomplishment of every single mantra in its proper sequence.
"If there are three *hūṃ* syllables within any heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*), one will be able to accomplish all the ritual matters described above.
The heart-mantra with the three *hūṃ* syllables is as follows:
'Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ' (with the first *hūṃ* drawn out from the throat). The mantra for eloquence (*pratibhāna*) is as follows:"
"Oṃ tathāhuḥ | dhurati | saraṇati | dhāraṇi | huṃ phaṭ. With this mantra, sprinkle water three times over the body to perform purification.

"Furthermore, regarding the methods for superior, middling, and inferior accomplishments (*sādhana*), as explained in other sutras, those seeking accomplishment must understand the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas of mantras. This sutra comprehensively encompasses the *maṇḍala* rites performed by the three families:
the *śāntika* rite of the Buddha Family mantra; the *pauṣṭika* rite of the Avalokiteśvara Family mantra;
and the *abhicāruka* rite of the Vajra Family mantra."
From the armpits to the crown of the head is the upper part;
from the navel to the armpits is the middle part;
and from the feet to the navel is the lower part.
"Within the mantras, one should distinguish three types of accomplishment (*siddhi*). Within these three families (*kula*), each is further divided into three; this must be well understood.
Among the mantras of the three families, the mantras of the Vidyārājas constitute the superior accomplishment;
all other messengers (*dūta*), *ceta*, *cetaka*, and so forth, constitute the inferior accomplishment."
The śāntika rite, the pauṣṭika rite, and the ābhicāruka rite are each present within the three families; one must skillfully understand their respective sequences.
“If, within the Buddha Family, one employs a Buddha-mother mantra for the *śāntika* rite, the Buddha-mother mantra is as follows:

‘Namo bhagavate uṣṇīṣāya | oṃ ru ru saṃpuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane samucchata-saṃdhani svāhā. If, within the Avalokiteśvara Family, one employs the Avalokiteśvara-mother Bhaṇḍalavatsinī mantra for the *śāntika* rite, [the mantra is as follows:]”
The mantra of the Mother of Avalokiteśvara is as follows:

*Namo ratnatrayāya* (1) | *Oṃ* (2) | *Kāñci* (3) | *kāñci* (4) | *bhagavati mārīce* (5) | *Svāhā* (6). If one employs the mantra of Vajraśṛṅkhalā, the Mother of the Vajra Family, for the *śāntika* rite within the Vajra Family.
The mantra of Vajravārāhī is as follows:

"Namaḥ stutāratrāya | Namaḥ śveta-vajra-pāṇaye | Mahā-yakṣiṣeṇa-pataye | Namaḥ raudra-dṛṣṭaye | Namaḥ saṅkale saṃtike | Kūṭadhi kūṭadhine gacchate | Kūṭadhine | Svāhā. Furthermore, within the Buddha Family, the most supreme vidyārāja mantra of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa is for the pauṣṭika rite.
The mantra of the Vidyārāja is as follows:

"Namo bhagavate śrī-ṣaṇmukhāya sarvataraṅgoddhātāya śamaya śamaya saṃtarpaya dharmarājapūjite mahāmṛteye sarvādhyāśayadhani svāhā. Furthermore, within the Avalokiteśvara family, the Vidyārāja Hayagrīva mantra is used for the puṣṭika rite.
The mantra of the Vidyārāja is:
"Oṃ amṛtodbhava bhamo bha va namas. Furthermore, within the Vajra Family, the mantra of the Vidyārāja Supoṣa is used for the pauṣṭika rite.
The mantra of the Vidyārāja is as follows: "Namo ratnatrayāya."
Namo vīraṇāya vajrapāṇaye.

“Ṭha ṭha” (14). Furthermore, within the Buddha Family, the mantra of the Great Wrathful One Aparājita is for the *abhicāruka* rite.
The wrathful mantra is as follows:
“Oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍe maṇḍe jaye svāhā. Furthermore, within the Lotus Family, the mantra of the Great Wrathful One Śivavāha is for the *abhicāruka* rite.
The mantra for *Svāhā* is as follows:

“Namaḥ stanutaruṇāya | Namaḥ mahāśriye | Oṃ | Śokṣaye samaye | Saurmye | Sidi sidi | Svadhāya | Śve śve | Śvaṅke | Śvamre | Svaha | Avahata svadhāni | Svāhā. Furthermore, within the Vajra Family, the mantra of the Great Wrathful One, Kuṇḍalī, serves as the rite for *Abhicāruka*.
The mantra of the Wrathful One is as follows: "Namo ratnatrayāya."
Namaḥ ścaṇḍāya mahāvajrakrodhāya.
Oṃ hulu hulu. (The same as above,

“Amṛte hūṃ phaṭ. Furthermore, there are mantras that do not belong to the three families;

one should distinguish the three types of rites, such as *śāntika*, according to the syllables of those mantras. If, within a mantra, one observes the words “*śānti-kuru*,” “*svasti-kuru*,” the word “*saṃ*,” the word “*pra-saṃ*,” the word “*upa-saṃ*,” or the word “*svāhā*,” one should know that it is a *śāntika* mantra.
If there is the word "pauṣṭika," one should know that it is a pauṣṭika mantra;
if there is the word "kuru," one should know that it is an ābhicāruka mantra.
Furthermore, if a mantra’s words and meaning are benevolent and compassionate, one should know that it pertains to the function of *śāntika* (pacification);
if a mantra’s words and meaning are fierce and wrathful, one should know that it pertains to the function of *abhicāruka* (subjugation/terrifying);
if a mantra is neither benevolent nor fierce, one should know that it pertains to the function of *pauṣṭika* (nourishment/enrichment).
"If one wishes to swiftly accomplish *śāntika*, one should employ the mantras of the Buddha Family;
if one wishes to swiftly accomplish *pauṣṭika*, one should employ the mantras of the Lotus Family;
if one wishes to swiftly accomplish *abhicāruka*, one should employ the mantras of the Vajra Family."
"This sutra is profound and wondrous, like the God among Gods; it is said to be the supreme among the supreme. If one relies upon this Dharma, there is no undertaking that will not be accomplished."

"Although this sūtra belongs to the Vajra Family (Kulika), by following the Buddha’s instructions, one can also accomplish the practices of the two higher families. It is just as when a king issues a command, he himself also acts in accordance with it; this practice is likewise so."

"According to this principle, one should know that if a mantra, though consisting of few syllables, has the syllable 'Oṃ' at the beginning and the syllable 'Svāhā' at the end, it should be known that this mantra can swiftly accomplish the *śāntika* rite.

Alternatively, there may be a mantra that has the syllable 'Hūṃ' at the beginning and the syllable 'Phaṭ' at the end, or the syllable 'Hum'; these are sounds of wrath. Any mantra possessing such syllables as these will swiftly achieve the accomplishment of the *abhicāruka* rite."

If there are mantras that lack the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, lack the syllable *svāhā* at the end, and furthermore lack the syllables *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*, or *vaṣaṭ*, one should know that such mantras are capable of swiftly accomplishing *puṣṭika* rites.

"If there is anyone who wishes to subdue various other spirits, such as *piśācas* and others, they shall quickly achieve success by using the mantras taught for messengers (*dūta*) and *ceta* [servants].
Furthermore, if there are mantras from other sections that claim to accomplish all matters, they can only accomplish what is taught within their own section and do not apply to other sections."

Furthermore, there are sutras that expound mantras for the purpose of eliminating poison and disease; since these are taught, they are also capable of removing all other forms of suffering, and one should understand that they thus apply universally to all uses.
One must thoroughly know the respective classes [of mantras], be well-acquainted with the appropriate applications of the mantras, and also understand their efficacious power;
furthermore, one must skillfully comprehend the methods for cultivating mantra-practice, and according to whatever aspiration is sought, one should recite and maintain that specific mantra.

Chapter Two: Distinguishing the Characteristics of the Ācārya *Susiddhikara-sūtra*, Chapter Two: Distinguishing the Characteristics of the Ācārya "Furthermore, I shall now explain the characteristics of the ācārya."
Since all mantras are obtained through this, one should know that the ācārya is the most fundamental.
What are his characteristics?
They are as follows:
With limbs perfectly formed and adorned with merit;
skillfully knowing and understanding both mundane and supramundane dharmas;
and always abiding in accordance with the Dharma, never practicing what is contrary to the Dharma.
Possessing great compassion and pity for sentient beings;
born into a noble family with a naturally disciplined and gentle disposition;
and bringing peace and happiness to all who dwell together with him.
Possessing intelligence, wisdom, and unimpeded eloquence;
able to maintain patience while harboring no view of self;
skillfully understanding profound meanings and having deep faith in the Mahāyāna.
Even when committing a minor offense, one should maintain great dread;
one’s physical, verbal, and mental actions must be well-disciplined and gentle, and the mind should always be joyful;
one should read Mahāyāna sūtras and reverently follow the teachings of the Dharma.
One must diligently recite mantras without interruption so that all the siddhis to be accomplished are fully realized;
furthermore, one must be skilled in drawing maṇḍalas.
They constantly possess the four means of integration;
seeking the Great Dharma, they take no pleasure in minor conditions and are forever free from stinginess;
and having previously entered a great maṇḍala with a teacher, they have received the empowerment ritual.
Furthermore, one's former teacher should praise them, saying:
"O Virtuous One, from this day forward you are worthy to bestow empowerment and serve as an Ācārya!
Only after receiving such authorization is it appropriate to personally compose the sequence of rules for the maṇḍala, and only then is it appropriate to transmit the mantras to disciples.
If one relies upon this, the mantras one receives will quickly attain accomplishment; there is no need for doubt.
If one does not receive them, yet chants the mantras at the residence of an Upādhyāya or Ācārya, one will merely expend effort in vain and ultimately fail to obtain the fruit.
"Now, the law for disciples is that they serve their ācārya with reverence, just as they would toward the Three Jewels and the Bodhisattvas. Why is this?

Because he is able to grant them a place of refuge and serves as the primary cause for all virtuous deeds; through him, one attains peace and happiness in the present life and reaps the fruits in the future. It is by relying upon the ācārya that one shall, before long, succeed to and attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

For this reason, you should revere them as if they were Buddhas and become their disciples; serve your ācāryas without indolence, diligently upholding their instructions without omission, and you shall attain *siddhi* regarding the Vidyārājas and Vidyārājñīs they bestow—of this you must have no doubt.

3. Chapter on Distinguishing the Characteristics of Recitation. *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Three: Distinguishing the Characteristics of Recitation. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the characteristics of the practice for achieving success through the recitation of mantras."
One must ensure that the three karmas are pure both internally and externally;
the mind must not be distracted and must never be interrupted;
one must constantly cultivate wisdom and be able to practice the One Dharma.
They accomplish all matters and are further free from stinginess;
their speech is without impediment;
they dwell among the assembly without fear, and all that they undertake is successfully accomplished.
They constantly practice loving-kindness and patience, remaining free from all flattery and deception and devoid of illness;
they always speak truthful words and are skillfully proficient in the affairs of the Dharma;
and though young in years, their faculties and physical limbs are all fully perfected.
One should constantly give rise to reverence and faith toward the Triple Gem;
practice the subtle and wondrous Mahāyāna sūtras;
and never harbor a mind of retreat regarding any virtuous merit.
Such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment.
One who always maintains reverence toward all bodhisattvas and mantras,
and gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings— such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment.

"One who always delights in tranquility and does not delight in the midst of crowds, who constantly practices truthful speech and maintains a mind of pure mindfulness—such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment.
If one hears of the sovereign power of the Vajradhara Bodhisattva and gives rise to sincere faith, joy, and a desire to hear more—such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment."

"If a person has few desires, is content with all things, recites and maintains the mantra, and contemplates the sought-after objective without ceasing day or night, such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment."
"If a person, upon first hearing the dhāraṇī sūtras and teachings, has their body hairs stand on end and their heart leaps with great joy, such a person shall attain accomplishment."
"If a person sees their own siddhi in a dream, as described in the sutras—delighting in mental tranquility and not dwelling among the multitude—such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment."
"If a person always honors and respects their ācārya as they would the Buddha, such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment.

If a person recites mantras for a long time without obtaining results, they must not abandon them; rather, they should redouble their vows, increase their diligence, and persevere until success is achieved—such a person will swiftly attain accomplishment."
Chapter Four: Distinguishing Companions. *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Four: Distinguishing Companions. "Furthermore, the characteristics of companions shall now be explained."
Adorned with merit, they are born into a noble lineage;
they always delight in the True Dharma and do not practice what is contrary to it;
furthermore, harboring deep faith, they are free from all fears.
He is diligent and never regresses, reverently practicing the Honored One’s teachings and always speaking truthful words;
his sense faculties and physical marks are all perfectly complete, and his body is free from disease;
he is neither too tall nor too short, neither too stout nor too coarse, nor is he emaciated; his complexion is neither too dark nor too pale, being thus free from such blemishes and ailments.
Accompanied by merit, one endures other sufferings through patience;
one is skillfully versed in mantras, mudrās, and maṇḍalas;
and one follows the sequence of offerings and all other ritual regulations.
They constantly cultivate pure conduct and accord with all matters through patience;
their speech is harmonious and elegant, causing others to delight in hearing it;
they are free from all conceit and possess a powerful memory that never forgets.
They uphold the teachings and practice them without shirking responsibility;
they possess great learning and wisdom, with a compassionate heart free from anger;
they constantly mindfully practice generosity and are skillful in discernment.
One must constantly recite the mantras of the Vidyārāja;
the mantras one maintains should be identical to those of the practitioner;
furthermore, one should clearly understand the methods for binding the boundaries and protecting the body.
Having obtained such companions, one will swiftly achieve accomplishment.
Their three karmas are well-disciplined;
they have previously entered a maṇḍala under a teacher.
They returned to practice the Buddha-dharma and did not study the provisional or inferior teachings;
they skillfully understood the sequence of what practitioners required without waiting for verbal instructions,
providing whatever was needed at the very moment it was sought.
One who possesses such qualities is a superior companion.
With body and mind virtuous, free from mental distress, resolute and firm,
never retreating from the resolve— by obtaining such a companion, one will swiftly achieve accomplishment.
"One who does not harbor expectations of or greed for great wealth and profit, and who possesses such virtues, is called an excellent companion.
Furthermore, they do not abandon the practitioner’s mind.

If one wishes to accomplish various medicinal elixirs, they should act as a powerful condition and must not abandon their natural noble precepts; one who possesses such virtues is called an excellent companion."

"One should have no expectations or desires regarding the practitioner; until the attainment of *siddhi* is fully accomplished, one must never abandon them. Even if many years pass without realizing *siddhi*, one should never harbor a mind of abandonment or retreat. Even if great suffering or other hardships were to afflict the body and mind, one should not forsake them."
One endowed with such virtues is said to be a supreme companion.
If one possesses the various virtuous qualities mentioned above, they will be capable of accomplishing the most sublime and superior matters;

even if one lacks those aforementioned virtues, provided they clearly understand the ritual rules for mantra accomplishment, are well-versed in the wisdom of all maṇḍalas, and possess high intelligence, further augmented by merit and excellence in recitation—such a companion can likewise accomplish the most sublime and superior matters.

"In order to accomplish the supreme goal, his companion of merit shall, fortnightly, perform empowerments (*abhiṣeka*) and fire offerings (*homa*) for the reciter; at all times, he must provide whatever incense, flowers, and lamps are available, and perform all other protective rites and selections according to the sequence, assisting in whatever is required."
It is not merely that they assist in practicing the aforementioned matters;

if there is any deficiency or lapse in the recitation and upholding [of the teachings], these companions of merit, relying upon the sūtras and the Dharma, shall instruct them with reason so that no dharma or practice is neglected. Furthermore, they shall extensively explain the causes and conditions of all practices, item by item. One who possesses such qualities is the most excellent companion.

"When a practitioner recites daily or performs ritual acts and occasionally forgets them, this merit will accompany them wherever they go, assisting them in their practice so that everything becomes complete."

When one wishes to accomplish the medicinal rites, one must constantly press the medicine with the hand, or grasp a stalk of grass and use it to press it; even though the tasks of recitation and ritual performance are many, one must never neglect or forget this.

When the practitioner is about to conclude the recitation, their companion must stand nearby and observe them; if the practitioner becomes fatigued during the chanting, or if there is concern that they might forget to perform the ritual for dispatching the deities, the method for setting aside the rosary, or other such rites, the companion should assist in performing whatever the practitioner has forgotten.

"His companion must constantly recite [mantras], perform offerings, and cultivate merit through all activities, dedicating it all toward fulfilling the aspirations of the mantra-holder. Whatever instructions are given, they should be communicated only with the companion."
If one wishes to accomplish the most supreme matter, one must further permit a companion who speaks in harmonious accord without any discrepancy.

The food consumed by this companion must be the same as that of the practitioner; the practitioner’s own food must be prepared according to the prescribed rules. One who possesses such qualities is fit to be a companion for the superior practice of tranquility.
The merit of the third companion is likewise as previously described.

Chapter Five: Selecting the Site *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Five: Selecting the Site "Furthermore, I shall now explain the places for the accomplishment of mantra recitation: in which direction or region one must dwell to swiftly attain accomplishment."
"The place where the Buddha attained the Way and subdued the four Māras is the most supreme for swiftly attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*).

Because the banks of the Nairañjanā River are free from all obstacles, one will swiftly attain *siddhi* at that location; even if there are many Māras, they cannot create hindrances, and whatever is sought will be accomplished without exception—such a place brings swift accomplishment.
Alternatively, it may be at the place where the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma."
Or the city of Kuśinagara, the place where the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa;
or the city of Kapilavastu, the place where the Buddha was born.
These four aforementioned locations are the most supreme and excellent; free from all obstacles and disturbances, the three kinds of *siddhi* will certainly be accomplished there.
Furthermore, regarding the superior locations spoken of by the Buddhas, there are also the superior locations spoken of by Bodhisattvas: the eight great stupas of the Buddha.
Or there may be famous mountains abounding in forests, with many flowers, fruits, and flowing springs; such places are called superior locations.
"There may be a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) abounding in flowers and fruits, with flowing streams that people find delightful; such a place is called an excellent location (*viśeṣasthāna*).

Furthermore, there may be a forest hermitage where there are many deer and no one to hunt them, and which is free from beasts such as brown bears, black bears, tigers, and wolves; such a place is called an excellent location."
“Where there is neither excessive cold nor excessive heat, and which is pleasant and agreeable to the mind—such a place is called a superior location (śubha-sthāna).
Or it may be by the side of a mountain;
or on a mountain peak as a solitary high terrace.”
Alternatively, where there is flowing water on the slopes of a mountain, such a place is called an excellent site (*śubha-sthāna*).

Furthermore, where there is an excellent site with green grass covering the ground and many trees and flowers, and wherein there are trees suitable for performing *homā* (fire sacrifice), such a place is called an excellent site.
"Either before a stūpa where the śarīra relics are enshrined;
or at a place in the mountains where the śarīra relics are enshrined;
or by the banks of the four rivers;"
There may be a forest hermitage (araṇya) adorned with various lush and magnificent groves where few people dwell;
or a cemetery (śmaśāna) where smoke never ceases;
or the bank of a great river.
Or by the side of a large pond;
or having gone to a place where many cattle once resided;
or beneath a solitary, towering tree where spirits dwell and the sun’s shadow does not shift.
Whether it be at a single shrine in a large village,
or beside a crossroads,
or by the side of a dragon pond— such places are called "excellent locations."
"Alternatively, in whatever country the Buddha has traveled, such a region will swiftly attain accomplishment.
In any land where the people have faith and obedience, reverently honor the Triple Gem, and propagate the True Dharma, in such a place one will swiftly attain accomplishment."
"Furthermore, there are lands where many virtuous people abound and all possess compassion; in such places, one will swiftly achieve accomplishment.

Having obtained such a supreme and wondrous location, one must select and clear away impurities, shards, rubble, and other such things from the ground, as is explained in detail in each section of the Maṇḍala Chapter."

According to the methods for *siddhi*, one must properly distinguish the locations for the three families (*trikula*), and furthermore, one must distinguish between the *śāntika* rite, the *pauṣṭika* rite, and the *abhicāruka* rite.

These three dharmas must further be distinguished according to their superior, middling, and inferior qualities to constitute the ritual procedures; then, in accordance with what is appropriate for one's mind, by performing various activities such as purifying the site, smearing it with ointments, and sweeping it clean, one will swiftly attain the accomplishment of the *siddhi* dharma.

Chapter Six: The Ritual for Holding Mantras from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. Furthermore, I shall explain in detail the ritual rules for the restraint and holding of mantras; if one follows these procedures, one shall before long attain all accomplishments (siddhi).

If a wise person upholds these mantras, they should first sever all anger; they should not give rise to anger even toward the devas, nor should they harbor resentment or malice toward other mantra-holders.
One should not arbitrarily interpret the mantras, nor their powers and ritual rules;
one should cultivate profound reverence for all mantras and their rules;
and one must carefully protect against evil persons.
Why is this? Because it can obstruct great matters and destroy them.

Even if one perceives faults in the physical conduct of an ācārya, one should not give rise to arrogance, resentment, or engage in various kinds of right-and-wrong talk; the mind should ultimately never entertain such unwholesome thoughts.
If this is the case regarding transgressions, how much more so when acting according to the Dharma?
Even if one harbors great anger, one must never use the mantra one holds to bind another vidyārāja, nor inflict harm or punitive suffering;
furthermore, one should not perform rites for subduing enemies.
One who has not previously received mantras from an ācārya should not be granted them.
Furthermore, even if one has received mantras from an ācārya, they must not be given to someone who lacks reverence for the Triple Gem or who follows non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika).
One should not grant them the mudrās, nor the mantras, nor the methods of efficacy, nor the universal practices; none of these should be bestowed upon such a person.
It shall not be bestowed upon those who have never previously entered a maṇḍala.
One should not leap over any sentient beings, whether they be bipeds or even those with many feet; nor should one step over or trample upon any of the ground-mudrās.
That is to say:
one does not step over or tread upon hammers, wheels, clubs, pestles, conch shells, vajras, and the like, nor those made of raw materials;
furthermore, one does not step over or tread upon the roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits of various medicinal herbs.
Nor should one abandon impure and defiled places.
"If one wishes to achieve success in the mantra-dharma, one must abide by its regulations and should not raise objections against the correct principles of the Mahāyāna;
if one hears of the profound, rare, and inconceivable conduct of the Bodhisattvas, one should give rise to sincere faith and harbor no doubts."
A mantra practitioner should not exchange signs of efficacy with another practitioner who holds a different mantra;
nor, on account of a minor transgression, should one immediately employ rites of subjugation.
"One who delights in accomplishment should not engage in singing, chanting, or flirtatious speech;
for the sake of adorning the body, one should not apply ointments, powders, or flower garlands;
nor should one leap, run hurriedly, or engage in improper conduct."
Nor should one float about naked and play in the river.

To speak briefly, one should not engage in any physical mockery, nor any form of jesting; nor should one commit any wrong verbal karma, such as lying, deceitful speech, divisive talk that separates those who are in harmony, or harsh and abusive language. None of these should be done.
In responding to others, one does not rely on excessive words; one never practices or learns useless talk.
Furthermore, one does not dwell together with followers of external paths or with *caṇḍālas*; even if such persons come to question or challenge one, one does not converse with them.
One does not engage in conversation with outsiders, speaking only with one's companions.
"When reciting mantras, one should not speak even with one's companions, except at other times;
unless it is for one's own necessity, one should not converse with companions.
Furthermore, one should not smear oil upon the body."

Furthermore, one should not eat onions, garlic, radishes, sesame seeds, wine, vinegar, or any other leafy vegetables; nor should one eat rice flour, bean cakes, steamed beans, sesame cakes, or food made into balls—all of these should not be eaten.

One should not eat any food favored by the Vināyakas, nor the remnants of offerings, sesame, non-glutinous rice, bean porridge, or milk porridge; furthermore, one must not eat food that has been stepped over or touched.
"One shall not ride upon any vehicle or saddle-mounted conveyance;

nor shall one employ any ornaments for adorning the body—namely, mirrors, flowers, face-powders, medicinal ointments, or parasols—unless there is a specific cause or necessity. Furthermore, one shall not rub hand against hand, nor foot against foot."
One should not defecate or urinate in any water;

one should not eat by holding food in the hand at the edge of the bank, nor should one eat from a bronze vessel used as a hammer, but rather place the food on various leaves without folding them over.
"One does not lie upon large or small beds or couches, nor does one lie down in the same place as others.

When wishing to lie down, one lies down in purity, contemplating wisdom; one does not lie face-down nor lie on one's back, but lies on the right side like a lion king. While lying down, one does not sleep with eyes wide open."
"One should not eat a second time in a day;
one should not practice fasting;
one should not eat excessively."
One should not eat sparingly; if there is doubt regarding food, one need not eat it.
One must not look at any forms of frivolous play, large crowds, or even women.
One should not be attached to the dwellings, fine foods, and other such things received by means of body, speech, and mind;
nor should one reject the poor dwellings and coarse food that are received.
Furthermore, one should not wear purple garments, nor should one wear old, tattered clothes or soiled clothing.
When reciting mantras, one should wear undergarments and must not disparage oneself by saying:
"I have committed many transgressions; there is no way for me to attain the three kinds of *siddhi*."
"Even if, due to past karma, one's body is afflicted by various illnesses, one must not neglect the recitation; the mantra received shall never be abandoned.
Then, either within a dream or from the sky, a voice will appear and announce:
'You should not hold this mantra.'"
Even though he heard this repeatedly, he did not abandon it;
nor did he feel anger toward those who reviled and scolded him with evil words. Why was this?
Because they were all Māras.

One must simply apply oneself with diligence; one should not allow the mind to regress or harbor evil thoughts, nor should one pursue various false objects or abandon restraint over the sense faculties. One should always maintain purity while reciting the mantra.
"If one desires to attain the accomplishment of great siddhi, the mantra one recites and maintains should not be used to subjugate goblins and imps;
nor should it be used to provide protection for oneself or others;
nor should it be used to rescue those in distress or to restrain various poisons."
One should not perform other mantras that are not held by the True One; nor should one frequently employ any mantras for various purposes;
furthermore, one must not contend with others to test the power of their efficacy.
"If one seeks siddhi, one must bathe at the three times of day;
one should perform recitation at the three times, bathing each time with water consecrated by mantra.
The water-mantra is as follows:"

“Oṃ hūṃ gānā vajra ṇaḥ. With this mantra, one should recite it seven times over water and bathe; then all māras and vināyakas will not cause harm or affliction. It is not to be used without the mantra.”
The mantra for earth and water is:

"Oṃ ni-kha-na bha-su-ṭe svāhā. With this mantra, one should recite it seven times over the earth, then mix a small amount of water with the soil and knead it together. By thus smearing it upon the body and performing an ablution according to the ritual rules, all Vināyakas shall not cause harm or affliction.
The mantra for warding off *vināyakas* is:
"Oṃ amṛte gaṇa gaṇa huṃ phaṭ. If this mantra is recited seven times, all *vināyakas* will be warded off; one should then bathe [the image].
The mantra for bathing is:
"Oṃ amṛtībhava hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra seven times and bathe as you please. While bathing, do not engage in idle conversation; you must maintain mindfulness by reciting the bathing-heart-mantra.
The Heart Mantra for Bathing is:
"Oṃ hūṃ hāḥ kili kili huṃ phaṭ. Recite this mantra until the bathing is completed; then, scoop up water and pour it over the crown of your head.
The mantra for self-consecration is:
"Oṃ hakahari hūṃ phaṭ. With this mantra, one should cup water in both hands, recite it three times, and sprinkle it upon one's own crown; this is to be done three times.
Next, the mantra for binding the topknot is as follows:
"Oṃ susiddhikari svāhā. Recite this mantra three times over the hair and form a topknot upon the crown of the head.

If a bhikṣu forms a fist with his right hand, extends the thumb, and bends the index finger to press down upon the tip of the thumb, making the index finger round and curved; he should recite the mantra three times and place this mudrā upon the crown of his head.
The mantra for binding the hair of the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ śikhi śikhāyai svāhā. The mantra for binding the hair of the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ śikhāyai svāhā. The mantra for binding the hair of the Vajra Family is: [as above].
"Recite: 'Oṃ śikhā svāhā. Next, one should wash the hands three times, rinse the mouth three times, and bathe the principal deity."
The mantra for rinsing the mouth, drinking water, and sprinkling for purification in the Buddha Family is:
*Oṃ mahā-jvala hūṃ*. The mantra for rinsing the mouth, drinking water, and sprinkling for purification in the Lotus Family is:
*Oṃ tucche tucche ruru ruru svāhā*. The mantra for rinsing the mouth, drinking water, and sprinkling for purification in the Vajra Family is: [as above].

"Recite: 'Oṃ jvalita vāriṇi hūṃ svāhā. Having rinsed the mouth, drunk water, and performed the sprinkling purification (*prokṣaṇa*), face the direction where the deity resides. Visualize the deity, recite the mantra, and perform the mudrās. Take three handfuls of water, imagining that you are bathing the deity and offering *argha*; or, while reciting the mantra according to your intention within the water, proceed to the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).”
The mantra for offering water to the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ tathāgata-vajra-buddha svāhā. The mantra for offering water to the Lotus Family is:
"Oṃ vari vari hūṃ phaṭ. The mantra for offering water to the Vajra Family is:
"Oṃ viśvavajri svāhā. As for the mudrā: with both hands palms upturned and sides joined, use the two index fingers to pinch the tips of the two thumbs;

the remaining six fingers are joined and slightly bent. With this mudrā, scoop up water and offer it as a bath to the deity three times while reciting the mantra. This mudrā is used throughout the three families.

Furthermore, at that place, recite the mantra you maintain for as many times as you are able; only then may you proceed to your regular site of recitation. Until you have reached that location, do not harbor anger or envy, and do not follow after sensory objects. With body and mind pure, maintaining a reverent visualization of the original deity, proceed slowly. Firmly uphold the prohibitions and precepts as previously established, constantly maintaining them without forgetfulness.

Having arrived at that place, one should immediately perform all ritual activities according to the Dharma and engage in recitation; one must always construct maṇḍalas and perform offerings and recitations in accordance with the Dharma.
"If you should become weary, you must recite Mahāyāna sūtras or construct caityas; you must never neglect other virtuous deeds and must daily take refuge in the Triple Gem three times.

You must repent of all other sinful karmas three times, and at the three periods of the day, you must vow to generate the mind of great bodhicitta. If you act in this manner, you shall attain accomplishment."
One should make vows at the three times of day to accomplish sublime matters.

To eliminate all transgressions, one should constantly act in accordance with the teachings by performing various wholesome deeds, practicing generosity, and possessing great compassion. One should not give rise to stinginess regarding the teachings of the Dharma, always maintain patience, and be diligent without retreating. With deep devotion and faith, one should keep the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti) in mind.

One should carefully contemplate the words and meanings of the sūtras one has heard, constantly recite the mantras and the Dharma-chapters, and must make offerings to the mantras and the Dharma-sūtras. Relying on the sūtras, one should skillfully paint a sublime maṇḍala and enter it oneself to bring it forth.

First, the bhikṣus enter with sincere faith; then the bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās enter in succession, all of them firmly resolving their minds toward bodhicitta, maintaining a mind of determination, and possessing right view.

"Once one has entered the maṇḍala, one should be granted the methods for binding hand-seals (mudrā) and the sequential rules for upholding mantras. One should correctly and extensively proclaim the rules for mantra practice on the eighth or fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, or on the fifteenth day and the final day of the month, or on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month. On such days, one should increase offerings, recite according to the ritual, perform the homa rite, maintain the prohibitions and precepts, and constantly and diligently keep them in mind; by increasing all such matters, one will swiftly attain accomplishment in the mantra."
"When performing the homa, one must hold a vajra in hand and recite the mantra of Krodhavajra one hundred and eighty times, or one hundred and eight times, for the accomplishment of all rites."
The mantra of Krodhavajra is as follows: "Namo ratnatrayāya."

[Chapter] Twelve: "Regarding the application of various vajra rites: one should take wood scorched by a celestial fire, or *kaṭuka* wood, or wood from a funeral pyre, or white sandalwood, or red sandalwood—whichever is available—and carve it into a three-pronged vajra."

"When performing homa and when reciting mantras, one should always hold it with the left hand; because it is capable of accomplishing all matters, it is called a *vajra*, and it is the means for excellent accomplishment."
If one constantly holds this vajra, all *vināyakas* who create obstacles and difficulties will become terrified and flee in all directions.

By smearing the vajra with red sandalwood incense paste and placing it before the deity, one should employ the aforementioned mantra to consecrate flowers and incense as offerings for all ritual activities; through the subtle secrets of the Vajra, all other matters whatsoever can be accomplished.

"When performing any ritual activity, one must always wear the rosary cord on the right hand; anoint it with incense and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, or one thousand and eighty times."
The mantra of Vajravidāraṇa’s jewel-noose is as follows; the homage is the same as before:

“Oṃ kili kili glāni svāhā. This Great Seal of the Vidyārāja is named Mañjuśrī; it can accomplish all vidyārāja mantras, can augment and fulfill the syllables and phrases of mantras, and can also accomplish various other ritual matters and the protection of the body.
She is not merely the mother of the various vidyārājas, but also the mother of all vajras.

"If it is a rosary string for the Vajra Family, one should place a single *mūlanara-akṣa* bead within the thread and then tie it as a knot; since this is the case for the Vajra Family, the other two may be understood accordingly."
For a rosary of the Buddha Family, one should employ the mantra of the Buddha-mother;
for a rosary of the Lotus Family, one should employ the mantra of Pañcarakṣā, known as the mantra of the Mother of Avalokiteśvara.
The mantra of the Mother of Buddhas (*Buddhamātṛ*) is:
“Namo bhagavatyai uṣṇīṣāya | oṃ | ru | ru se | pru | jvala | tiṣṭha | siddha | locani | sarvārtha-sādhani | svāhā. The mantra of the Mother Avalokiteśvara is:

“Namo tārāya | Oṃ | Kaci | Mikaci | Kaṭe | Kaṭe | Vāgvati | Miraje | Svāhā. One who wears or carries this mantra-rosary will not be obstructed by the Vināyakas; their body shall attain purity, and they shall swiftly fulfill all their desired aspirations.

"When performing the ritual procedure, one should fashion a ring from *kuśa* grass and place it upon the ring finger of the right hand. One should recite the three-and-a-half-syllable heart mantra of the relevant family one hundred and eight times or one thousand and eight times, and then place [the ring] upon the finger."
The Heart Mantra of the Buddha Family is:
“Oṃ jina-jik. The Heart Mantra of the Avalokiteśvara Family is:
“Oṃ āḥ ruḥ. The Heart Mantra of the Vajra Family is:

"Oṃ [as before] Vajratīkṣṇa. When performing offerings, when reciting mantras, or when performing homa, one should wear a ring of grass. By wearing this ring, karmic obstructions are eliminated, the hands become purified, and all actions become auspicious.

Furthermore, take white cotton thread and hemp fibers, have a young girl dye them red or the color of *uragasāra* gold, and join them together to form a cord. Recite the mantra for each knot; once seven knots are completed, place them before the deity and recite the mantra over the cord one thousand and eight times.

"When reciting mantras, performing homa, attending to bodily needs, or at dawn and dusk, one should always wear it tied around the waist; even while sleeping, one must ensure that the semen is not lost by constantly wearing it."
The mantra for the *sūcaka* is:

"Oṃ kara kara pāṭani śikharadharani siddha svasti svāhā. Whether during recitation, during *homā*, when combing the hair, when putting on clothes, when draping the shoulder, when lying down, when performing ritual purification (*śauca*), or when bathing—whenever one puts on or takes off clean upper garments, one should consecrate them all with this mantra.
"If one is about to relieve oneself, one should wear wooden clogs;

however, when approaching the presence of the Honored One, or before the Upādhyāya, the Ācārya, or various venerable elders, one must not wear them. In the presence of these honored ones, one should make offerings through body, speech, and mind."
"If you wish for siddhi to be swiftly attained, you should always pay homage and respect whenever you see a caitya or the community of bhikṣus;
if you encounter an image of an external deity, you should merely join your palms or recite a gāthā;
and if you see a venerable person, you should likewise offer salutation."
If you hear the sublime Dharma, give rise to deep reverence and faith;
if you hear of the inconceivable marks of a Bodhisattva or the various feats accomplished through mantras, you should all rejoice with hearts full of exultation;
if you desire accomplishment, you should always advance with vigor and never give way to indolence.
One must constantly maintain mindfulness regarding these established regulations; if one does not do so, one violates the prohibitive precepts, incurs grave offenses, and achieves nothing.

With the body and all other faculties perpetually in meditative concentration, one should not be greedily attached to worldly desires, but should always diligently practice in accordance with these disciplinary regulations without neglect or forgetfulness.
If one mistakenly commits various transgressions during the early morning, one must repent by evening;
if one mistakenly commits various karmic acts at night, one must sincerely repent when morning arrives.

One must always remain pure and perform recitations, homa offerings, and other such rites according to the Dharma; one should constantly abide by the fundamental precepts and direct the mind in this manner to pass the days. Within the precepts of the Vidyārāja, one must always maintain focused attention, so that before long one attains the stage of the *siddhi* level.
7. Chapter on Offering Flowers: Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Seven, "Offering Flowers. "Furthermore, the three categories of rites shall be explained in detail.
These three categories consist of the śāntika rite, the pauṣṭika rite, and the ābhicāruka rite, along with all other rites."
"Each of the three families has three grades of mantras, namely:
those spoken by noble beings, those spoken by devas, and those spoken by terrestrial devas.
These constitute the three families."
"Those spoken by the noble ones refers to the speech of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas; these are the mantras of the noble ones.
Those spoken by the devas refers to:"
That which is spoken by the devas from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven down to the Trayastriṃśa Heaven is the mantra of the celestial devas;
that which is spoken by those dwelling on earth—
namely, by yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, nāgas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhūtas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth— is the mantra of the terrestrial devas.
"If one performs the śāntika rite, one should employ the mantras of the Noble Ones;
if one performs the pauṣṭika rite, one should employ the mantras of the devas;
if one performs the ābhicāruka rite, one should employ the mantras of the earth-dwelling spirits (bhūmideva)."
"If one seeks the supreme accomplishment, one should employ the mantras of the Noble Ones;
if one seeks the middling accomplishment, one should employ the mantras of the devas;
if one seeks the inferior accomplishment, one should employ the mantras of the earth-dwelling spirits."

"In this way, each of the three families has three grades of accomplishment; when performing the three types of rites, one should equally employ various colored flowers produced on both land and water, distinguishing them well according to their names and forms based on their respective families."
One should offer the mantra-flower while making this aspiration:
"This flower is pure, and its place of origin is likewise pure; I now offer it, praying that you will graciously accept it."
"Success shall be granted.
The mantra for offering flowers is:
"Aḥ karā aḥ karā sarvabuddhaye dhara pūrti svāhā. Using this mantra, one consecrates the flowers and makes offerings to the three families.
If making an offering to the Buddha, one should use white flowers with fragrant scents;
if making an offering to Avalokiteśvara, one should use white flowers grown in water;
if making an offering to Vajrapāṇi, one should use various kinds of fragrant flowers.
If one makes offerings to the terrestrial deities, one should offer various flowers gathered according to the season.
Those flowers that should be offered are:
the *mālatī* flower, the *pāṭala* flower, the lotus, and the *campaka* flower.
...the nāgapuṣpa flower, which resembles the mother-śatapatra flower; the vakula flower; the kumuda flower;
the sāla tree flower; the mallikā flower; the jātī flower;
the yūthikā flower; the śephālikā flower; the kuruṇṭaka flower; and the karṇikāra flower.
The *mālatī* flower, the *mutunini* flower, the *tṛṇa* flower,
the *vandanapuṣpa* flower, the *bhaṅga* flower, the *nāgamañjarī* flower,
the *arjuna* flower, the *jāmunu-kuñcana* flower, the *naṅkana* flower, and the *cūtamrakṣita* flower.
The *lihua* (flower of benefit), *mukula-campaka*,
*kadalī*, *kunda-nīla*, *pāṇi-ja*, *utpala*, *tagara*,
*kundana*, *kāramada*, and so forth.

Regarding the flowers grown in forests, hermitages, and both on land and water, such as those mentioned above, one must properly know the application of the three families, the three grades, and the three levels of flowers for offering.

For offerings to the Buddha Family, one should use *maṇḍārava* flowers, *dāḍima* flowers, *kundana* flowers, *mallikā* flowers, *yūthikā* flowers, and *nāgakesara* flowers; such flowers as these are for offering to the Buddha Family.

For offerings within the Avalokiteśvara Family, the *utpala* flower, *kumuda* flower, lotus flower, *sāla* tree flower, *śephālikā* flower, *bhandīra* flower, and *dāḍima* flower—such flowers as these are superior for offering to the Avalokiteśvara Family.
One should use blue lotuses, *pāṭala* flowers, leaves, flowering branches, and others not specifically mentioned, for general offerings within the Vajra Family.
As stated above regarding the flowers, those that are white are used for the *śāntika* rite;
those that are yellow are used for the *pauṣṭika* rite.
Those that are purple are for performing *abhicāruka* rites.
"Among these flowers, those with a sweet taste are for performing *śāntika* rites;
those with a pungent taste are for performing *abhicāruka* rites."
For those of a mild flavor, one performs the pauṣṭika rite.

One should employ various flowers according to their kind: branches and blossoms produced in pure locations, newly sprouted shoots, *kuśa* grass, small herbs, medium-sized tree flowers, or large tree flowers. Any such flowers may be used as appropriate.
"It is said that the *jāti-sumana* flower is to be offered exclusively to the Buddha;
the red lotus (*padma*) exclusively to Avalokiteśvara;
and the blue lotus (*utpala*) exclusively to Vajrapāṇi—each of these being designated as the most excellent."
"In the Buddha Family, use *jāti-sumanā* flowers for performing *śāntika* rites;
use red lotuses for performing *pauṣṭika* rites;
and use blue lotuses for performing *abhicāruka* rites. The other two families should be treated accordingly."
Superior, middling, and inferior colored fragrant flowers are to be used according to the specific requirements of the rite.
"Alternatively, one may use flower garlands or loose flowers; offering these to the Queen of Heaven (Devī) is said to be most excellent.
Purple and white *karamara* flowers, when offered to the Wrathful Lord (Krodheśvara) and his messengers, are said to be most excellent."

"Flowers such as the *kuṭaja*, *tilaka*, *bāla*, *kārṣmarya*, *asana-ruvuka*, *vilva*, and *kaṭphala*—whichever one of these is taken will universally serve for offerings to the three families (*trikula*), as well as for the three types of rites for averting calamities (*śāntika*) of superior, middling, and inferior grades. Furthermore, by combining various flowers to form garlands, or by offering clusters of various flowers, they universally serve for the nine types of rites."

"Among all flowers, only those that emit foul odors, those growing on thorny trees, and those with bitter or acrid flavors are unfit for offering; furthermore, any flowers not previously enumerated in detail should also not be used.
Moreover, flowers such as the *mālatī*, *ketakī*, *atimuktaka*, *mṛgaśṛṅgī*, and *campaka* should likewise not be employed."
"Regarding the ninefold long-term offerings:

saffron, *śamī* flowers, *prāyaṅgu* flowers, *kuru* grass, and so forth, as well as rice blossoms mixed with sesame seeds—these are offered; among all the various flowers and other items mentioned above, these are the most supreme."
If there are no such flowers available for offering, one may instead use white non-glutinous rice that has been selected and crushed until soft; this also applies to all nine types [of offerings].
One must not interchange the various flowers; however, if the prescribed flowers cannot be obtained when performing the ritual, any flowers that are available may also be used for offering.
"If one makes offerings of flowers, one should offer flowers while reciting the specific *mantra* of that particular family (*kula*).

If no flowers are available for offering, one should substitute with the leaves of the *surabhi*, or *maruva*, *tāḍa*, *tamāla*, *kṛṣṇamallikā*, *mandūka*, or *elā-arka*, as well as the leaves of *lāṅgalī* and other such plants."

"If these branches and leaves are unavailable, one should employ the roots of *vānaka*, spikenard (*uśīra*), clubmoss (*selaginella*), and *śatāvarī*, as well as the roots and fragrant fruits of various medicinal herbs that are likewise suitable for offering.
These include: cloves, nutmeg, mace, and *kakkola*; such fragrant fruits may all be used interchangeably with flowers for the purpose of making offerings."

"If one does not have flowers, leaves, roots, or fruits as described above for offering, then having previously seen or heard of offerings of flowers, or having personally offered flowers oneself, it is most excellent to perform the visualization and mental transport of the offering according to what is appropriate."

"Regarding the offering to the Honored Dharma, although there may be offerings of flowers, fruits, and so forth as previously described, if one can with a sincere and reverent mind join the palms and offer flowers and fruits to the Honored One upon the crown of the head, such an offering of mind and intention is supreme and beyond compare. One should always perform such offerings; if one does not harbor doubts, one will attain accomplishment."

8. Chapter Eight: The Substances for Unguents and Medicines from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the methods for the substances of unguents and medicines belonging to the three families (*trikula*). By means of these, one who makes offerings according to the respective mantras will be able to accomplish all manner of merit."
The names of those fragrant medicinal substances are:
nut grass (*kattṛṇa*), *kuṭha*, *agaru* (sandalwood), *vālaka*, *uśīra*, *sariva*, boiled incense,
aloeswood (*aguru*), saffron, white sandalwood, and purple [sandalwood].
Sandalwood (*candana*), *varaṇa* (the two together), *phalgu*,
*prāgvaṃśa-mālā-dhāraṇī-śarala* (five-needle pine), *sappileka-patramga-khaḍga* (juniper wood),
and *dāru-parṇika-kāleya-khaḍga* or *culirira* (lifu).
*śukti*, *karpūra*, *bālaka*, *aguru*, *pāṭalā*, *kṣīravidārī*, *punnāga*, *candana*,
*kapittha*, *jātīphala*, *phalinī*, *hariṇī*, *śivāṅgī*.
Svālinī-śakalā, mandūka, leather, tālīśa-pattra,
tagara, nāgaramothā, maruva, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, nalada, elā, and miyaka.
Jvalanākṣeśvara-vārivāsibhiḥ, dāhūṇi-yañjetapūṣpa-hiṅgu-svati-cūrṇaka-kodrava-gulma-jarad-dhūpa-kodrava-parajvara-khaḍga.
Furthermore, there are *paṃpanna*, *lambā*, *saṃkucitā*, *yamadevī*, *maṅgalyā*, *caṇḍā*, *dūru*,
*sahakāra*, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *prasānta*, *sāvakī*, *sallan*, and so forth.
As for resinous liquids, namely:
nāgakesara, yattūraśa, saccharasa, guggulu, kunduruka, śallakī, śvāsaka, and others that are fragrant resins from trees, these should all be properly blended according to their respective families.
"Using three substances—various grasses, fragrant roots and juices, and fragrant flowers—one blends them to form an ointment for offering to the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*).

Furthermore, using the bark of various fragrant trees, white sandalwood, aloeswood (*agaru*), celestial wood (*devadāru*), incense from boiling resin (*kṣipta-gandha*), and similar types, along with fragrant fruits, one blends them as previously distinguished to form an ointment for use by the Lotus Family (*padmakula*).
Moreover, using various fragrant herbs, roots, flowers, fruits, and leaves, one blends them to form an ointment for use by the Vajra Family (*vajrakula*)."
There may be ointment perfumes composed of various root fruits, or those blended by predecessors with superior fragrances, which also pertain to the three families.
Alternatively, one may use only aloeswood incense mixed with a small amount of camphor as an ointment for offerings to the Buddha Family;
or use only white sandalwood incense mixed with a small amount of camphor as an ointment for the Lotus Family.
Alternatively, one may use only saffron mixed with a small amount of *nāgakesara* as an unguent for use in the Vajra Family;
furthermore, red sandalwood may be used as an unguent, which is applicable to all [families], including the Vajra and others.
"Use *jātīphala*, *kakkola*, *sumana*, or *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *sarpis*, and *elāpattra* as unguents to offer to all female messenger deities (*dūtī-devatā*).
Furthermore, use *tagara*, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, and whole *jātīphala* as unguents to offer to the queens of the Vidyārājas.
Additionally, use white sandalwood (*candana*), *agaru*, and *kuṅkuma* as unguents to offer to the Vidyārājas."
Furthermore, one may use the bark of various fragrant trees as unguent to offer to the messengers;
or use whatever fragrance is available as unguent to offer to the earth-dwelling devas;
or use agarwood alone as unguent, which may be employed in all instances for the three families, the nine types of ritual methods, and for the queens of the vidyā-rājas.
"If one performs a *śāntika* rite, use white incense;
if a *pauṣṭika* rite, use yellow incense;
if an *ābhicāruka* rite, use purple incense that is odorless."
"If one wishes to achieve the great siddhi, one should use the aforementioned liquid incense along with fragrant fruits;
if one wishes to achieve the middling siddhi, one should use hard-wood incense and fragrant flowers;
if one wishes to achieve the lesser siddhi, one should use roots, bark, incense, flowers, and fruits to prepare an ointment for offering."
"One should not use blended fragrant substances on the body of a sentient being;

that is to say, substances such as *nakha* (claw-fragrance), musk, *urasāra* (purple sandalwood), and the like, as well as wine or vinegar, or those that are used in excess, or those not beloved by the world—all these should not be used for making offerings."
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of incense, namely:
unguent incense, powdered incense, pellet incense, and pill incense; one should use any one of these to draw the mandala as flowers and offer them daily."
When about to offer it, one should make this vow:
"This incense is as fragrant as the wondrous incense of the heavens; it is pure and provides protection. I now offer it to you; please graciously accept it and cause my aspirations to be fulfilled."
The mantra for the scented ointment (*vilepana*) is:

"Aṅgāra aṅgāra sarvabhūtebhyo bhuṭṭe svāhā. Having recited this mantra over the scented ointment, one should subsequently recite the mantra of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭamantra*) to purify it according to the ritual rules and offer it to the Honored One.

If one seeks various perfumes but cannot obtain them, one should take any available unguent and recite the mantra over it; furthermore, having consecrated the incense with the specific family’s unguent mantra, one should offer it to the deity.
Chapter Nine: The Classification of Incense Burning Rituals in the Susiddhikara Sūtra Furthermore, I shall now explain the incense-burning rituals for the three families.
That is to say:
aloeswood, white sandalwood, saffron, and so forth, which are taken for offering according to their respective order; or, the three types of incense may be blended and used for all three families;
or, a single type of incense may be taken and used according to whichever family it corresponds to.
The names of the incenses are as follows:

śrīveṣṭaka resin, sarjarasa, gandhasāra, guggulu, sallakī, nālika, kunduruka, turuṣka, karpūra, jātīphala, harītakī, granthiparṇa, kuṅkuma, saugandhika, agaru, vālaka, candana, tamālapattra, devadāru, nārikela, pāribhadraka, uśīra, śarkarā, vacā, and various fragrant fruits.

"If one wishes to accomplish the mantra rites of the three families, one should blend incense: the resin of the *śrīveṣṭaka* tree is suitable for all three families and may be offered universally to all deities;
*guggulu* (安息香) is suitable for offerings to yakṣas;
and *kunduruka* (薰陸香) is suitable for offerings to all devas and devīs."
Sāgarasāra incense is offered to the earth-dwelling devas;
śalākī incense is offered to the female messengers;
and gandharvasa incense is offered to the male messengers.

"Nāga-mada incense, gandharvasa incense, sācalasa incense, kun-luk (olibanum) incense, guggulu incense, sarjikā incense, and śrīveṣṭaka incense—these seven resinous incenses, when blended together and burned, are effective for all nine types [of rites]."
It is said that among these seven types of incense, resin incense is the most superior, heartwood incense is middling, and the remaining flowers, leaves, roots, and so forth are inferior.
Incense made by blending storax, aloeswood, saffron, and the like is the first;
adding white sandalwood and granulated sugar makes it the second type of incense.
Furthermore, add guggulu and frankincense as the third incense.
These three blended incenses may be used individually for any purpose and will apply universally to all matters.
Moreover, for the terrestrial devas and those who provide protection, one should use *sajjara*, sugar, and *harītakī*, blending them to form an incense for making offerings to them.
"Furthermore, there are five fragrances, namely:
granulated sugar, śrīveṣṭaka, sarjarasa, harītakī, and rock honey; when blended together, they form a fragrance that may be employed for all matters pertaining to the three families."

Alternatively, there may be a single incense that universally applies to all matters, such as a superior incense esteemed by all people or an exquisite blended incense; if such a fragrance does not exist, one may use whatever is available, which likewise applies to the three families, while all other ritual applications are as previously described.
The method for compounding incense must be skillfully distinguished according to its intended use; when blending roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits, they should be offered at the appropriate time.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of incense that one must know:

namely, natural incense (*svabhāva-gandha*), stick incense (*varti-gandha*), powdered incense (*cūrṇa-gandha*), and pill incense (*guḍika-gandha*); one must also know the specific applications for each.
"If for the śāntika rite, use incense made of powder;
if for the ābhicāruka rite, use powdered incense;
if for the pauṣṭika rite, use incense made into pills."

"To encompass all applications, one should combine the incense of self-nature with counting-sticks and pills; place it with granulated sugar and blended powdered incense, or resin incense. For pill incense, one should use fine honey for the blending;
alternatively, one may substitute ghee or milk for the honey when blending the incense."
One should place a small amount of clarified butter upon the natural incense, using the specific incense prescribed for burning in the relevant section.

"If such [specific] incense cannot be obtained, one may use whatever incense is available that first conforms to the relevant section; first recite the incense mantra of that section to consecrate the incense, and then recite the mantra one maintains while performing the method for blending the incense."

One should not place incense such as *nakha*, musk, or *candana*; nor should one employ blended incenses such as *manjika* and the like; furthermore, one must not exceed the proper measure so as to produce an unpleasant odor rather than a fragrant one.

"By means of the fragrances of these forest trees and resins, one can transform the intentions of all people; may the gods, who are my constant sustenance, now accept this offering out of compassion."
The mantra for burning incense is:

“ĀGARA ĀGARA SARVA BHŪTAYADHARA PURATI SVĀHĀ. After reciting this mantra over the incense, one should recite the specific mantra of the deity being worshipped while burning the incense, offering it according to the ritual rules.
Chapter Ten: The Ritual for Lighting Lamps from the Susiddhikara Sūtra Furthermore, the ritual for lighting lamps in three categories shall now be explained.

By relying on the Dharma, one brings joy and accomplishment to all the celestial beings and rishis; one may fashion lamp bowls from gold, silver, or refined red copper, or even from porcelain or earthenware.
Among these five types, whichever one is selected and employed according to the ritual will bring joy to the deity.

Regarding the method for making the lamp wick: it may be made from white cotton flowers, or from new cotton cloth, or from the fibers of the *nāgakeśara* tree bark, or from clean new cloth; one should use various fragrant oils favored by the assembly, or fragrant clarified butter (*sarpis*) and oil.
"For the *śāntika* rite, use superior fragrant oil;
for the *pauṣṭika* rite, use intermediate fragrant oil;
for the *abhicāruka* rite, use inferior fragrant oil."
"If fragrant wood oils are used for *śāntika*;
if sesame oils are used for *pauṣṭika*;
if white mustard seed oils are used for *abhicāruka*."
The *āmrātaka* fruit oil is used by the Queen of Mantras and by the various female seers (*ṛṣikā*);
the fruit oils of various trees are used by the Lords of Mantras;
and the fruit oils of bitter trees are used by the gods and by Mahākāla.
If fish fat is used, it is for making offerings to the *bhūtas*;
if the fat of various domestic animals is used, it is for making offerings to the *yakṣas*;
if *bhallātaka* oil or sesame oil is used, it is for making offerings to the lower classes of gods, as well as for the four sisters, the *Cāmuṇḍās*, and so forth.
If a vetāla arises in a cremation ground, use the fat of a whole dog.
Among all oils, buffalo ghee is superior and is suitable for all three classes of rites.
Furthermore, white cow ghee is used for śāntika rites;
Yellow ox ghee is used for *sādhana*;
black ox ghee is used for *abhicāruka*.
If there are specific [ghees] belonging to particular families, one should distinguish them and use them accordingly.
"Oil produced from flower stamens is used for pauṣṭika;
oil produced from fragrant substances is used for śāntika;
and oil with a foul odor is used for ābhicāruka."
As briefly explained above, one should skillfully observe the rules for lighting lamps; even if these have not been mentioned here, they should be applied with careful scrutiny.
Although there may be lamp oil that does not belong to a specific *kalpa*, it is also permissible to offer it after consecrating it with the mantra of one's own *mūla-kalpa*.
“The lamp can dispel obstructions and burn away impurities; I now offer it, may you graciously accept it out of compassion.
The mantra for the lamp is:
“Oṃ āloka āloka sarvabuddhayādya pūjite svāhā. Having recited this mantra, one should then recite the root dhāraṇī and consecrate [the offering] with it.
Furthermore, because the rite of purification (*śodhana*) removes all faults, one should practice it according to the instructions given in the preceding chapter.

**Chapter Eleven: The Chapter on the Offering of Food** *Susiddhikara Tantra* "Next, I shall explain the method for offering food, so that all celestial beings (*devas*) may be fully delighted and [the practitioner] may swiftly attain accomplishment (*siddhi*)."
"To summarize the offering of food:
one should use round and long roots, various fruits,
cakes made with ghee, and cakes made with oil."
Various soups and broths;
or various kinds of gruels and other foods and drinks—
these four types of food may be offered universally to all the families.
The *māravaḍra* fruit is common to all three families; furthermore, the pomegranate and *juna* fruits are also common to all three families.
To indicate their respective order, each is assigned to one specific family.
"If the taste is sweet, it is used for śāntika;
if the taste is sweet and sour, it is used for pauṣṭika;
if the taste is pungent or bland, it is used for ābhicāruka."
"If there are *tāla* fruits, *jambū* fruits, *bilva* fruits, *nīpāra* fruits, or other foul-smelling fruits that are not pleasing to the assembly, one should not offer them."
"Or there may be fruits of superior flavor, which are abundant in the world and most precious; by offering such fruits, one attains the supreme accomplishment (*uttama-siddhi*).

Or there may be various fruits whose flavor is of secondary excellence, which are easy to find in the world and not prized for their cost; by offering such fruits, one attains the middling accomplishment (*madhyama-siddhi*).

Or there may be various fruits whose flavor is bitter, pungent, bland, or the like, which are plentiful in the world and of the lowest price; by offering such fruits, one attains the inferior accomplishment (*adhama-siddhi*)."
"If one wishes to make an offering according to one's desire, one should take female-named fruits.
That is to say:
persimmons, apricots, peaches, and other such fruits should be offered to the goddesses."
Fruits produced by trees that lack a bitter taste are offered to the Mantra Consorts and Queens;
*śrīphala* fruits may be offered to all the wrathful deities (*krodha*) of the three families;
and *vaṇa* fruits are offered exclusively to all the yakṣas.
One offers the *kapittha* fruit to Śrīdevī;
one offers the fruit produced by the *pāyasa* tree to Pārṣadagaṇeśvara.
"There are many other such fruits, each with its own distinct name; according to what one observes, one should use them for offering based on their flavor."
Whether by the side of a village or in a pure place such as an araṇya, if there are roots of plants whose taste is sweet and delicious, taking them to offer will also bring accomplishment.

The root of the vinālikā is suitable for all uses; furthermore, there are other roots of plants with extraordinary flavor, whose stalks, branches, and leaves may also be offered—not only for the celestial deities, but also for use among human beings.
"Those roots that grow in the mountains and possess a delicious flavor are for offering to the Buddha Family; furthermore, cooked yam roots are also suitable for the Buddha Family.
Moreover, the roots of *kācilindika*, *vinālikā*, *vāyasī*, *kukkuṭī*, and other round roots that grow in water are used for the Lotus Family.
Furthermore, all medicinal round roots that are bitter, pungent, or bland, as well as various kinds of wild yams, are used for the Vajra Family."
“Furthermore, those with round roots that are white in color, with fragrant scent and extremely sweet taste, are for offering to the Buddha Family;
those with round roots that are yellow in color, with fragrant scent and a taste that is neither too sour nor too sweet, are for use in the Lotus Family;
and those with round roots that are red in color, with a bitter, pungent, or faint scent, and a taste that is not sweet, are for use in the Vajra Family.”
Thus, the *śāntika* rites and other methods of these three families, as well as their superior, middling, and inferior grades, are all universally applicable.

To speak briefly: one should properly accord with each family according to its superior, middling, or inferior grade and offer [the substances] accordingly; by making such distinctions, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
The explanation of these round roots, long roots, their growth, and their ritual application is as follows:
one should not use onions, garlic, leeks, or cakes with an extremely foul, pungent, or bitter flavor for making offerings.
“Śaṣṭika rice, urubīka rice, puppa cakes, vānaka cakes, and other flour-based foods; or various sesame balls;
or various white sugar sweets, modakas, mātuluṅga fruits, piṇyāka cakes, bhaṇiṇaguśika cakes, and aśukāvatsya cakes.”
These are: finger-food (śalākā-bhakṣa), cake-food (piṇḍaka-bhakṣa),
food exceeding the *raśceṭaka* [time], *śākulīya*-food, *papphaṭa*-food, *pūraṇa*-food,
*maṃsa-pūpa*-food, *vinodaka*-food, *puṣpavarta*-food, *rāvaṇika*-food, and *arkapuṣpa*.
Īrṣyāka food, Kujñika food, Rāmaṅga food, Khaṃsa food, Saktika food, Pṛthakcillika food, Śrīphalaka food,
Vaiśvika food, Cchinnaka food, Ṭanaraka food, and Yonabhu food.
Lākā food, Citra-puṣpa food, Karkara food,
Gūṇa-paṭṭa-śilinda-kakā food, Khāda food, various karpāsa-bīja-puṣpa food,
Rāja-hasa food, Śaraka food, and Kṛta-pūraka food.
Food, *kāmuka* food, *kusārika* food, *tripuṭa* food, *śaṇava* food,
*harīnaka* food, *śikhaṇḍaka* food, *mīna* food,
various *praṇīta-riṣṭaka* foods, *dibika* food, and *jalahasiti* food.
The food of Niyama, the food of Kakarabhinna, the food of Varagata,
the food of Vattimka, the food of Kṣiptika, the food of Gajakarṇika, and so forth.
Regarding the aforementioned foods, they may be prepared with granulated sugar or clarified butter;

or they may be made from sesame oil. Using them according to the specific ritual manual of their respective family (*kula*) and offering them in accordance with the dharma, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
"Rice flour foods belong to the Buddha Family; they are used for śāntika rites and superior accomplishments.
All wheat-flour foods belong to the Lotus Family; they are used for pauṣṭika rites and middling accomplishments.
Sesame and bean foods belong to the Vajra Family; they are used for ābhicāruka rites and inferior accomplishments, and so forth."
"Among all varieties of food and flavors, those adorned with white sugar should always be offered within the Buddha Family;
if it is śrīveṣṭaka food, it is for the Lotus Family;
if it is modaka sweets, they are for the Vajra Family."
If for the yakṣa named Pūpaka, use the mantra;
if for the queen named Strībhakṣā, use the subsequent mantra.
As for "the one named Strībhakṣā":
The food of Kṣemamālī and the food of Pātrapūraka—among all these foods, those that are the most excellent in flavor should be used for offering when seeking supreme accomplishment;
those of secondary flavor are used by the other two families. Since these are not fully detailed here, one may use whatever food is available for the eight classes of beings and others as required.
"At the time of offering food, first spread out cloths, fruit leaves, and so forth to adorn the site.
First place the *sāṣṭika* food, the *ulūpika* food, and the *pūpa* food; in this manner, first perform the common rites for the three families."

Furthermore, one should offer whatever food and drink are required by the specific division according to one's capacity. One must offer, in accordance with the ritual rules, cooked rice of non-glutinous rice, rice that ripens in sixty days, rice with barley milk, rice of non-glutinous rice that grows spontaneously without being sown, and millet rice;
as well as various fragrant and exquisitely delicious soups and stews, along with various bean-based broths.
"One seeks the supreme accomplishment through milk-boiled barley rice and uncultivated, self-grown non-glutinous rice;
one seeks the middling accomplishment through non-glutinous rice and its cooked rice, as well as sixty-day ripened non-glutinous rice;
and one seeks the inferior accomplishment through millet and its cooked rice."
"The śāntika rite is the supreme accomplishment;
the pauṣṭika rite is the middling accomplishment;
and the ābhicāruka rite is the inferior accomplishment."
Offerings of cooked rice, roots, fruits, and rice-gruel should be presented according to the categories of superior, middling, and inferior:
"The *śāntika* rite belongs to the Buddha Family as the superior;
the *pauṣṭika* rite belongs to the Lotus Family as the middling."
