The *ābhicāruka* rites belong to the lower Vajra Family.
Regarding the supreme, middling, and inferior *siddhis*, one must properly understand their application according to the specific category in accordance with the ritual rules.
"Among soups and broths, those that are sweet in flavor are for use in *śāntika* rites;..."
Those with a sour or sweet taste are for pauṣṭika rites;
those with a bitter, pungent, or bland taste are for abhicāruka rites.
Milk porridge is for śāntika rites.
Pomegranate porridge, curd porridge, and the like are used for pauṣṭika rites;
kṛsara porridge— meaning porridge made with old sesame,
non-glutinous rice, beans, and so forth— is used for ābhicāruka rites.

"As previously explained regarding the various flavors of food and so forth, which may differ according to region, one should present them while contemplating their superior, middling, or inferior qualities;
or one should offer those flavors praised by the multitude or those that one personally loves;
or one should follow the sequence for offering food as taught in the mantras of one's own specific family (*kula*), for if it differs from that, accomplishment will not be attained."
Regarding food, those that are visually striking and those with foul odors are for use in the Vajra Family.

As previously stated, ointments, lamps, food offerings, and so forth each follow their respective families; one should rely on the specific chapter for rites such as *śāntika* (pacification) and others, observing whether the nature of the mantra is joyful or wrathful.
Next, one should further contemplate: "What purpose does this accomplish?
Furthermore, by investigating minutely, what aspirations does it fulfill?
Having observed and understood this, one should offer the previously presented food according to one's capacity.

"In the ritual of offering, if one sees the use of *kāmika* food, one should offer *sāṣṭika* rice, *ūrubilaka* rice, and other foods prepared according to one's means, such as molasses, curd, cooked rice, roots, fruits, and milk porridge."
This *kṛmika* food may be offered universally to all [deities], with the sole exception of those for whom *abhicāruka* rites are performed.
Regarding the ritual procedures for making offerings, if one observes the use of *ciñcā-udumbara* food, this refers to adding two or three kinds of superior, exotic foods to the *kṛmika* food.
"If one observes that *kṛsara* (rice and sesame) is used among the offerings, it means that one should place double the amount of the previously mentioned *kāñjika* (sour gruel) food.
If one observes that the 'three white foods' (*trimaṇḍala*) are used among the offerings, they should consist of milk, curd, and ghee with rice;
furthermore, if the 'three sweet foods' are observed, they consist of ghee, honey, and milk with rice."

"If among the offerings there are *sarvabhojya* (all kinds of food), *sāyaliya*, *laṅgaliya*, *pūpalikā*, *tilapiṣṭaka*, rice with curd, roots, or fruits—taking any one or two flavors from among the aforementioned foods, place them upon rice-fragrance, various flowers, and leaves; put these into a large vessel filled with water and discard it at a distance from the place of recitation."

"If, within the ritual of offering, one sees the *śāntika* food, one should employ *svastika*, milk porridge, rice blossoms, ghee, honey, milk, and barley rice boiled with milk, as well as *ciñcāphala* and other such foods; it will certainly eliminate calamities, so have no doubt."

"If, within the ritual of offering, one sees that *puṣṭika* food is required, one should employ curd-rice, curd-gruel, *modaka* (joy-balls), *ulūpikā*, granulated sugar, *śrīveṣṭaka*, and so forth; these will certainly fulfill one's wishes—of this there is no doubt."
"If, within the ritual of offering, one sees that there is food for the *abhicāruka* [subjugation rite], one should use red non-glutinous rice, or *kunduruka* seeds;
or rice colored red;
or sesame cakes, *sapphaka*, *pūpalī*, *yavāgū*, *kṣāra*, and so forth. These will certainly subdue the māras; have no doubt."

"If one holds the mantras of yakṣas but lacks the ritual for offering food, one should present offerings according to this method: namely, red non-glutinous rice, roots and fruits, honey-water, honey-sugar, rice-flour cakes, and the like;
for those who hold the mantras of female deities and others, one should offer soup and rice, bean stews, various sweet syrups and water, *prāṇa*, *pṛṣṭhaka*, *śāka* (vegetables), and various fruits."
All goddesses should be offered this food.

Those who seek the supreme accomplishment through the offering rites of their own specific family (*kula*) should offer various foods, roots, fruits, incense, and so forth—those that are commonly spoken of by all as being delicious, abundant, and precious. Seeking the supreme accomplishment, one should thus present such superior flavors as offerings.

As briefly explained above, the various methods for offering food each follow their respective families; the ritual procedures for whatever matters one seeks have all been concisely set forth. Should the flavors of food differ in other regions, one should observe their colors and tastes and offer them accordingly to their kind.

"When about to present the food, first purify and smear the ground, sprinkle it everywhere with scented water, and thoroughly wash all the leaves. Afterwards, spread upon it lotus leaves, *pāṭala* leaves, leaves from trees that produce milky sap, or new cotton cloth and the like; thereafter, place the various delicacies upon these leaves for use."
"For *śāntika*, one should use the leaves of aquatic plants and other extraordinary trees, such as the plantain (*kadalī*) and so forth;
for *pauṣṭika*, one should use the leaves of the *balādarka* tree, the *argha* tree, or whatever is available at the time;
and for *abhicāruka*, one should use the leaves of female trees, namely:"
For instance, one may use leaves from a young plantain tree, lotus leaves, or leaves from the *kṣīravṛkṣa* (milk-tree) family;
furthermore, for the mantras of female ṛṣis (*ṛṣikā*), one uses *parṇaka* leaves from a dry tree;
and for the terrestrial deities (*bhūcaradevatā*) and others, one employs blades of grass.

"One who seeks the superior, middling, and inferior dharmas must thoroughly understand and practice this: first, smear and sprinkle the ground, then spread out the leaves; next, one should wash the hands, rinse the mouth, and swallow water, after which one must partake of the food."
First, offer the *sāstika* grain;
next, offer round and long-rooted fruits;
and next, offer various gruels.
Next, serve the soup;
next, serve the rice;
next, serve the milk curds, each being served according to its respective ritual procedure.

If one constructs a maṇḍala or intends to accomplish various rites and attains the various meditative states, one should increase twofold the offerings of pure food, drink, flowers, fruits, and the like.
"When first performing the recitation, one should offer whatever has been prepared and whatever flavor has been obtained, according to that specific root ritual.
Furthermore, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, as well as during solar and lunar eclipses or earthquakes, one should perform extensive offerings."

Regarding the items required for the homa ritual, one should first prepare them and place them before the principal deity. Whenever the practitioner wishes to eat, they should first set aside a portion of food and likewise place it before the deity. If one intends to eat after performing the homa, one should prepare the food in advance and set it out prior to making the offerings.

Once the prepared food has been set out, one should then begin the recitation. One should offer various flowers, medicinal herbs, and food and drink; one must constantly maintain this mindfulness without neglect or forgetfulness, remaining in accordance with the original ritual method.
"If one says that recitation is performed at one time, then offerings of various roots and fruits should be made at that same time;
if one says it is performed at two times, then offerings should be made at those two times;
if one says it is performed at three times, then offerings should be made at those three times. By following the ritual in this manner, one shall quickly achieve accomplishment."

"If a practitioner who recites [mantras] fails to offer food and drink, thereby violating the rules of their own *kula*, that person will be beset by demonic obstacles; their body will lack luster, they will suffer from wind-disorders, dryness, hunger, and thirst, and they will constantly harbor evil thoughts. They will be unable to achieve accomplishment in the mantra of their chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), all because they fail to offer fruit and food to the deity."
One should perform extensive offerings on the aforementioned dates, such as those in the first and second months, and present them to the principal deity along with their retinue.
When first beginning the recitation, one should prepare *śāntika* food on those same dates and discard it in the four directions at a distance from the place of recitation.

In this regard, it is not mentioned; or, even if the specific section does not prohibit it, one should not employ those things that seek higher accomplishment through inferior flavors, nor those types of prepared food that are foul-smelling or offensive.

One should constantly offer milk-rice; among the various classes [of mantras], those seeking the superior, middling, or inferior *śāntika* rites, as well as those who practice the general mantras of the devas, should perform worship in this manner.
If there is no food as originally prescribed, one should consecrate whatever has been obtained with the mantra of its respective family, saying:
"This medicinal offering is fragrant and delicious; it is worthy of being presented to the Honored Lord!"
"I now offer this; please accept it out of compassion.
The mantra for preparing the food is as follows:

"Āgara āgara, sarvabhūtidhāra, pūrṇi, svāhā. This mantra is universally applicable to all three families (*trikula*). After reciting this mantra over the food, one should then recite the specific mantra of the deity being worshipped and offer the food.

*Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Scroll One. On the ninth day of the second month in the twenty-fifth year of the Engi era, by Eijun of the Daibenzō-in. 12. Chapter on Distinguishing the Times for *Siddhi*. *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Twelve on Distinguishing the Times for *Siddhi*, Scroll Two:
"Furthermore, I shall now explain the auspicious times and seasons for accomplishment; once the practitioner has understood this, they may immediately..."
Regarding the pursuit of *siddhi*, as for the seasons: the eighth month, the twelfth month, the first month, the second month, and the fourth month.
During these five months, on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, one should perform the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasādhana*).
In the fourth month, there will inevitably be the difficulty of rain;
in the second month, there will inevitably be the difficulty of wind;
and in the first month, there will be various difficulties.
Only the month of Mārgaśīrṣa (the waxing moon) is free from all obstacles;
during the eighth month, there are the obstacles of thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts.
All such obstacles as described above are signs of accomplishment.
“During these five months, one should seek to perform the rites for supreme accomplishment (*uttamasādhana*), and one should also perform the *śāntika* rites;

furthermore, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight within these same five months, one should perform the rites for middling and inferior accomplishments (*madhyama- and kanyasasādhana*), as well as the *pauṣṭika* and *abhicāruka* rites.”
"One should accomplish the most supreme objects during a lunar eclipse;

during a solar eclipse, one may accomplish objects of the superior, middling, or inferior grades. Alternatively, on the first, third, fifth, seventh, or thirteenth day of the moon, one should perform the accomplishment of all matters."

"If one performs the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasādhana*), one should select the most excellent lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and planetary periods (*tithi*); it should be understood that for middling and inferior methods, the same principle applies accordingly.

Among all lunar mansions, the Ghost Mansion (*Ārdrā*) is the foremost; if performing a fierce accomplishment (*tīkṣṇasādhana*), one should likewise rely on fierce lunar mansions and planetary periods, or else act in accordance with the three types of ritual matters, and the accomplishment itself is performed based on those three matters;
or else, as explained in the specific root-text."
Alternatively, one may follow the instructions of the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā).
Between the first and fifteenth days of the twelve months, one should perform all accomplishments and rites;
or else, one may select the day indicated by the tutelary deity.
Alternatively, one may also achieve accomplishment on the thirteenth day of either the waxing or waning moon in any month.
July and August are the latter part of the rainy season; during this time, one should perform *śāntika* rites.
September and October are the beginning of winter; during this time, one should perform *pauṣṭika* rites.
The third and fourth months are the latter phase of spring; at this time, one should perform the *abhicāruka* rites.
The first and second months are the initial phase of spring; at this time, one may accomplish all matters.
The fifth and sixth months are the initial phase of the rainy season; those who wish to achieve success should perform the *kṣudrasiddhi* rites.

In this manner, during the seasons of spring, winter, and after the rains, one should likewise accomplish the three kinds of *siddhi*. Within these, the nine grades are distributed according to their respective categories.
"When accomplishing the lower grade during the first watch of the night;
when accomplishing the middle grade during the middle watch of the night;"
During the latter part of the night, at the time of supreme accomplishment:
"The first part of the night is the time for performing *śāntika* rites;
the middle part of the night is the time for performing *abhicāruka* rites."
During the latter part of the night, this is the time for performing the *puṣṭika* rite.

Regarding these three types of rites, they are distinguished into nine grades; one should understand their respective timings according to their corresponding categories, and discern the superior, middling, and inferior signs that appear during those specific periods.
"However, during solar or lunar eclipses, one should immediately perform the rite regardless of the specific time or duration.
For all rites of fierce accomplishment (*tīkṣṇa-sādhana*) and *abhicāruka* (sorcery), the times of solar and lunar eclipses are most highly conducive."

In all undertakings for accomplishment (*sādhana*), one should fast for three days, two days, or one day; it should be understood that these periods correspond to the superior, middling, and inferior grades of the rite.

Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on Perfect Accomplishment (*Pariniṣpanna-siddhi-paṭala*) from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the deficiencies in the auxiliary requirements for accomplishment according to the fundamental rites."

If you fear that your physical strength will not sustain you, do not practice total fasting. Once the required number of recitations has been completed and you wish to initiate the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*), you must further perform recitations and *homa* offerings. Present offerings of flowers and incense, offer various praises, and maintain the visualization of the *iṣṭadevatā*. Take a thread of white cotton and have a young girl join it together; perform the ritual as before, tie seven knots, and recite the mantra seven hundred times.
At dawn, by binding it around one’s waist, one will not lose semen during sleep.
The *kumāri* mantra of the Vajra Family (Buddha Family) cord:
*Oṃ jaye kumāri śukra hūṃ dhāri svāhā.* The *kuṇḍalī* mantra of the Lotus Family (Padma Family) cord:
“Oṃ lu-kṣaṃ kuru kuruṇi svāhā. This is the mantra of the Vajra Family. The mantra of Samantakī is: “Oṃ kulandhari bandha bandha huṃ phaṭ.
One should recite the verses of supplication during the beginning, middle, and end [of the ritual]. If the specific root practice lacks such verses of supplication, one should insert them;
however, these three mantras are to be used for their respective families.
One should daily bind and wear this recitation cord while performing rituals to manifest its spiritual power.
When constructing a maṇḍala, during the time of recitation, or on auspicious festival days, one must always bind and wear it to eliminate obstacles and hindrances.

Furthermore, take equal parts of eye-salve, *sruva*, *añjana*, *śarkarā-madhu*, camphor, *pippalī*, clove bark, *tagara* incense, and naturally occurring rock honey; grind and sift them into a powder. Mix this with the froth from a horse’s mouth and grind it finely, then recite this vidyā over it one hundred times.

At the time of accomplishment, one should wash the face repeatedly and apply medicinal ointment to the eyes to remove sloth and mental torpor; when obstacles arise, they will be forewarned by seeing them in dreams.
The Mantra for Closing the Eyes in the Buddha Family:
“Oṃ jvala locane svāhā. The Mantra for Closing the Eyes in the Lotus Family:
“Oṃ milocini svāhā. The Mantra for Closing the Eyes in the Vajra Family:

"Oṃ bandhura kaṇḍi svāhā. These three mantras of this family are used for eye medicine; alternatively, by reciting them over water alone and washing the face and eyes several times, one may also eliminate the hindrance of torpor and sleep.

"If, while performing the accomplishment, one becomes weary from recitation, one should mix white sandalwood incense with water, recite the Family Heart Mantra over it seven times, and drink three handfuls."

When one wishes to achieve accomplishment, one should first sprinkle water over the body and observe auspicious signs. When about to achieve accomplishment, the appearance of auspicious signs is as follows:
a conch shell, a wheel, a hook, a fish, a clockwise-turning seal, a white lotus banner, a *svastika* seal, a full vase, a *śrīvatsa* seal, a vajra, and a flower garland.
Or they see upright women adorned with necklaces;
or they see pregnant women or those carrying clothes and utensils;
or they see joyful young maidens.
Or they may see a pure-practicing Brahmin wearing new white garments;
or they may see vehicles, elephants, horses, medicinal roots, and fruits;
or they may see extraordinary occurrences.
Some hear the sound of thunder;
some hear the sound of Vedic recitation;
and some hear the sounds of various musical instruments, such as conchs and horns being blown.
Or they may hear the calls of peacocks, partridges, parrots, geese, cranes, and auspicious birds;
or they may hear the sounds of kind words that bring consolation and healing,
namely, words concerning their well-being, peace, and the fulfillment of their desires.
Some see auspicious clouds, lightning, gentle breezes, or fine rain;
some see flowers raining from the heavens;
or they encounter exquisite fragrances and behold soaring rainbows.
"Among these signs, that which descends from the sky is the supreme accomplishment;
that which appears in the air is the middling accomplishment;
and that which appears on the ground is the inferior accomplishment."
Regarding these three signs and nine grades of distinction, all that appears as described above is auspicious; those who perceive them otherwise will not achieve success.
Having seen these signs, one should give rise to profound joy, and with such a mind, subsequently perform the ritual methods for accomplishment through skillful means.
Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on Invoking for Accomplishment from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Next, the method for invoking for accomplishment shall be explained."
The aforementioned times, lunar mansions, and auspicious signs have been explained in detail within the rituals for constructing maṇḍalas and the methods for accomplishment.

If unfavorable signs appear, one should immediately perform homa with cow’s ghee using the Mother of the Family mantra one hundred and eight times; thereafter, when performing the rite, one will also attain the accomplishment of siddhi.
"The site of the maṇḍala previously distinguished should also be prepared for accomplishment according to those [instructions].
For superior accomplishment, one should perform it on a mountain;
for middling accomplishment, one should perform it by the side of a pond."
If one performs the accomplishment at a lower level, it may be done anywhere, or at a place corresponding to the mantra.
If one does not perform it according to these specific locations, the accomplishment will be somewhat delayed.
Within a *caitya* containing bone relics (*śarīra*), all mantras of the Inner Dharma (Vajrayāna) will attain accomplishment.

"Among the accomplishments of the eight great *caityas*, such as the Buddha’s birthplace and others, this is the most supreme; yet, at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there are no obstacles whatsoever that can hinder accomplishment. Even Māra does not create obstacles there, let alone other classes of beings."
Therefore, all mantras will certainly achieve accomplishment.
"Whatever fierce accomplishments there may be, they are performed in a cemetery;
or else in an empty room."
One should perform the accomplishment either in a temple dedicated to a single deity where no others reside,
or beneath a solitary tree in a remote place, or by the side of a river.
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of a female yakṣī, perform it in a forest;
if one wishes to accomplish the dharma of a nāga king, perform it by a spring;
if one wishes to accomplish the dharma of wealth and nobility, perform it upon the roof of a house."
If one wishes to accomplish the rite for summoning messengers, one should perform it at a place where people gather;
if one wishes to accomplish the rite for entering various caverns, one should perform it within a cave.
This is the place for the secret classification of accomplishment.

Having determined the site through discernment, one should first abstain from food; the ground should be purified according to the ritual for purifying the maṇḍala site, or according to the ritual for the recitation chamber. When the location is thus cleansed, spiritual efficacy is swiftly attained.
"First, using the mantra for accomplishing all tasks, or alternatively reciting the mantra of Kuṇḍalī, scatter white mustard seeds and other substances upon the ground to ward off all obstacles;
take four stakes made of khadira wood, each measuring two finger-widths in length, with one end split and chiseled into the shape of a single-pronged mallet;
then smear the stakes with red sandalwood incense paste."
Furthermore, wrap it with vermilion thread;

form a fist with the seal of the Vajra-stake and hold it, and recite this mantra one hundred and eight times while driving it into the four corners so that the tips of the stakes are slightly visible.
Prepare a single white banner and suspend it from a long bamboo pole at the eastern side of the maṇḍala.
Recite the Vajra-Wall mantra over iron filings one hundred times to fashion three-pronged vajras with their tips joined together; these encircle the maṇḍala to serve as the Vajra Wall.

Furthermore, recite the Vajra-Railing mantra over iron filings one hundred times to likewise fashion three-pronged vajras; place each of these horizontally upon the vertical vajras and encircle the maṇḍala to serve as the Vajra Railing.
"The gate of the outer maṇḍala is protected by the mantra of Kuṇḍalī and the vajra-mudrā;
the second-tier gate is protected by Hārītī;
and the gate of the central courtyard is protected by Aparājita."

These gate-protectors are common to all three families; alternatively, one may employ just one of them to protect all three gates. These three holy ones all crush all obstacles and cannot be destroyed; this is the secret protection for accomplishing the ritual objects.

"In the center of that altar, five precious objects are buried; however, when constructing a maṇḍala at a place where people gather, those five precious objects should not be buried, but should simply be placed beneath the object being fashioned.
This is likewise the case when constructing a maṇḍala in a courtyard, within a room, or inside a Buddha hall."
"In these five locations, it is sufficient merely to recite the mantra and sprinkle scented water; purification is thereby accomplished without the need for digging the ground.
If one performs this rite within one's original recitation chamber, accomplishment will be swiftly attained.
However, one should not perform rites for accomplishment in caves, nor should one do so in ruined dwellings."

"When one is about to construct a maṇḍala, during the evening seven days prior, with a mind of profound reverence, one should visualize the various deities as if they were present before one's eyes and address them thus:

'O all the deities within the three families, and the deities and their retinues within this very treasury, I have for a long time performed recitations, homa, and maintained the precepts. With this sincere heart, I make this offering to you; I pray that on the seventh day you will descend to the ritual site. Out of compassion for me, accept this humble offering and, through your great loving-kindness and compassion, grant me accomplishment.'"

In this manner, continuing until the seventh day has passed, one should offer the formal petition at the appointed time and then perform the ritual. Furthermore, with *argha* water, flowers, incense, food, drink, and hymns of praise, one should make special offerings to each of the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*) at the end of every day, doing so for all three directions;

likewise, one should apply fragrance to the hands while reciting mantras, pressing those hands upon the object to invite the deity, and again invite the deity by fumigating the object with burning incense.

Furthermore, having fasted and selected an auspicious day, one should briefly construct a maṇḍala using articles for invitation, or simply create a circular maṇḍala of a single color with only one gate opened. In its center, place an eight-petaled lotus measuring two cubits; the remaining outer enclosure may be made of any size as desired.
"First, place the lords of the three families within the inner courtyard. To the north of the western gate, place Maheśvara and his consort.
To the right of the Buddha, place Tejorāśi; to the left, place Buddhalocanā.
Next, to the right of Avalokiteśvara, place Mahāśrī; to the left, place Ṣaḍbhuja."
Next, place Mañjughoṣa on the right side of the Vajra and the Heart-mantra of the Vidyārāja on the left side;
at the southern side of the western gate, place the wrathful Kilikili and the vajra hook.
All that has been described above should be installed within the inner court.
Next, in the outer court, one should place the deities of the eight directions, as well as the lords of mantras who are capable of accomplishing all matters;
the lords of mantras for whom the mind has offered repeated prayers in both the inner and outer courts should all likewise be installed.
Place Kuṇḍalin at the northern side of the outer gate, and Aparājita at the southern side of the gate; invite and make offerings to each with their respective heart-mantras.
Place the articles for accomplishment upon lotuses and offer them.
Alternatively, one may place a full *karṣa* jar upon a lotus flower and set the article for accomplishment upon it;
or one may place a casket upon a lotus flower and store the article within it;

or one may place an earthenware vessel upon a lotus flower and store the article within it. Having placed the article either within the pericarp of the flower or directly upon the lotus flower, one should press it with the hand and recite the mantra over the object one thousand or one hundred times.
Next, again recite the mantra while casting flowers upon the object;
next, burn incense made by blending ghee with *gandha-anusmṛti* (anusthāna) to fumigate it;
next, lightly sprinkle the object with scented water.
Next, one should again recite the mantra of the Family Mother over the object; for all the deities present within the maṇḍala, one should each recite their respective mantras over the object.
Next, perform the homa with cow ghee;
alternatively, use cow’s milk, or a mixture of ghee, honey, and sesame seeds for the homa, followed by a homa of curd-rice.

All the substances mentioned in this root ritual should be subjected to homa; one should perform homa for each using all the mantras contained within the maṇḍala, and for each, one should recite the respective mantra while sprinkling the substances with scented water.

"Just as the methods for illuminating objects were previously explained, so too should one perform this recitation: looking at the object with one's own eyes while mentally reciting the mantra. By performing the ritual in this manner, the object is immediately consecrated through invocation; indeed, by applying this method of invocation to any object whatsoever, one will swiftly attain accomplishment."
"In all the rites of offering and sacrifice belonging to this primary practice, each and every one should be performed with this rite of invitation.
Within the maṇḍala, it is also universally applicable for the consecration of objects and universally applicable for the illumination of objects;
if one performs the *sādhana* therein, those who create obstacles shall find no opportunity, and it is also universally applicable for the purification of objects."
According to the ritual of empowerment, it applies both to the objects of empowerment and to one's own person.
This is the secret, supreme maṇḍala capable of accomplishing all matters; if this rite is performed, success will be attained before long.
Chapter Fifteen: The Ritual for Amending Deficiencies in the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "I shall now explain the ritual for amending deficiencies. [If] there is a deficiency or omission..."
Once the object has been received and maintained, one must bathe three times daily;
perform offerings and *homā* three times a day while pressing the hand upon the object;
change clothes three times a day; and on festival days, observe fasting. All such practices as these offerings must be increased in frequency.
Perform prostrations, repentance, sympathetic joy, entreaty, and the making of vows during the three periods of the day;
recite scriptures and construct maṇḍalas during the three periods;
and take refuge and receive the precepts during the three periods.
Protecting the body during the three periods [of the day], if one practices the rite in this manner, accomplishment will certainly be attained.

Should there be any deficiency due to negligence, one must immediately recite the *Kulamātṛ* mantra twenty-one times to fulfill the requirement; if this method is omitted, accomplishment will likewise be deficient.

Alternatively, if there is a deficiency, one must further recite it one hundred thousand times and again construct this maṇḍala to compensate for the prior deficiency, only after which may one proceed to achieve accomplishment.
"In that maṇḍala, one should establish four gates at the four corners and arrange the boundary lines as previously described.
On the eastern side, place the Buddha;
on his right, place the Ūrṇā-kośa (the hair-treasure); and on his left, place the Śoṭī (the *uṣṇīṣa*)."
On the right side, place Buddhalocanā; on the left side, place Buddhākṣī.
On the right side, place Cakravartin-uṣṇīṣa; on the left side, place Sitātapatrā-uṣṇīṣa.
On the right side, place Tejorāśi; on the left side, place Vijayā-uṣṇīṣa; on the right side, place Abhyudgata-uṣṇīṣa.
Place Subhūti on the left side and Ānanda on the right side.
Place the alms bowl in the southwest corner;
place the mendicant’s staff in the northwest corner; place Hārītī on the right side and Aparājitā on the left side.
Outside the maṇḍala, place that which can accomplish all tasks; in the center, place a wheel, upon which one places the object to be accomplished, or the principal deity.
"In the outer enclosure, place the gates of the eight directional deities; on both sides, place the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, each invited with their respective root mantras;
or invite them all together using the *hṛdaya-mantra* of the family (*kula*). Having made offerings according to the ritual rules, perform the *homā*;
as for these various deities, one may also place their respective mudrās."
Or, having placed it upon its seat and purified the sacrificial fire with the root mantra, one performs one hundred and eight *homa* offerings of clarified butter and honey;

furthermore, using curd-rice and sesame seeds, one performs one hundred *homa* offerings for each with their respective root mantras. When these rites are completed, one recites [the mantra] one hundred times again; this is the secret method for remedying transgressions.

"All items offered must be fragrant and delicious; the food presented should consist of *uṇṇāra* offerings mixed with sugar and curd. For one who performs this rite, all the Honored Ones will be fully satisfied and delighted, and one will swiftly attain accomplishment."

Not only to fill omissions, but one should also construct this maṇḍala every half-month, on festival days, or even daily to make offerings to the various deities; by doing so, all will become abundant and one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
If one cannot determine the specific times, one may perform it according to one's capacity.

"As previously explained regarding the maṇḍala rites of the Buddha Family, these rites for the Lotus Family are likewise identical to them; the only difference is that one should construct it as circular, with its dimensions determined according to one's preference."
Facing east, place Avalokiteśvara;
on the right side, place Hayagrīva, and on the left side, place Viśvarūpa;
on the right side, place the Three-Eyed One, and on the left side, place the Four-Armed One.
On the right side place the Six-Armed [Mahācīna-kumāra], and on the left side place the Twelve-Armed;
on the right side place the One Who Fulfills All Wishes (Sarvārthasiddhi);
furthermore, on the right side place Yaśomatī, and on the left side place Mahāśrī.
To the right, place Tārā; to the left, place Caṇḍa. Near the door, to the right, place Śvetā;

to the left, place Phaṇaravasinī. In the center, place the lotus. Outside the maṇḍala, place the deity of this family who can accomplish all tasks. This is the method for the Lotus Family’s Maṇḍala for Supplementing Deficiencies.
"As previously described for the Buddha Family maṇḍala, this Vajra Family is likewise; however, it must be made square, and its dimensions may be according to one's preference."
On the eastern side, place Vajrapāṇi;
on his right, place the Vidyārāja, and on his left, place Mañjughoṣa;
on the right, place the wrathful Krodha-Śamkara, and on the left, place Vajrāṅkuśa.
On the right side place the staff; on the left side place the great sword.
On the right side place the fist; on the left side place the *khaṭvāṅga*.
On the right side place the *triśūla*; on the left side place the *paraśvadha*.
On the right side, place Krodhāgnimukha;
on the left side near the door, place Vajrabhairavanetra; and on the right side near the door, place Vajrāparājita.

Outside the maṇḍala, place the deities of the primary family who can accomplish all tasks; all other outer enclosures and methods of offering are as previously described. This is the method for supplementing deficiencies in the Vajra Family.

Having thus completed the offerings, one should pray for auspicious dreams. At dawn, having bathed and put on clean white garments, one should offer rice blossoms, green *kūlaka* grass, and fragrant white flowers upon the ground where the maṇḍala was prepared. Then, after smearing the area all over with cow dung and sweeping it clean, one performs the *tripuṭa-homa*. To the right, one places curd, *kūlaka* grass, ghee, honey, sesame seeds, and cooked rice; all the materials for the homa are placed on the right side.

To the left, place the argha vessel; the sruva ladle and the various other offering ladles should be placed in front, separated by the clarified butter (soma). Next, using the mantra for accomplishing all tasks, sprinkle the substances and so forth. Invite the presiding deity of the family (kula-nātha) and install him for worship. Using the root mantra, invite with the argha water, and likewise install that principal deity as well.
Place *sū* before oneself, place fire before the *sū*, and place the object of accomplishment between the *sū* and the fire.
First is oneself, next the *sū*, next the object, next the fire, and next the principal deity and the lord of the family.

"As with the five aforementioned items, one should know that they are to be placed in sequence: place the *Tijaṇi* mantra on the left side of the Lord of the Family, and place the *Sarvakarmasādhana* mantra on the right side, arranging them in the order specified in the previously explained *homa* ritual."

"First, spread out blue *kūlūka* grass and place upon it rice mixed with curd; scatter *śāli* grain flowers as an offering of *svastika*, and make offerings of excellent, beautiful incense. Then, perform the *homa* rites according to the ritual rules, placing the object to be accomplished in a vessel made of gold, or silver, refined copper, stone, conch, shell, wood, or a *vamika* earthenware vessel."
Spread the leaves of the aśvattha tree upon which to place the vessel;
or spread the leaves of a milky sap-bearing tree;
or the leaves of the arka tree.
Alternatively, one may take and spread out leaves of the plantain tree, or lotus petals,
or fresh, clean white cotton cloth as a seat.
"Furthermore, one should first spread five layers of leaves upon the ground and place the articles for accomplishment thereon;
then, one should cover those articles with another five layers of leaves—
whether these be loose leaves or various kinds of cloth."

Alternatively, regarding various miscellaneous items, one should first understand the vessels in which they are to be placed. Then, with an undistracted mind, perform the *tripatāka* ritual; illuminate the objects with the light of the mind and sprinkle them. Holding a ladle, gently grasp the clarified butter (*sarpis*) and place it over the objects while reciting the root mantra. Upon reaching the syllable *svā*, pour it into the fire-pit; upon pronouncing the syllable *hā*, return to touch the objects and withdraw back to the vessel of clarified butter.
In this manner, the contact with objects at the three locations during the coming and going must not be interrupted; this is called the *tripatā homa* method.

Whether one recites it one thousand times or one hundred times, or contemplates the mantra in its extensive or abbreviated forms, or again achieves the lower, upper, light, or heavy stages—even down to twenty-one recitations of the *homa*—this is termed the general limit for the number of recitations.

"At the time of the *tripaṭha*, one should use a ladle to sprinkle water over the objects until they are all thoroughly moistened. When first placing the objects, first sprinkle them with water; next, press down and recite the mantra;
next, examine them again;
and finally, present the offerings."
When the homa is completed, one must likewise proceed as follows.

Regarding the three signs of accomplishment described in the context of the siddhi-maṇḍala, if such signs appear while performing this rite, they must be restrained; one should know that accomplishment will be attained before long.
If the substance is large, place it on the right side; if it is something to be held in the left hand, place it on the left side, and then perform the three-fold tossing (*triparyāsa*).
If the substance is a sentient being, fashion its image and perform the homa while touching its head with the ladle;
if it is one's own person, perform the homa by touching the crown of one's head with the ladle.
If one performs the *tripakṣa* rite for the sake of another, one should simply utter that person's name while performing the *homa*.
Furthermore, there are three distinctions regarding the objects of accomplishment:
first, merely uttering the name; [the other two follow].
Second, cover and separate it with an object;
third, simply expose it so that it may be seen by the eye.
In all such cases, perform the homa using ghee.
If ghee is not obtained, one should use cow’s milk, or milk mixed with ghee;
alternatively, one may use the "three sweets";
or, depending on the specific requirements of the accomplishment (*siddhi*), one should use curd.
One may perform homa according to what was previously explained;
or one may perform homa with sesame seeds for weapons.
If a vetāla is to be accomplished, one should perform homa with the heartwood of a hard tree.
Alternatively, one may use various other liquid fragrances such as *sugandha*;

or, observing the specific characteristics of the object and the particular nature of the accomplishment (*siddhi*), one should take various types of fragrant substances that correspond to the rite and perform the homa.
If one has prepared dog meat, one should likewise use its fat; the same applies to all other types of meat.

As for the object of accomplishment, it may either be drawn and placed before one while reciting the *sādhana* ritual, or one may perform the *homa* rite as previously described. One should extensively perform the *sādhana* ritual and the *homa* of that object; having done so, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.

"Having washed and rinsed the *tripatāka* until it is pure, and having completed the consecration according to the ritual, one should offer worship and maintain it before the *iṣṭadevatā*. Furthermore, one should present various kinds of food and drink as offerings to the *iṣṭadevatā* and perform sacrifices to the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*). One must also duly offer worship at the site of the *homa*. Then, using various cleansing powders and *āmala* fruit, one should bathe oneself according to the ritual; at the hour of midday, one should press the object with the hand while performing recitation."

Furthermore, one should separately prepare the thread and, according to the previous ritual, perform the recitation; likewise, for the armlet, the *bhasma*, and the mustard-seed water, each must be consecrated with recitation as before.

"When one wishes to perform the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*), one must first recite over the articles for protecting the body so that they may be employed later. By thus reciting over these various protective items, they will all prove effective whenever used at the time of accomplishment; therefore, one must first recite over them in advance. One should also prepare offerings such as flowers, consecrating them with mantras and placing them nearby. Subsequently, one should construct the maṇḍala according to the ritual rules, make offerings in accordance with the dharma, and perform the accomplishment."
Recite the mantra while using it to distinguish the various ritual matters; wrap the five-colored boundary-line cord around the four stakes.

Recite the Mañjuśrī (Muṇḍarī) mantra and place the flask before the outer gate; tie both ends of the wrapped cord to the neck of the flask, leaving them slightly loose. Whenever entering or exiting, one should call upon Mañjuśrī and lift the cord to enter;
this cord may be consecrated by reciting the Mañjuśrī mantra, or it may be consecrated by reciting the mantra of the specific root practice.
"Regarding the methods for dispelling obstacles as previously described, one should first purify the site and then perform the ritual.

At that time, one should offer sacrifices outside to the great world-protectors of the eight directions along with their retinues. Upon the flask, place a *vajra* or a branch bearing fruit; then, either recite the mantra of the *vidyārāja* of the relevant family over the flask and the thread, or use the *hṛdaya* (heart-mantra) of the family."
Alternatively, one may recite the mantra of the Family Mother (Kulamātṛ) to protect that place;
or, one may install the various mudrās belonging to the respective family in their original directions to ward off all obstacles.
"Recite the Vajrakilaya mantra one hundred times over the stake.

One end of the stake should be fashioned in the shape of a three-pronged vajra or a single-pronged vajra; having done so, drive it into the four corners outside the purification chamber, or if constructing a maṇḍala, drive it into the corners of the boundary lines. This is called the Vajrakilaya rite."
To accomplish all rites, that maṇḍala may be made using dry powdered pigments;
or using various kinds of fragrant powders;
or using liquid colors applied with a brush made of cow hair.

Outside each corner, draw a three-pronged vajra; throughout the boundary paths, fashion them entirely in the shape of three-pronged vajras. Recite the Vajraprākāra mantra once more, and within the shape of these boundary vajras, further place one vajra across each; this should be done everywhere in this manner, which is then called the "Vajra Railing."
One should further recite the Vajrāṅkuśa mantra; having done so, nothing shall be able to destroy it. Therefore, one performs the rite of accomplishment within this [maṇḍala].
"At each of the gates and outside the gates, place a vajra. As for the method of accomplishment, one may perform it either within a pure chamber or in the open air;
the maṇḍala should measure five cubits, or seven, or eight."
Alternatively, one may contemplate the specific task to be accomplished and act according to its magnitude:
"Place a *vajra* in the center of all the gates, and place vases upon each of the corners;
in front of the outer gate, place a vase capable of accomplishing all tasks."
On the inner side, facing east, place the Dharma-wheel mudrā;
on the right side, place the Buddha-eye mudrā, and on the left side, place the Buddha-ūrṇā mudrā;
on the right, place the tusk mudrā, and on the left, place the śakti mudrā.
To the right, place the five types of Buddha-uṣṇīṣas, arranging them in sequence on both the left and right sides.

Within the Buddha Family (*buddhakula*), arrange all the deities in whatever order suits you on the left and right; finally, place Ānanda and Subhūti at the two outer edges. Next, below and near the entrance, place Aparājita.
"Next, place the Vidyārāja Siddhārtha on the eastern side of the outer enclosure;
place the Honored One Mahāsthāmaprāpta on the northern side;
and place the Honored One Mañjuśrī on the southern side."
On the west side, place the Honored One Maheśvara.

On the east side, to the right, place Brahmā and the various devas of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu); to the left, place Indra, extending upward from the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven down to the terrestrial deities.
"In the southeast, place the Fire God (Agni), with the various ṛṣis as his retinue;
in the south, place King Yama, with the piśācas, bhūtas, and mātṛs as his retinue;
in the southwest, place the deity Niriti, with the various rākṣasas as his retinue."
At the western gate, place the deity Varuṇa, with the hosts of nāgas as his retinue;
at the northern gate, place the Earth Deity, with the asuras as his retinue;
in the northwest, place the Wind Deity, with the garuḍas as his retinue.
In the north, place the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, with the yakṣas as his retinue;
in the northeast, place the deity Īśāna, with the kumbhāṇḍas as his retinue.
Furthermore, in one place on the eastern side, place the Sun Deity (Sūrya) together with the planets;
in one place on the western side, place the Moon Deity (Candra) surrounded by the lunar mansions (nakṣatras);
and at both sides of the western gate’s curve, place the Nanda and Upananda Dragon Kings.
"Regarding all the mantras and vidyās of the messengers and their like within the Buddha Family, they should be installed at will on the four sides of the outer enclosure.
Thereafter, one should invoke them according to the ritual, and perform the offerings, homa, and recitation in successive order."

In the very center, one should install the principal deity or the object of accomplishment; just as the rites for protecting the body and so forth are explained in the Maṇḍala rituals, these should likewise be performed in their proper sequence. This is the Maṇḍala ritual for accomplishing various objects belonging to the Buddha Family.
No obstacles whatsoever shall find an opportunity to prevail; within this, the ritual acts will be swiftly accomplished, and all the Honored Ones will increase their protection.
As before, construct a maṇḍala using five colors, but change it to a circular shape; in the center of its eastern inner court, place the lotus seal.
To the right, place the Seven Tārā Vidyās; to the left, place the Seven Auspicious Vidyās.
Next, place the Six Great Vidyārājñīs on both sides;
to the right, place Pañcarakṣā; to the left, place Yaśomatī.
On both sides near the gate, place the One-Braided Vidyārājñī and Hayagrīva;
in front of the outer gate, place the Vase that Accomplishes All Aims;
at the gates and corners, place vajras, with a lotus placed in the center.

In the outer enclosure, one should place Brahmā, Indra, Maheśvara, and others; the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; the Bodhisattvas Vimalacaryā, Prabhāmandita, and Alaṃkāra; the Dragon Kings Ananta, Śaṇḍa, and Upaśaṇḍa; and the Vidyādhara King Śaṅkha together with all the Vidyādharas, just as the World-Protectors were previously placed in their respective directions. Within this section, all the messengers and various classes of mantras and vidyās should be installed according to one's preference. The sequence of installation is exactly as previously described; thus, no obstacles whatsoever shall find an opportunity, and one should perform the rites of accomplishment within this [enclosure].
"Perform as previously instructed and according to the prior boundary lines; place Susiddhikara on the eastern side of the inner court.
To his right, place the Vidyārājñī Vajragrasanā, and to his left, place the Vidyārājñī Vajramuṣṭi;
to his right, place the Vidyārāja Śumbha, and to his left, place the Vidyārāja Kṛtīcila."
To the right is placed the Honored One Vajra; to the left is placed Vajratuṇḍa.
To the right is placed the Vajramātṛ-gadā; to the left is placed Vajrasaṃkara.
To the right is placed the Vajrāṅkuśī consort; to the left is placed the Māmakī consort.
"On the eastern side of the outer enclosure, place the messenger Vijñāna, the messenger Vajramati, Maheśvara and his consort, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, and the various yakṣas."

"Place a vessel capable of accomplishing all tasks at the outer entrance; then, within the Vajra Family, sequentially arrange the mantras and vidyās of all the messengers (dūtas), as well as the bhūtas, piśācas, gandharvas, mahoragas, vidyādharas, and the world-protectors of the eight directions, each in their respective positions within the outer enclosure."
Thereafter, one should perform the invocation and offer ritual worship according to the dharma, beginning the homa and recitation for the sake of accomplishment.
For the invocation of the various deities, one should employ the mantras of the Vidyārājas;

alternatively, one may use the mantras of the Kulas (Family Mothers) to invoke them. One should place a flask for each of the deities present within the maṇḍala. All the rites pertaining to the maṇḍala as previously described apply here as well; this method of accomplishment is exactly the same.
"If one performs the rites of accomplishment within these maṇḍalas, one shall attain siddhi even if one does not fully possess the methods for protecting the body.
For those deities have their own vow:
'If anyone invites us to the maṇḍala and makes offerings according to the Dharma with a sincere heart, we shall grant whatever boons they seek.'"
Therefore, one should know that in this regard there will be no obstacles and protection will surely be granted.

If one employs the heart-mantra of the family (*kula-hṛdaya*) and the mother of the family (*kulamātṛ*), or the vidyā-consort, the mantra capable of accomplishing all tasks, as well as the body-protection mantra within the family to perform the invocation, the protection of the various realms will swiftly achieve accomplishment; this is the secret method of the three families.
"Furthermore, the secret maṇḍalas of the three divisions are explained.

As in the Path of the Dharmadhātu, one places a *vajra*; in the center, one places the mudrā of the presiding deity of the family; before that, one places the presiding mantra-lord, or as previously stated, one places a *kalaśa* (vase), with its contents placed within a vessel and set upon the vase."
"In the eastern side of the inner court, place the seal of the Tathāgata;
in the northern side, place the seal of Avalokiteśvara;
and in the southern side, place the seal of Vajra."
On the right side of the western face, place Rudra; on the left side, place Vaiśravaṇa.
Just as the Maṇḍala of the Vidyārājas was explained previously, this one should also be arranged in this same sequence.
To the right, place the Vidyā of the Family Mother; to the left, place the Vidyā for Accomplishing Activities. It is the same for the two families of Lotus and Vajra on the left and right!
On the western side, place KṢĀRĪ to the right and LAKṢMĪ to the left.
"Place the alms bowl and the *cīvara* at the two corners on the eastern side;
place the *daṇḍa* and the *kuṇḍikā* water flask at the two corners on the northern side;
and place the *vajra* and the *mudgara* at the two corners on the southern side."
Place the *cakravāla* and the precious vase at the two corners facing west.
Outside the gate, establish a separate location to place Aparājita; in front of the eastern gate, place Hārītī;
in front of the southern gate, place Kūṭadantaka.
To the north, in front of the gate, place the *Icāketaka*.
In the outer enclosure, arrange various mudrās as desired; perform the invocation and offerings according to the ritual. This is the secret universal maṇḍala.
In this practice, all substances prepared for accomplishment will attain siddhi; even Mārīcī cannot find an opportunity here, let alone any other vināyakas.

One should offer various fragrant flowers, lamps, and diverse foods after manifesting them through recitation; this offering should be performed in the same manner as that prescribed for recitation and for the maṇḍala. If it is performed within a purified chamber, it is likewise the same; however, the various offerings to the lord of the maṇḍala should be increased fourfold—this is the secret method.

"Once the offerings have been completed, one should next perform the ritual sacrifice outside according to the Dharma. One should offer lamps fueled by ghee with fresh and pure wicks to the Principal Deity, and each and every item must be presented with an *argha* offering. If one performs the ritual in this manner, the Principal Deity will swiftly grant signs of efficacy."
"Recite the Mantra of the Vidyārāja over white mustard seeds;
or use the Mantra for Accomplishing All Affairs;
or use a mantra that has previously been mastered through practice. Place these near the object of accomplishment to ward off all obstacles, which will then immediately disperse."
Furthermore, place the primary seal of the root mudrā on the left side;
or, simply reciting the mantra of Mahābala, place it on the left side, and position a male figure at each of the eight directions.
First, in the east, that person is dressed in the regalia of Śakra, holding a vajra, with appearance and form exactly like Śakra;
in the south, that person is dressed in the regalia of Yama, holding a daṇḍa staff;
in the west, that person is dressed in the regalia of a Nāga King, holding a noose.
In the north, the person assumes the attire of Vaiśravaṇa, holding a *gadā* staff in hand;
in the northeast, the person assumes the attire of Īśāna, holding a trident;
in the southeast, the person assumes the attire of the Fire God (*Agni*), appearing like a *ṛṣi*, and holds a water jar (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary.
In the southwest, that person is dressed in the attire of a rākṣasa king, holding a horizontal sword in hand;
in the northwest, that person is dressed in the attire of a wind deity, holding a bannered flag in hand.

“Śakra is white; Yama is black; the Nāga King is red; Vaiśravaṇa is golden; Īśāna is whitish-yellow; the Fire God is the color of fire; the Rākṣasa King is the color of a pale black cloud; and the Wind God is blue; the garments they wear are all likewise.”

"All those persons must receive the precepts and be made utterly pure; they must possess great courage and bravery, be skilled in the methods for protecting the body, be handsome in appearance, in the prime of youth, and robust. All the weapons they carry must be consecrated through recitation; they must wear flower garlands interlaced around their necks and both shoulders, be equipped with white mustard seeds, and be well-versed in the signs of obstacles."
"If obstacles arise, one should immediately scatter white mustard seeds and strike them with them, or throw a flower garland;
or if many obstacles appear and manifest great terrors, one should brandish the weapons one holds at them from a distance."

If they should press him closely and strike with weapons, he should scatter white mustard seeds and throw flower garlands while brandishing weapons; at the time of being struck, he must not move from his original position. If he moves from his original position, they will gain the advantage; therefore, he must remain motionless in his place.

"Regarding the invincible mudrās for protecting the body found within this treasury: recite and offer them while keeping them by one's side. If a great and violent danger should arise, one should personally strike at it using those various mudrās;
or else, using white mustard seeds over which mantras have previously been recited with efficacy, one should scatter them while chanting to strike down the obstacle."

If they still do not cease, one should go outside and provide them with excellent food and drink in great abundance, performing sacrifices according to the ritual for those various obstructing spirits.
There are nine kinds of general protections for the Dharma, namely:

expelling obstacles; binding the boundary of the ground; binding the boundary of space; binding the boundary of the maṇḍala; binding the boundaries of the directions; binding the vajra wall; binding the vajra railings; protecting objects; and protecting the body, thereby removing all obstacles.

"When performing the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*), one must keep such dharmas in mind. If one cannot identify the protective deities of the various directions, one should place their respective weapons there;
if even this is not possible, one should place the *nārāca* weapons in all directions;
or else, one may draw a bow and fix arrows in all directions."

Alternatively, one may employ assistants who have mastered the treasury of teachings, possess wisdom and skillful means, have achieved merit through recitation, and maintain pure conduct; these should stand at the entrance to assist in managing various affairs and warding off obstacles, providing aid throughout both the inner and outer courtyards.

"Whatever tasks there may be, they must all be completed by evening; as soon as the sun has set, one should begin the rites for accomplishment (*sādhana*). If one feels fatigued during the interval, one should go outside the maṇḍala, take water in the mouth to rinse, and hold three handfuls of this rinsing water while reciting the Mañjuśrī-krodha (Kuṇḍalī) mantra, or recite the heart-mantra of one's own tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) over a small amount of cow’s ghee and drink it;

thus, all exhaustion shall be cured. Furthermore, mix long pepper (*pippalī*) with honey, recite the Mother-mantra of the Buddha Family (*buddhakulajananī*) over it, and apply it to the eyes; thus, drowsiness and the inability to rise shall be immediately cured."
"First, with a sincere mind, stand facing east and observe the various deities, taking refuge and making your petition.
Among the three kinds of auspicious omens, whichever favorable sign you perceive, accomplish the rite with a joyful heart; as it was with the initial omen, so shall it be for the accomplishment."

Therefore, the practitioner should observe the preliminary omens: first, one must for a brief moment contemplate the Vidyārāja Susiddhikara, and next, circumambulate to the right while discerning the various ritual vases.

When entering the maṇḍala, one should circumambulate all the vases encountered to the right; having arrived, one prostrates to the deities and surveys them thoroughly, offering arghya to each with their respective root mantras, or otherwise making offerings with the heart-mantra of the family.

One should summon the Lord of Mantras with the mantra of a Vidyārāja, and having summoned the Lord of Vidyās with the Vidyā, one should gaze upon their respective mudrās and recite their respective mantras and vidyās; or, one may simply gaze upon a single universal mudrā and recite its mantra and vidyā. If one acts in this manner, one will swiftly attain siddhi.
"The accomplished object may be placed within an argha vessel;
or placed upon a flask;
or held within cupped hands."
Either one may merely bring it to mind;
or place it in a vessel made of *varaṇa* wood;
or place it upon leaves.
All the vessels prepared before the central deity within the inner sanctum should be smeared with ox-gall (*gorocanā*); next, one should perform protection using white mustard seeds;
then, reciting the mantra, one should offer *mālātī* flowers to those objects.
By applying cow bezoar, one achieves the state of being restrained;
by using mustard seeds, one achieves protection;
and by making offerings of flowers, one achieves radiance. These three methods should be performed in their proper sequence and must not be omitted or neglected.

"Place the articles for accomplishment before the deity, ensuring that no other objects intervene between them. These articles for accomplishment are to be protected by means of two methods: first, mudrās;
second, white mustard seeds."

In order to cause the object of accomplishment to swiftly manifest its efficacy, one should repeatedly offer arghya, flowers, incense, and other requisites, as well as curds; furthermore, one should make offerings to those who assist in the accomplishment, so that they may protect the object by remaining constantly at that site.

"Having thus arranged and made offerings, one should then press upon it with the hand or gaze at it with the eyes; reciting slowly with an undistracted mind, one should repeatedly manifest its splendor throughout the process. In this manner, one should continue the recitation throughout the night without interruption."
During the three periods of that night, one should perform offerings in succession with *argha* water and other substances.

If it is necessary to go outside to rinse the mouth, one should have an assistant take one’s seat and continue the recitation; whatever the practitioner may forget or omit, the assistant must compensate for all such deficiencies.
"If a great calamity should arise during the time of recitation, those who assist in its accomplishment should repel that calamity.
If it cannot be restrained, the practitioner should personally scatter white mustard seeds to ward off the calamity."
"When those who assist recite this object, if such difficulties as heavy rain and lightning appear in the east, one should know that these are the calamities of Śakra."
In the southeast, this calamity appears, namely a great being of fiery color;
or it may appear like the setting sun—one should know that this is the calamity of the Fire God (Agni).

In the south, this calamity appears, namely corpses of most terrifying form, crying out with loud voices and holding great swords with which they sever noses; holding skulls filled with human blood which they drink, their heads ablaze with fire—one should know that this is the calamity of Yama.

In the southwest, this obstacle appears: namely, rain consisting of excrement and filth falls upon the maṇḍala, along with various terrifying forms; one should know that this is the obstacle of Nīlāṅga.
In the western direction, there are such calamities as rain, thunder, lightning, and hail; one should know that these are the calamities of the dragon kings.
In the northwest, this difficulty manifests: namely, the arising of a great black wind; one should know that this is the difficulty caused by the Wind Deity (*Vāyu-deva*).
In the north, this difficulty manifests: namely, male and female yakṣas harassing the practitioner; one should know that this is the difficulty caused by the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
In the northeast, there appears this obstacle: namely, beings with the heads of elephants, pigs, and dogs, each holding a mountain of fire; one should know that these are the obstacles of Īśāna.
One should know that when various devas manifest above with great majesty and power, this is the "difficulty of the upper heavens.
As for the difficulties of the lower regions, one should know that earthquakes and fissures in the earth are the "difficulties of the asuras."
"It is only when performing the supreme accomplishment (*uttamasiddhi*) that these obstacles manifest.

Such obstacles appear during the middle watch of the night; one should know that for ordinary [accomplishments], the signs of obstacles in the supreme accomplishment are likewise great, and those for the middling and inferior accomplishments should be understood accordingly."

During the three periods of the night, these constitute the superior, middling, and inferior signs; when they correspond to the proper time, there is accomplishment, but if they do not correspond to the time, there is no accomplishment.
"The three types of signs are:
warmth, smoke, and light."
These three signs should appear in succession.
If the superior accomplishment is achieved, one possesses all three signs;
if the middling accomplishment is achieved, one possesses the first two signs.
If the accomplishment is of an inferior grade, only the first sign will appear.

Alternatively, if one recites with devotion and the three signs appear in succession during the first watch of the night, one should immediately restrain their light by means of the Family Mother’s mantra,
or restrain those signs by means of the Heart-mantra of the Vidyārāja.
Furthermore, one may recite mantras while applying or sprinkling cow bezoar,
or press with the hand,
or sprinkle with clarified butter (ghṛta).
Alternatively, one may scatter flowers;
or scatter white mustard seeds;
or simply sprinkle water to seal and stabilize the visualization, whereupon one may immediately utilize it and fulfill one's aspiration.

"Alternatively, if one has already entered the period of restraint during the first watch of the night, one may continue with the recitation until the designated time arrives before partaking [of the substances]; the methods for accomplishment therein should be understood accordingly."
"In the first watch of the night, the lower siddhi is accomplished;
in the middle watch of the night, the middling accomplishment is obtained;
and when the dawn light appears, the supreme accomplishment is obtained."
Regarding those accomplishments achieved at midnight, once one has performed the ritual prohibitions according to the dharma, it is permissible to utilize them even until dawn.
The lower levels of accomplishment should be understood accordingly.
"Regarding those who assisted at the original time [of the ritual], it is not auspicious if they do not partake [of the substance].

Even if the substance has been prepared, if one does not partake of it immediately nor preserve it, and fails to partake of it by dawn, that substance will become like a withered flower or foul food, unfit for use. Because the mantra was invoked through recitation to enter into the substance, once the proper time has passed, its efficacy is lost."

Furthermore, although the signs of accomplishment may initially appear, they do not yet constitute actual accomplishment; if one restrains those signs at that time, one will later achieve accomplishment by performing rites such as the manifestation of light, as well as making offerings and receiving empowerment on various festival days.
If, after three years, it is not accomplished, one should know that this object cannot be achieved.
For the supreme method of accomplishment, the limit is three years;
for the middling accomplishment, it is six months.
If the lower grade of accomplishment is achieved, there is no restriction on the time;
the same applies to the methods for rectifying a damaged accomplishment.
Chapter Sixteen: The Method for Recovering Stolen Accomplished Objects from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "I shall now explain the method for recovering objects that have been stolen."
When the object has been completed, or at the time of performing the rite of accomplishment, the object may be stolen;
at the time of the theft, one may either see the thief’s form, or simply lose the object without seeing the thief.

At that time, one need not select an auspicious day nor observe a fast; having aroused a state of wrath, one should immediately perform this maṇḍala rite. It should be constructed as a triangle using the ashes from cremated corpses, with only the western gate opened, and the principal deity placed before the outer gate.
In the eastern corner of the inner court, place the Vidyārāja Susiddhikara.
To his right, place Vajracanda; to his left, Mahācanda.
To the right, place Vajramuṣṭi; to the left, Vajrāṅkuśa.
To the right, place Vajrakīlikīla; to the left, place Vemacitra.
To the right, place Śeṣa; to the left, place Piṅgala.
To the right, place Aśvinau; to the left, place Śaṃkara.
To the right, place Vajra; at the right gate, place Kāli;
at the left gate, place Nandamukha; to the left, place Vajrasena;
and to the right, place Sumahā as well as all the other great wrathful deities.

For the sake of accomplishment, one should arrange the ritual sequence and perform the formal invocation according to the Dharma, making offerings in succession with red flowers, red food, and so forth.

"The *ābhicāruka* rites previously described should be performed here; the principal deity stationed outside the gate should be worshipped according to the Dharma with exquisite flowers and other offerings. Furthermore, the deities of the eight directions placed in the outer enclosure, as well as the various messengers (*dūta*) and other honored ones of the respective families, must likewise be offered worship in this manner."
"In its center, perform the homa rite; the hearth shall be triangular, exactly as described before. Use seven pieces of khadira wood, anointing them with one's own blood, and perform the homa;
alternatively, use *kṛtavedhana* wood or the charred remains of funeral pyres for the homa.
Once the fire has been kindled, mix funeral ashes with one's own blood and perform the homa."
Furthermore, one should perform homa by mixing four substances—poisonous medicine, one’s own blood, mustard oil, and red mustard seeds;
then, fashioning the shape of the thief from these four items and sitting upon it, one should cut and dissect it piece by piece with the left hand while performing the homa.

If there is one who can subdue anger and is proficient in the Dharma, they should perform this rite. The thief, seized by panic and terror, will bring the stolen object and personally hand it over; the practitioner should then bestow fearlessness upon him and at that time perform for him the *śāntika* rite.
If this is not done, he will die.
Alternatively, one may further increase the items to be offered and place them secretly before the Honored One.

Furthermore, if the articles for accomplishment have been stolen over a long period and one wishes to reclaim them, one should immediately construct this *Sarvakarmasādhana-maṇḍala* common to the three families; it should be drawn as a square with the seal of the Vidyārāja Susiddhikara installed at the center.

"On the southern side of the inner court, place Vajrakrodha, Mahākrodha, Māmakī, Vajrāṅkuśa, Vajrabhakṣa, Vajramuṣṭi, Vajrajvālā, Vajramātṛkā, Vajrabhairava, Vajraśaṅkhalā, Kīlikīla, Prajñāvajra, and Vajrāparājita, as well as all the great wrathful deities and all the messengers."
The great accomplished ones, lords of mantras, and others are to be installed in order on its southern side.

On the northern side of the inner courtyard, one should install in their respective order according to the ritual: the Fulfiller of All Wishes, Avalokiteśvara, Hayagrīva, the Many-faced and Many-handed One, the Manifestor of Many Forms, Yaśomatī, Mahāśrī, Rakṣami, Śvetā, Pañcarakṣiṇī, Tārā, Candra, Māra, and all their mantras and vidyās, as well as all the messengers.

"On the eastern side of the inner court, place the various other Buddha-uṣṇīṣas such as the Suvarṇacakravarti-buddhoṣṇīṣa; the Buddha-ūrṇā, Buddha-netrī, Buddha-śakti, Buddha-danta, Buddha-maitrī, and other vidyārājas such as Aparājita, as well as mantras capable of accomplishing all tasks."

The various other mantras and their respective messengers are to be installed in order, according to the ritual rules, on the eastern side; those near the two sides of the gate and outside the gate are likewise to be installed according to the ritual rules as before.
"In the outer enclosure, place the deities of the eight directions.
On the southern side of the western gate, place Brahmā and his retinue;
on the northern side of the western gate, place Maheśvara together with his queen, Nambati, and other attendants, as well as the seven Mātṛkās, the eight Dragon Kings, and their respective retinues."

The Asura Kings and their retinues—those deities of great majesty who had taken refuge in the Buddha—were each installed in due order and according to the Dharma within the outer enclosure; they were then invoked with utmost sincerity and offered successive offerings.

"To the west outside, place a homa fire pit. Fashion an image of the thief out of wax and place it within a winnowing basket; then, according to the ābhicāruka rite, perform invocations, offerings, worship, and homa.
Next, cut that image with a knife and perform homa [with the pieces]."
Alternatively, one may perform it according to the *ābhicāruka* rites taught in one's own family (*kula*);
or one may perform it in the same manner when the deity steals [the substance] itself or when it is accomplished even though it was not given.
From the fifth day to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, performing rites during this interval is said to be supremely auspicious.

Furthermore, one may strike the form with a staff or whip, burn it with fire, and beat it with various fierce implements; one may pierce its body parts using mustard seeds as vajra-stakes according to the ritual method;
and one may cause harm by inflicting whatever suffering one desires upon it, having smeared its entire body with black mustard oil mixed with salt.
Furthermore, cover the corpse's form with the shroud used for its burial;

wrap it with red thread and offer red flowers while reciting the mantra. Staring at it with eyes wide in wrath, insert words of reproach into the mantra and strike it every day. If someone brings an offering, one should then cease.
"In the middle of the night, one should perform this fierce rite: using *kubjaka* wood and black mustard oil, perform a *homa* offering;
furthermore, mixing together poison, one's own blood, mustard seeds, oil, salt, and black mustard seeds, perform a *homa* while reciting the name of the thief eight hundred times;
or alternatively, simply use one's own blood mixed with salt to perform the *homa*."
"If such a *duḥkhadhāraṇī* does not return the object, one must immediately perform the fierce rite unto death.
One should perform everywhere the rites of killing as taught in the *ābhicāruka* rituals, and insert the words of killing within the mantra."
If someone brings an object and requests that a certain practice be ceased, one should grant them joy;
if they have already used that object and bring another to replace it, one should likewise cease that matter;
or if they have already used the object and have nothing to replace it, yet come to express regret and apologize, one should still cease that matter and bestow joy upon them.
If those items have been lost or given away to others, one should cease the matter regarding whatever remains and bestow it upon the recipient with joy.
One should perform homa using the Vajra-Cintāmaṇi mantra, or perform homa using Mahākrodha or Aśuci-krodha;
or one may perform homa using the mantra for recovering lost objects as taught in the specific family (kula) concerned.
However, these three types of mantras are common to the mantras of the three families:
“Oṃ āryānaye svāhā. Having invited the Fire God, one should offer three balls of food—one mantra for each ball—into the fire to make offerings to the Fire God.
Furthermore, the *homa* mantra is:

"Oṃ ānatace nyasva vagena jñuppi jñipini pāya svāhā. Again, hold one piece of clarified butter (*sū*), recite the mantra once, and burn it; do this three times to make offerings to the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*).
The Vajra-family Wrathful Vajra Mantra:
“Oṃ kili kili vajra-krodha hūṃ phaṭ. With this mantra, perform the fire-offering rite (homa) by reciting it once for each oblation.
The mantra for accomplishing the homa rite: "Namo ratnatrayāya. (1)
Namo vīra-vajrapāṇaye. (The second phrase.)
Mīhā yakṣa-sa (as above) kṣe-na baṇḍa-ye (three syllables);
Oṃ (as above) hu (four syllables); Gara.
Gara-vajra-pañca-kumāra-tāta.
Maṭha-vajra ṣaṭ-kūṭānāṃ.
Dunā vajra saptaguṇa hana hana.
vajra-astaghuṭa ghāta ghāta!
The nine-sentence *vajra*-banner;
as for the banner:
Vajra daśakuṇāla nara nara.
Vajra ekādaśa jvalaya jvalaya vajra dvādaśa.
Minarāya minarāya vajra (13) [syllables]
Cchinna cchinna vajra (14)
Pinna pinna vajra (15th phrase)
"Vajra hūṃ phaṭ (16).
"By reciting this mantra and performing the homa rite, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.

If one obtains the actual object or a substitute for it, one should then protect that object as well as oneself; on festival days, one should perform the rites of illumination and so forth in their proper sequence."
"Among those, the accomplished objects and the lesser accomplished objects shall all have one portion offered to the World-Honored One;
one portion offered to the Ācārya;
and one portion offered to the previous practitioner who achieved success."
One portion is offered as a gift to companions and others;
one portion is taken for oneself and divided into two parts:
one part for personal use, and one part offered as a gift to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and so forth.
