"All material things are like this: first offer *argha* water to the Honored Ones and others, and afterwards take your own portion. For those who have previously attained accomplishment, offer their portion with *argha*; as for the value of that offering, one should take double its worth for one's own use. What is meant by 'value' here is the act of making an offering."
If the ācārya is absent, one may take back the share and use it oneself after repaying its value; as for that "value," the sense of shame and remorse felt in one's heart constitutes the value.
When exiting the maṇḍala to offer to those who have previously attained accomplishment, one should speak these words:
"May all you who have previously attained accomplishment accept your respective portions.
Holding the arghya vessel in hand, one should chant thus for a second and third time:
"If there is no one to take it, you should give it to your companions; do not harbor any doubt or hesitation.

Because they possess a devout mind, because they offer worship, because they maintain the precepts, and because they attend upon their fellow travelers, they are those who have already attained [merit]. Therefore, they should receive their share."
When the third proclamation is made, his companions should respond thus:
"We are indeed those who have previously attained accomplishment.
The practitioner himself shall then divide the objects equally with his companions.
If the substance is so small that it cannot be divided—such as agallochum, cow bezoar, and the like, which are indivisible—one should mentally determine its portion and consume it for oneself.

“There are such objects that are for the use of a single person alone and cannot be divided, such as wheels, swords, and so forth; one should perform their accomplishment according to what is taught in their respective original texts.”
The central pillars and other such components must likewise not be divided.

Within the primary ritual (*mūla-vidhi*), even if the quantity of the substances for accomplishment is small, one may add to the original amount to perform the accomplishment for oneself and one's companions; or, one may perform the accomplishment based on the proportions of a person already accomplished, achieving success even if the amount is reduced by half; or, one must strictly follow the specific proportions prescribed in the primary ritual.
"When a traveler distributes goods to his companions, he should issue this instruction:
'You shall follow me in whatever tasks I assign.
Once they have given their assent, he should then bestow the goods upon them."

Alternatively, if one person achieves the benefit of others and, based on this treasury of teachings or other dharmas, intends to distribute [the merit] equally among companions and others, the distribution of goods according to their respective contributions must be impartial and without favoritism.

Once the object has been accomplished, one should first make offerings to the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity), generating deep shame and remorse, and then respectfully request [the deity's permission] before dividing it; this applies to all the rites of every *kula* (family).

The middling and lower levels of accomplishment should be understood according to this principle: one should give rise to a profound sense of shame and remorse, offer respectful service and worship, and bestow material wealth; furthermore, one’s every movement and action should follow the other’s instructions, thereby repaying the value of the object through such deeds.
Once the object has been consecrated, first offer *argha* water and distribute it according to the ritual rules.

Recite the root mantra and perform the hand gestures (*mudrā*), while contemplating the principal deity with the mind and reciting the mantras of the Vidyārāja and Vidyārājñī; continue this contemplation until its completion, and thereafter enjoy the object.

Ascending into the sky at will, he shall reach the abode of the various sages; there, none shall be able to harm or despise him, and even if there were enemies, they would be unable to cause him injury.

That practitioner must constantly recollect the tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā) and never neglect it. The articles for accomplishment must always be kept in mind or beheld with the eyes. Because of the mantras and rites of the Vidyārāja, all sages will revere him; because of the Vidyārājñī, he shall have no fears. He must not neglect performing the samaya-mudrā, the family (kula) mudrā, or gazing upon the articles [of accomplishment].
Upon meeting a seer, one should first show respect and inquire: "Welcome;
are you well, and from where have you come?
If the seer asks anything in return, one should answer with kind words.

"When wandering through the air, one should not pass over shrines, nor over solitary trees, crossroads, the dwellings of sages, city walls, sacrificial altars, assemblies of Brahmins, or the abodes of practitioners of false doctrines; for due to such overweening pride, one who passes over these will surely fall."

Those who fall due to negligence should recite the mantras of the Vidyārājas and engage in meditative contemplation; whether they have already fallen or are on the verge of falling, they shall thereby regain their original station.

"Although space has no form or color, when one with the divine eye perceives the path, it is as if a skilled practitioner reaches the destination as soon as they resolve their mind upon it; likewise, even while remaining unmoving in meditative concentration, one reaches it."

Therefore, they travel upon those paths previously perfected; by the power of their merit, garments appear spontaneously according to their wishes. They enjoy palaces, flowers, groves, gardens, and various birds, as well as celestial maidens sporting with song, dance, and music. All manner of sensual delights blaze with radiant light, just like the wish-fulfilling jewel-trees at the beginning of a kalpa that can satisfy every aspiration.

For the sake of dwelling, there are gem-studded seats; beneath flowing channels, soft grasses carpet the ground; various necklaces and ornaments serve as articles for adornment and enjoyment; auspicious trees bear ambrosial fruits; and even whatever places one desires or remembers appear before one.

Even though this is so, one must always protect the body and never neglect it; one should dwell in pure groves, on mountain peaks, or on islands in the ocean, rivers, or sandbanks, staying in those places for the sake of recreation. There, one will encounter the sublime environments described previously, or dwell together with the hosts of sages who have already attained perfection.

Chapter Seventeen: The Chapter on the Ritual Procedures for Accomplishing All Branches of the Susiddhikara Sūtra "I shall now further explain the ritual procedures for accomplishing all branches of *siddhi*.

If the object is not accomplished, one should restrain it according to the ritual, guard it, conceal it, or discard it; then, as before, one should again perform the preliminary recitation rites up to the rites for accomplishment.
Having done this, if it is still not accomplished, one should increase one's diligence and again perform the recitation and the rites for accomplishment.
If, after seven such cycles have been completed, it is still not accomplished, one should perform this rite, and success will be certain.
That is to say: begging for alms;

diligently reciting mantras with great reverence; circumambulating the eight holy sites; prostrating and walking the path; or alternatively, reciting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* seven or one hundred times;
or holding superior objects to offer as gifts to the *Aṅga*.

Alternatively, by the side of a river leading to the sea, or on a sea island, one should construct one hundred *stūpas*. Before each *stūpa*, one should perform recitation according to the ritual rules for one thousand repetitions. If, at the end, the hundredth stūpa emits light, one should know that the rite is definitely accomplished.

Furthermore, if one constructs one thousand *stūpas* and recites [the mantra] one thousand times before each one, even if one has committed the crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), once the full number is completed, there is no need for further ritual procedures and success will be naturally attained;
moreover, by reciting all mantras one *koṭi* times, they will certainly be accomplished.

If one recites while performing the rite for twelve years, even those with heavy karmic offenses will achieve success, and even if the ritual requirements are incomplete, accomplishment will still be obtained.
Furthermore, once the number of recitations and the prescribed time have been completed, one should immediately perform the *vṛddhi-homa* (prosperity rite);
or alternatively, one may construct this *sarvakarmika-maṇḍala* (maṇḍala for accomplishing all matters) and perform the four kinds of *homa* therein.

Whether on a mountain peak, at a place where a herd of cattle previously dwelt, or on an island in the Ganges, one should level the ground and construct a maṇḍala measuring one hundred and eight cubits.

One hundred and eight vases should be placed therein, with pillars erected at its four gates to form the entrances. At each gate, a jeweled pavilion should be established and adorned in various ways; garlands made of various flowers and branches should be hung upon the gate pillars and the corner banners. Butter lamps should be arranged all around the site, numbering one hundred and eight, and one hundred and eight incense burners filled with various famous incenses should also be set out within the maṇḍala.

One side of the inner court measures seven cubits, and one side of the outer court measures three cubits; the remainder is the central area. All procedures for invocation, offering, and so forth are to be conducted exactly as previously prescribed according to the *homa* ritual.
"Next, one should explain the specific procedure for the center: place the root mantra within the *kalaśa* flask, and perform the *homa* rite on its four sides.
Within the inner enclosure (*abhyantarāvaraṇa*), place all the deities of the Buddha Family on the eastern side;
place all the deities of the Lotus Family on the northern side."
On its southern side, place all the deities belonging to the Vajra Family;
on the western side, place the god Rudra and Vaiśravaṇa, each together with their respective retinues.
"As previously described, the messengers and other honored deities who cannot be accommodated within the inner courtyard should be placed in the outer courtyard.
The guardians of the directions and their respective retinues should each be placed in their original positions;
the lords of the three families, as well as Rudra and Vaiśravaṇa, should first be established in their original locations."
Next, one should further place the Vidyārājas, Vidyārājñīs, and the Lords of Mantras who accomplish specific tasks, arranging them in order along with their various messengers;
furthermore, one should place the Honored One Khaṇḍakapālin and the Honored One Aparājita in front of the outer gate.
Having thus completed the maṇḍala according to the ritual procedure, one should perform the sequence of invocation and offerings using the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) of the respective family.

Then, while performing recitation in the four directions, one should subsequently perform the homa rite within the hearths placed on the four sides of the flask, each according to its own family; this is called the "homa for the enhancement of the deities."
For the food offerings, use *nāra* as the oblation.
Having performed this rite, all the Honored Ones will become empowered.
"Having thus completed the recitation and *homa*, one should further perform the *homa* of clarified butter (*sarpis*) with the mantra of the Family Mother."
Next, perform homa with milk porridge mixed with ghee using the mantra of the principal deity;
further, perform homa with sesame seeds and the three sweets using the mantra of the Family Mother (Kulamātṛ);
and again, perform homa with ghee using the mantra of the Family Mother.

Having performed this rite, one shall obtain all the Honored Ones; they will immediately be fully satisfied, and through the accomplishment of increase and perfection, they will all rejoice and swiftly grant success.
If one constructs this maṇḍala up to seven times, accomplishment is certain.

If, despite performing the recitation and circumambulating the eight stūpas as previously described up to seven times and constructing this maṇḍala, success is not attained, one shall then subdue the deity through the *ābhicāruka* rite of harsh treatment. One should fashion an image of the deity out of wax and perform the recitation while holding its mantra.

First, recite the mantras of the Family Mother and the Vidyārāja; place the mantra of the principal deity (iṣṭadevatā) in between and perform the homa according to the ābhicāruka rite. Anoint the image with mustard oil, and it will immediately be seized by a violent fever.

If one subdues another who is possessed, such that the entire body is in pain, one should strike them with a whip or with flowers out of anger, using the two aforementioned mantras while maintaining a mind of wrath; this is like the methods for punishing malevolent spirits or punishing a tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā).
One must act according to these teachings and may not act arbitrarily.

"If the Honored One appears and grants you accomplishment, once your original vow has been fulfilled, cease the previous rites and perform the *śāntika* rite. Alternatively, mix together poison, your own blood, sesame seeds, oil, salt, and red mustard seeds, and perform *homa* throughout the entire night; at that time, the Honored One will become terrified and cry out:
'Stop! Stop! Do not do this!'"
"Then [the deity] immediately grants the accomplishment.

If, after performing the ritual in this manner for three days, [the deity] still does not come to grant the accomplishment, one should further apply oneself with courage and a fearless mind, cutting one's own flesh and performing *homā* three times. Thereupon, the tutelary deity will appear to seek that person's favor, and whatever wish is sought in the heart shall be granted as an accomplishment."

If there are any deficiencies or transgressions, they shall be pointed out one by one; even if one has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, if one performs the homa sacrifice with pieces of flesh for nine nights, the deity will certainly come and grant accomplishment.

This is the method for engaging in a ritual contest with a mantra. One must protect one’s body according to the Dharma with a fearless mind; only then may one perform it, and it will certainly not be in vain.
Once the accomplishment has been attained, one should immediately perform the śāntika rite; if any transgressions have been committed, they must be rectified.
"Among all matters of accomplishment, this maṇḍala is supreme; by performing the three types of rites within it, one obtains the three kinds of fruits.

Within it, one should perform all various activities as well as homa; the subjugation of the deity is like the subjugation of a malevolent spirit. For every offering, one must use fresh items, and the same applies to the materials for the homa."

"One should not be negligent regarding this dharma; one must bathe for purification and protect the body according to the ritual rules without showing disrespect. Only after clearly understanding the treasury of teachings may one employ this rite to punish the *iṣṭadevatā*; if one violates this, it will result in self-harm."

*Susiddhikara Tantra*, Middle Volume. On the third day of the fifth month of the twenty-fifth year of Ōei, by Eijun of the Daitō-in. Chapter Eighteen: The Classification of Accomplishments (*Vibhāga-siddhi-pariccheda*). Lower Volume.
"I shall now further explain the accomplishment of the *siddhis* of the three families. One proceeds through the air with sovereign mastery."
The supreme is [the attainment of] the highest vehicle; concealing one's form and hiding one's traces is the middling accomplishment (*siddhi*); and mundane affairs are the inferior *siddhi*.

Having established these three types of accomplishments—the superior, middling, and inferior—pertaining to the three vehicles and mundane matters, they are further differentiated according to their respective levels of superiority, mediocrity, and inferiority.

"Through the supreme accomplishment methods of the three families, one attains the state of a Vidyādhara and travels through the air, achieving the five supernatural powers; furthermore, there are many varieties, such as the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava),
the attainment of the stage of a Pratyekabuddha,
or the realization of the rank of a Bodhisattva."
Some understand all matters;
some possess eloquence and extensive learning;
some achieve the status of a Vettāla.
Some become yakṣiṇīs;
some obtain cintāmaṇi jewels;
and some obtain inexhaustible hidden treasures.
Possessing such superior qualities and so forth is called the method for the supreme-superior accomplishment (*uttarottara-siddhi*).
Regarding the methods for accomplishment within the three families: by concealing the traces within the body, one attains great power;
and though previously indolent, one comes to attain diligence.
Entering the palace of the asuras, he obtains the elixir of longevity;
he becomes a *piśāca* celestial messenger,
or is able to command spirits.
Some may achieve mastery over the tree deity Śalabhañjika;
some may become widely learned, such that even before hearing something, they realize its profound meaning and principles;
or they may succeed in compounding medicines, whereby merely by applying them to their feet or heads, they can travel great distances without fatigue.
All that has been explained above are methods for middling and superior accomplishments.
"The methods for inferior accomplishment in the three families cause the multitude to behold one with joy,
or to bring people under one's control;
Alternatively, the ability to punish evil persons, subdue hostile hosts, and perform other such inferior tasks is termed the "inferior-middle" method of accomplishment.
If one wishes to accomplish medicinal substances and the like, there are three grades of accomplishment: the emission of light and flames constitutes the superior grade; [the others follow].
Smoke is the middling [sign];
warmth is the inferior.
"Furthermore, O Noble One, mantras constitute the superior accomplishment;"
That which is spoken by the devas constitutes middling accomplishment;
the mantras of the worldly devas constitute inferior accomplishment.
Furthermore, the mantras of the Buddha family constitute the superior siddhi.
The mantras of the Lotus Family (Padmakula) result in middling siddhi;
the mantras of the Vajra Family (Vajrakula) result in inferior siddhi.
"If one desires to seek an inferior accomplishment by means of a superior mantra, one shall obtain that inferior accomplishment."
If one seeks the superior [attainment] by means of an inferior mantra, one obtains the supreme accomplishment;
or if one achieves the superior or the inferior by means of a middling mantra, these too are equally accomplished.

One should know that within mantras these four virtues are complete, such that they can all produce great fruits according to their superior, middling, or inferior divisions—namely, enabling the fulfillment of the stage of a Pratyekabuddha.
That is to say, bringing the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of a bodhisattva to full completion, up until the attainment of Buddhahood, constitutes the great fruit and retribution.
Furthermore, accomplishing great virtuous conduct—meaning being surrounded before and after by numerous retinues—constitutes great virtuous conduct for one who fulfills such aspirations.

Furthermore, there is the stage of long-term abiding, which refers to attaining the status of a king, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), or a long-lived immortal (ṛṣi); for one who fulfills such aspirations, this constitutes the stage of long-term abiding.
The physical form and demeanor are vast and magnificent, and its majestic radiance shines afar; it teaches the cultivation of the vast and great.
One who possesses these four virtues can achieve the superior grade even with a mantra of the inferior grade;
conversely, if these virtues are not present within a mantra of the superior grade, then despite being of the superior grade, it functions as one of the inferior grade.

"The mantras spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas follow this sequence: even those spoken by many Buddhas and Bodhisattvas that belong to the lower grade can accomplish matters of the highest grade and so forth."
"Among the mantras spoken by the Honored Ones and others, there are those that possess only a single purpose;
namely,
the śāntika rite, the pauṣṭika rite, and the ābhicāruka rite."
Although each of these factors possesses its own superior, middling, and inferior grades, how could an inferior mantra ever accomplish a superior result?
It is just as when exquisite lotus flowers emerge from blue mud; of this there is no doubt.
How could a mantra of superior compassion and benevolence accomplish an inferior accomplishment of wrath?
It is like white sandalwood, whose nature is cool; yet if it is struck by the wind and rubbed together, fire naturally arises—not without its causes and conditions.
Although these various differences do not follow a fixed sequence, you should have no doubts regarding any other *siddhis*.
The *siddhi* of bodily parts constitutes the superior grade of accomplishment;
the *siddhi* of medicinal substances constitutes the middling grade of accomplishment.
The accomplishment (*siddhi*) of wealth and abundance is classified as the lowest grade.

Furthermore, if there is a person who has long practiced the recitation of a mantra of the lowest grade, even if they themselves lack the power to seek a higher grade from the deity, the higher grade will be spontaneously attained.

However, if one harbors doubt regarding a mantra of the highest grade, or if their recitation, maintenance, and offerings are not sincere, then despite it being a mantra of the highest grade, because of that light-mindedness in recitation, they may only dare to invite an accomplishment of the lowest grade.
Therefore, know that the practice of recitation depends entirely upon the mind.
For instance, even among the devas there are those who are poor, and within the ranks of the pretas there are those who are wealthy and powerful; as it is with these beings, so it is with mantras.
Each and every mantra possesses the three *siddhis*, namely:
superior, middling, and inferior; by reciting with a sincere heart, one shall obtain *siddhi* in all cases.

Chapter Nineteen: The Chapter on Invocation (*Sūksma-siddhi-kalpa Sūtra*) "Furthermore, if one wishes to enter the chamber of the *iṣṭadevatā*, one should first gaze upon the countenance of the Honored One, join the ten fingers and toes, and slightly lower the head."

Furthermore, fill a vessel with pure water; according to the rite to be performed, place the original offering flowers therein and also add scented ointment. Perform the *argha* offering according to the fundamental ritual, fumigating it with incense. One should recite the mantra over the *argha* seven times, and then, having made the invocation, perform the offerings according to the dharma.
"The vessel for the *argha* offering should be made of gold or silver;
alternatively, it may be made of refined copper or fashioned from stone."
Some are made of earth or wood;
some are fashioned from shells;
or they are made of bamboo strips.
Alternatively, one may use lotus leaves to fashion vessels,
or leaves from milk-producing trees;
when employing the aforementioned *argha* vessels and other implements, one must know the proper sequence for their use.
For *śāntika* rites, one should use white vessels;
for *pauṣṭika* rites, yellow vessels;
and for *abhicāruka* rites, black vessels.
To accomplish the superior, middling, and inferior siddhis, one should employ them according to what was previously explained.
For performing śāntika rites, place a small amount of barley in the arghya;
for pauṣṭika rites, sesame seeds should be used.
For ābhicāruka rites, one should place millet;
furthermore, for śāntika rites, one should place milk;
for pauṣṭika rites, one should place curd.
For an ābhicāruka rite, one should place cow’s urine or one’s own blood;

for rites applicable to all [three types], one should use rice-pollen, fragrant ointments, flowers, sesame seeds, and rings of kuśa grass, placing them in a vessel of refined copper filled with arghya water.
If this vessel is unavailable, one may use whatever is at hand for all general purposes.
At the time of invocation, one should employ the mantra of the vidyārāja of the relevant family as well as the mūdrā.
If the fundamental ritual manual already provides a mantra for invocation, one should employ that and not seek another.
First, invite the honored deity of the respective family (*kula*), and next, invite the consort of the vidyārāja; this should be done in the same manner for all three families.
If the fundamental manual lacks a mantra for invocation, one should employ the mantras of the vidyārājas and so forth to perform the invocation.
Although this root ritual explains the mantra for invocation, how could it be appropriate to invoke the Lord of the Family with a subordinate mantra?
If one invokes using the mantra of the root ritual, accomplishment shall be swiftly attained; one should not raise objections.
If this ritual manual includes mantras for invitation and dismissal, at the time of invitation, this mantra-lord shall go to the presence of the Lord of the Family and request:
"Now, [Name], for the sake of such-and-such a matter, respectfully invites... The same applies at the time of dismissal.
"Having completed what was to be done, I pray that the Honored One will bear witness and depart as you please.

To invite the female seers (*ṛṣikā*) and others, one uses the mantra of the Queen of the Vidyārāja; to invite the lords of mantras (*mantranātha*), one uses the mantra of the Vidyārāja. If there are lords of mantras who do not accept the invitation by the mantra of the Vidyārāja alone, one must use both the mantra of the Vidyārāja and the mantra of the Queen of the Vidyārāja; yet, they may still be invited accordingly.

As stated in other sections, when placing the *argha* water, one should recite the mantra: once for a superior [offering], three times for a middling one, seven times for an inferior one, and twenty-one times for the most inferior.

Regarding the *argha* ritual described above: first, with both knees touching the ground, one should place the hands upon a ring of pure *kuśa* grass, hold the *argha* vessel, and while burning incense to perfume it, make this invocation:

"I humbly entreat you, Venerable One, by virtue of your original vow, to descend to this maṇḍala; I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and accept this *argha* and these humble offerings."
“There is a Lord of Mantras named Vikiraṇa-ekajaṭa-krodha, who does not accept invocations by other mantras; one must use the mantra he himself has taught to bring about his descent when invoked.
His various retinues likewise do not accept invitations from other mantras; one should also employ the specific mantras of those retinues to summon them.”

One should perform the invocation using either the Family Heart Mantra (*kulacittamantra*), which is common to all three families, or the Root Mantra or the Mantra spoken by the Queen of Wisdom (*vidyārājñī*).
When employing these for invocation, one should append the syllable *ehi* [to the mantra] so that the deity may descend; this is even more secret and swiftly fulfills one's aspirations.
"When making the invitation, one should prostrate with a sincere heart and address the request three times:
'O Great Compassionate One, please descend to this ritual arena in accordance with your original vow.
If one lacks sincerity, even extensive recitation will be in vain."

Furthermore, one should treat even the mantras with the utmost reverence; holding the arghya vessel with both hands, wearing it upon the crown of the head as an offering constitutes the supreme siddhi;
placing it at the heart constitutes the middling siddhi;
and placing it at the navel constitutes the inferior siddhi.
"First, observe the painted image of the deity.
If the image is standing, the practitioner who recites the mantra should also stand when making the request;
if the image is seated, one should also sit when making the request."
Furthermore, observing that the image stands with its body slightly bent, you should likewise imitate this posture when making your invocation.

At the time of the invocation, first observe the direction in which the Honored One resides and face that direction while inviting; then, turn your body and place the *argha* vessel before the image of the Honored One.

Furthermore, there are secret visualizations for performing *śāntika* and other rites in various locations to invoke [the deity]; or, at other times, when one obtains flowers and fruits that accord with the deity’s preference, one should invite and offer them.

When making the invitation, one should join the palms with the fingers aligned toward their respective directions and invoke them with a sincere heart; alternatively, one may invite them by holding an *argha* vessel with both hands, and thereafter arrange and present the offerings received.
"If one wishes to accomplish superior, middling, or inferior feats, as well as *śāntika* and other rites, one must in all cases employ mantras and *mudrās* to perform the invocation."
If obstacles arise during the performance of various other rites for accomplishment;
or if Māras stir up disturbances;

or if the sufferings of the patient increase—at such times, because the circumstances are urgent and cannot be delayed, one should prepare an *argha* vessel and immediately apply the mind to invoke the *iṣṭadevatā* (chosen deity) to perform the rite of expulsion.

As described above, one should invoke [the deities] with *argha* offerings according to their respective scales when intending to achieve accomplishments; in times of urgent distress and other such matters, one should invoke them with a sincere heart.

Furthermore, if there are those who wish to take refuge in and revere the venerable masters of the various families (*kula*), they should constantly perform the ritual rules for invocation; the practitioner who maintains these recitations will swiftly attain accomplishment.

Chapter 20: The Chapter on Offerings (*Pūjā-varga*) from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, having performed the invocation of the Honored One, one should next proceed according to the respective families (*kula*) or specific rites (*karman*).
Observe their size and make offerings according to the prescribed rules; having completed the invitation, speak these words:
"Welcome, Venerable One!
Out of compassion for us, you have descended to this site of practice; please further show your mercy by accepting this humble offering and taking a seat here."
Again, arising with a sincere heart, he repeatedly prostrated and addressed the Honored One, saying:
"The Great Compassionate One has condescended to appear out of pity and to fulfill my original vow; this was not something I could have requested of the Honored One myself!"
"In this manner, one should rely upon this during all three periods.
As previously stated, one must prepare the offerings: first present the unguents;
next bestow the flowers and so forth, and then offer the incense."
Next, offer food and drink;
next, light the lamps.
Following this sequence, employ the mantra of the Wrathful King (Krodharāja) to purify all these offerings and make them pleasing to the mind, reciting each with its respective original color-mantra.

Having offered the scented unguents, list their names individually; as previously explained, then present the arghya water. In this same manner, the flowers, incense, food, drink, and so forth are all to be treated accordingly.
If one has no unguents, incense, flowers, or food and drink to offer, one should simply recite the respective seed-syllable mantra and perform this hand-seal to present the offering, declaring:
"No offerings could be obtained; I offer only my sincere heart."
"By subsequently performing the *argha* offering with a sincere mind, one's wishes will be swiftly fulfilled.
Apart from these, there are four types of offerings that are universally applicable across all sections and used in every context:
the first is the joining of palms (*añjali*)."
Second, by means of argha;
third, by using mantras and mudrās;
fourth, by merely directing the mind.

Among these virtuous practices, one should act according to one's capacity; or rather, among all forms of long-term offerings, there is none superior to the cultivation of the mind. As the World-Honored One has said, "In the practice of all dharmas, the mind is the foremost. If one can offer worship while directing the mind toward it, all aspirations will be fulfilled.
"If one wishes to accomplish other matters, one should dispatch those who create obstacles;

for if they are not dispelled, they may later cause harm. Therefore, one must first perform the rite of dispatching by reciting the mantra of a wrathful deity, or else using the mantra for accomplishing all matters belonging to the specific family."

Having dispelled the obstacles, one should next recite the mantra of the principal deity of the respective family (*kula*), while using the water consecrated by the mantra to universally invite the fire deity (*agni-deva*) and the *mudrās* associated with the *homa*.
The mantra for inviting the fire deity of the Buddha Family (*buddha-kula*) is: *Oṃ ānāyāhi veśmani vaha svāhā.* Recite this mantra three times to invoke the fire deity to consume the offerings.
The *homa* mantra:

“Oṃ āryānaye svāhā vakhānayā khaṇḍi khaṇḍi nibhaya svāhā. Next, holding cow’s ghee, recite this mantra once for each offering; perform this three times to make offerings to the Fire Deity (*Agnideva*).
The Vajra Family Wrathful Vajra Mantra:
“Oṃ kili kili vajra krodha hūṃ phaṭ. With this mantra, recite it once for each morsel of food and once for each burnt offering.
To dispel obstructors within the ground through ritual procedure, one should again use this mantra or the mantra of the Family Lord (kula-nātha) to sprinkle flowers and other offerings everywhere.

Furthermore, using the mantra and mudrā of the wrathful Kīlikīla, one should recite the mantra while forming the mudrā with the left hand to seal the fragrant ointments, incense, food offerings, flowers, and so forth, thereby purifying them and removing all impurities.

To purify one’s own body, one should cup fragrant water in the right hand; gazing at the water while reciting the Heart Mantra, one should pour it over the crown of one’s head to purify oneself and remove all impurities.

Furthermore, using the Sarvakarmasiddhi-mantra together with the Krodha-mantra, one should sprinkle scented water upon the seat with the mantra for the purpose of purifying it; moreover, reciting it seven times while sprinkling the site establishes the boundary, which can eliminate all impurities and achieve purity.

The Kilikīla Mantra: "Oṃ kili kili padma padmīnute bandha bandha huṃ phaṭ. Having completed the protection of the site with this mantra above, one should bind the boundary of space (*ākāśadhātu*). One should hold incense while reciting the Susiddhi mantra that follows; by fumigating the air with it, all impurities and evils are removed, and it becomes pure.
The Susiddhi Mantra:

“Oṃ susiddhikari jvalita nana munite jvala jvala bandha bandha gona gona huṃ phaṭ. This Susiddhi mantra of the Vajra Family is universally applicable for all rites, including the binding of the boundary (sīmābandha).
The mantra for binding the spatial boundary (kha-dhātu) of the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ jvala huṃ hūṃ. This mantra for binding the spatial boundary of the Buddha Family applies exclusively to its own family.
The Lotus Family mantra for binding the space-element is:
"Oṃ padmamiṇi bhagavati moha ya moha ya jñāna mohani svāhā. This Lotus Family mantra for binding the space-element applies exclusively to the Tathāgata Family.
"Next, one should employ the Family Heart Mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) to sprinkle scented water in all directions.

Then, using either the Root Mantra or the Heart Mantra of the Vidyārāja, or the Heart Mantra of the Lord of the Mantras or his Messenger—whichever is appropriate—one should bind the boundaries of the directions (*dig-bandha*).

Alternatively, one may perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) with these various Heart Mantras; the place thus bound will be like a constructed wall, and the sages and devas of that particular Family will constantly provide protection, such that no one can create obstacles."
If there are matters concerning the various classes [of spirits] that involve conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), one should dispel them by relying on the *Amṛtakuṇḍalī* ritual.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of protective rites that should always be performed within the inner sanctum of the maṇḍala.
That is to say:
the diamond wall;
the diamond city;
The Vajrakīla; the wrathful Kīlikīla;
and the wrathful Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
The Mantra of the Vajraprākāra (Vajra-Wall) Mother of the Family: "Oṃ śara śara vajra-vajraka-ra huṃ phaṭ.
The Mantra of the Vajrapura (Vajra-City): "Oṃ miṣa-pradara-rikṣa vajra-bhañjara huṃ phaṭ. The Mantra of the Vajrakīla (Vajra-Stake):
"Oṃ vajra-kīla hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the wrathful Kīlikīla.
"Oṃ kili kili vajra hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the wrathful Amṛtakuṇḍalī.

"Namaḥ staccatu-jñātāraye | Namaḥ vajra-krodhāya mahā-bala-prakramāya | Sarvabhayopadrava-vināśanāya | Oṃ hūṃ | Huru huru | Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha | Bandha bandha | Gana gana | Amṛtīkuru | Huṃ phaṭ. If within the primary rite there are such mantras as these for the Vajra Wall, they should be bound repeatedly.
When all matters have been concluded, one should next perform the recitation (*japa*).
At the time of recitation, first recite the Mother-mantra (*mātṛ-mantra*) of the relevant family.
The Mother-mantra for the Buddha Family, beginning with the homage, is as follows:
“Oṃ ru ru saphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane svāhā. This is the mantra of the Mother of the Lotus Family; its homage and visualization are the same as those for the mantra of Avalokiteśvara.
“Oṃ karmacandre karmacandre karmakare karmakare karmakarī karmakarī bhagavati mārīce svāhā. This is the mantra of the Mother of the Vajra Family.

“Namo rucikaṭaśriye (1) | Namaḥ saṃkale saṃdhikale (2) | Saṃsaṃsaṃ (3) | Saṃdhini (4) | Kāṭaye saṃdhini (5) | Svāhā (6). First, reciting this mantra of the Mother can protect the *iṣṭadevatā*, eliminate all sins, remove various calamities and obstacles, and bring one into accord with the gateway to *siddhi*. Reciting even the Buddha-family *Māmakī* mantra alone suffices for both families; by reciting it at the beginning and end, the various deities will provide increased protection.
"If that which has already been taught in the root ritual is to be recited, one should first recite this [mantra] and then follow the recitation according to the root ritual;
or, if there is a particularly superior mantra within the root ritual, one should also recite it first, provided it does not involve excessive complexity."

All matters as described above—the sequence of offerings up to the removal of impurities, the protection and purification, and the binding of the boundary—should be performed at the beginning of the recitation, during the performance of ritual acts, and whenever performing rites such as the śāntika.
"Whether by means of the mantra of the Lord of the Family,
or the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) of the Family,
or the mantra of the King of All Mantras;
One may use either the King of Susiddhi Mantras or the Sarvakarmika Mantra.

These five types of mantras are found throughout the three families; for whatever rite one performs, one should select one from its respective family and employ it—namely, for self-protection and protecting companions, summoning, sprinkling water, purification, and binding the boundary, treating them according to the ritual characteristics.
If a mantra is incomplete, it may be supplemented for the sake of increasing its power;

or, for the purpose of subduing a mantra, or for the sake of awakening, as well as for other matters not explicitly described, one should likewise select any one from among the five mantras of the relevant section and employ it, whereby one shall attain siddhi.

"The Family Heart Mantra can protect both the tutelary deity and one's own body; when protecting the body, one should recite it three or seven times, binding the hair on the crown of the head into a single topknot."
If one is a renunciant, one may tie the corners of the *kāṣāya*;
or one may tie a cord and fasten it to protect the body;
or by reciting mantras while touching the five places with the index finger, the protection of the body is likewise accomplished. These five places are as follows:
On the crown of the head, the forehead, both shoulders, below the throat, and over the heart.
One may use either ox-gallstone (*gorocana*) or white mustard seeds.
Alternatively, one may use either argha water or [the aforementioned substances] to protect oneself.
"If performing an ābhicāruka rite, one should protect oneself with the mantra of the Lord of the Family;
if performing a śāntika rite, one should protect oneself with the mantra of the Wrathful Vajra."
If one performs the pauṣṭika rite, one should employ the mantra of the Lord of the Family and the mantra of the Wrathful Vajra to protect it simultaneously.
"If the Mantra Lord appears and the practitioner feels fear, one should employ the mantra of the Lord of the Family to protect oneself;
however, at all times when performing various rites, one should constantly protect oneself with these two mantras, namely:"
Regarding the mantras of the Family Lords and the Wrathful Deities:

when the recitation is completed, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*). At the time of dismissal, one should protect the mantra-lord by using either the mantra of the Family Lord or the mantra of the Family Mother.
Alternatively, one may protect oneself by means of the *kula-citta* (family-heart) and perform the *yathāsukham* (as one pleases).

If one must go to a defiled place, such as an impure location, for some necessary business, one should first recite the *Uṣṇīṣa* mantra and form the mudrā; having sealed the five points of the body, one may proceed as desired, provided that one continues to recite the mantra constantly and does not let it be forgotten.
At the time of bathing, one should first recite the *Vighnāntaka* mantra to protect the body, and this should not be neglected until the bath is completed.
The *Vighnāntaka* mantra is that of the wrathful Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
When eating, one should use the mantra of the Lord of the Family to protect the body while maintaining mindfulness.
When about to lie down, one should protect the body with the *kulamātṛ-mantra*.

If, while performing various rites, one forgets to perform the protective ritual, it will cause demons to arise. To eliminate these demons, one should quickly recite and hold the *vidyārāja-mantra* of the relevant family to guard oneself; thus, no demonic obstacles shall find an opportunity.

"Once one has fully performed the aforementioned rites for protecting the body, establishing the boundary, and other such dharmas, one should then collect the mind and perform the recitation with a serene state of mind.
As for the seat upon which the practitioner sits, it should be made of blue *kuśa* grass; the seat should be four finger-widths high, two spans wide, and sixteen finger-widths long."
Such a seat should be utilized both at the time of the initial recitation and during the period of mantra-holding;
one may use *kāśa* grass, or other green grasses, or,
according to the ritual of the specific family (*kula*), it is most excellent to use wood from a milky sap tree.
The dimensions for making a bed or seat are also as described above, which should be cleared and leveled;

alternatively, one may fashion them from various leaves or branches and stalks as previously prescribed, selecting branches and leaves according to the specific requirements of the situation to serve as a seat.
"Sitting cross-legged upon the seat, one performs the *śāntika* (pacifying) superior accomplishment;
sitting in the half-lotus posture, one performs the *pauṣṭika* (increasing) middling accomplishment;
sitting with both feet hanging down, one performs the *abhicāruka* (subjugating) inferior accomplishment."

"When the offerings have been completed, one should arouse a sincere heart to praise the Buddha; next, praise the Dharma and the Saṅgha; next, praise Avalokiteśvara; and next, praise the Greatly Powerful Vajra of the Vidyārāja!"
The gāthā says:
“O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!
You skillfully guide all sentient beings;”
I now prostrate and pay homage to the ocean of merit held by blessings;
To the Dharma of *śamatha* which is Suchness, Which can purify the poisons of greed and hatred,
And skillfully eliminate all evil destinies— I now prostrate and pay homage.
To the Sangha who has attained liberation through the Dharma,
who dwells well in the stages of training,
and who is a supreme field of merit— I now prostrate and pay homage.
O Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara!
Praised by all Buddhas, you are able to generate manifold merits; I now prostrate and pay homage to you.
O Great Powerful Wrathful Body!
Well done, King of Vidyādharas;
you who subdue those difficult to subdue—I now prostrate and pay homage to you.

"Having thus offered this sincere praise to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should again join the palms with a heart of profound reverence and praise the marks and excellences (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and meritorious virtues of other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the verses for such praise should employ those spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves, and should not be composed by oneself."
Having finished the praise, one should arise from a sincere heart and repent for all transgressions, saying:
"I now take refuge in the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Arhats, Noble Sangha, and all Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions!"

We testify that from the past until our present life, our minds have been shrouded by afflictions as we have long wandered through birth and death; obscured by greed, hatred, and delusion, we have committed various evil deeds toward the Buddha, the Dharma, Bodhisattvas, the noble Sangha, our parents and elders, all sentient beings, and those with or without virtue.

Regarding all the evil deeds and karmic offenses committed in the aforementioned places—whether performed by myself, incited in others, or rejoiced in upon seeing them performed—I now, before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, sincerely repent for the vast accumulation of sins of body, speech, and mind. I repent for every offense created, just as the Buddhas know them to be. Arising with a heart of utmost sincerity, I take refuge for the remainder of my life in the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, the true path to Nirvana; I take refuge in the Triple Gem in order to eliminate all suffering of sentient beings.

Having thus taken refuge and prostrated with the crown of the head, he rejoiced and leaped for joy, generating the bodhicitta and seeking the supreme siddhi of the nectar of liberation, the fruit of Buddhahood:
"I shall rescue the immeasurable sufferings of sentient beings in the world and cause them to leave the evil realms; I shall eliminate their afflictions and enable them to attain liberation.
For all the various oppressions of suffering, I now give rise to great compassion and generate the bodhicitta to act as a refuge for those suffering beings."
They act as a refuge for sentient beings who have no protector;
they act as guides for sentient beings who have lost their way;
and they provide fearlessness to sentient beings who are terrified.

For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to suffering sentient beings, and for the purpose of eliminating the afflictions of sentient beings, I dedicate all the supreme resolve, cultivated wholesome deeds, and the six *pāramitās* arising from the past, present, and future, along with all my merits, entirely to all sentient beings. May they return to the right path, ascend together to the wondrous fruit, and swiftly attain the Buddha-way; until reaching *bodhi*, may I never give rise to indolence, but instead generate the *bodhicitta*, compassionately mind sentient beings, and give rise to great loving-kindness.
When will their manifold sufferings be extinguished?
For the sake of purifying the mind, they should constantly maintain the six recollections; with the mind abiding in a single object without distraction, they should not harbor self-clinging.
Furthermore, just as the Buddhas of the past and present have made vows, one should likewise make vows to give rise to all pure karmas;
to vow that sentient beings may accomplish all virtues;

and further to vow that the merits produced in the past and present may cause all sentient beings to obtain inexhaustible wealth and be able to practice giving, to increase wisdom and achieve great forbearance, to constantly cultivate wholesome qualities, to possess the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and to harbor great compassion—vowing that in every place where these classes of beings are born, they shall be endowed with the matters mentioned above.
"Next, one should join the palms and prostrate to the Honored Lord of the Family, calling to mind the Vidyārāja!
Then, perform all ritual activities according to the prescribed rules.
First, take the rosary with the right hand and place it in the left hand; holding it with palms joined, contemplate the rosary of the Vidyārāja and recite the mantra."
The Mantra for Purifying the Beads of the Buddha Family:
"Oṃ abodhi-miñjaye siddhe siddhārthe svāhā. The Mantra for Purifying the Beads of the Lotus Family:
"Oṃ amṛte laghu-kāri śrīye śrī-mālini svāhā. The Mantra for Purifying the Beads of the Vajra Family:

"Oṃ jili jili lāriṇi svāhā. (One phrase: Oṃ; two phrases: jili jili; three phrases: lāriṇi; four phrases: svāhā). With the right hand, press the tip of the ring finger with the thumb, extend the middle finger straight, and slightly bend the little finger; press the side of the middle phalanx of the middle finger with the index finger. The left hand is done in the same manner. Holding the prayer beads with the right hand is for general use in all applications.
If performing an ābhicāruka rite, one should raise the thumb and form the mudrā of counting the rosary beads.
Bodhi seeds are used for the Buddha family;
lotus seeds are used for the Avalokiteśvara family.
The rudrākṣa seed-bead is for use in the Vajra family;
these types of rosaries are the most excellent for each of the three families, and one should always hold them during all recitations.
Alternatively, one may use wood apple seeds (kataka),
or seeds of the tala tree,
or use earthen beads;
Or use conch beads;
or use crystal; or use pearls;
Or using ivory beads;
or using red pearls;
or various maṇi jewels;

Alternatively, one may use a rosary of throat-beads (*kaṇṭhamaṇi*), or other seeds from various plants, each according to its respective family (*kula*), observing their color and type to select and hold for recitation.

"If performing an *abhicāruka* rite, one should use various bones as the counting beads to swiftly attain accomplishment; furthermore, this serves to provide protection and increase the efficacy of the ritual."
The *dhāraṇī* for holding the rosary of the Buddha Family:
"Oṃ namo bhagavatyai sidhyanti siddhaye siddhiṣṭhe svāhā. The *dhāraṇī* for holding the rosary of the Lotus Family:
"Oṃ sumatiśriye padmamāmalini svāhā. The *dhāraṇī* for holding the rosary of the Vajra Family:
"Oṃ vajra-īdṛñjaye svāhā. Recite this while using the aforementioned bead-seal (mālāmudrā) according to the respective family (kula).
"When reciting, place the rosary at your heart, neither too high nor too low;
when holding the rosary, slightly lower your head and, with a mind of utmost sincerity, prostrate before the Triple Gem."
Next, prostrate to the eight great bodhisattvas;
next, prostrate to the retinue of the vidyārājas.

Next, one should recite the mantra while visualizing the lord of the mantra as if standing before one's eyes. In this way, with such sincerity, one must not allow the mind to be distracted by other objects.

"However, for those mantras that begin with the syllable *oṃ* and the syllable *vaśyakaḷ*, one should perform *śāntika* recitation and *pauṣṭika* recitation with a tranquil mind; these should all be recited slowly or mentally.

Alternatively, for those mantras that end with the syllables *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should know that they are all for the purpose of killing and should be recited with a forceful voice as *abhicāruka* recitation and other wrathful recitations."

"One should examine the number of syllables in the mantras of the three families: if there are fifteen syllables, one should recite them fifteen lakṣas of times; if there are thirty-two syllables, one should recite them three lakṣas; and for those exceeding this number, one should recite ten thousand times."
"When the above number of recitations has been completed as prescribed, one should examine its categories—whether superior, middling, or inferior;
or its three types of matters;
or observe what was taught by the Noble Ones."
It was spoken by the devas;
it was spoken for the sake of the earth-dwelling devas. One should carefully examine its categories and recite and maintain it until accomplishment is attained.

"If one does not first recite it fully and maintain it through mindfulness when performing the initial recitation, even the lower dharmas sought will not be accomplished, let alone the higher or middling siddhis."
For this reason, one should first perform recitation with a superior and exalted mind.

However, when first reciting and holding any mantra as previously described, one should divide the total number of recitations into ten parts; once the recitation is complete, one should then pray to the Lord of Mantras for the causes and conditions of *siddhi*.
If no signs appear, one should again perform the second and third supplications from the beginning;
if signs do appear, one should recite the mantra according to the ritual rules.
If there is no awakening, one should abandon it and not recite.

The rules for the supplication ritual are the same as those for the invocation ritual. When performing the supplication, if one sees the Lord of Mantras in a dream turning his back and departing, or not speaking with one, one must begin the recitation anew; this should be repeated two or three times.
If, in a dream, one sees the Lord of Mantras conversing with one, it should be known that this person will achieve accomplishment before long.
If there is no such sign, one should not perform the recitation; if one were to force oneself to recite, it may bring misfortune upon others.

When first beginning the recitation, one should commence in a clean and secluded place. From the first day of recitation until exhaustion, the number of repetitions must strictly adhere to the fixed requirement and should neither be increased nor decreased.
Regarding the previously mentioned method of recitation during the three periods:
one should perform the recitation during the first and last parts of the day; during the middle part, one should bathe and engage in various virtuous deeds.

The same applies to the three periods of the night; however, during the middle part, one should attend to matters of rest and recuperation, and perform the recitation during the latter part of the night.
"The *ābhicāruka* rite, the *āntardhāna* rite, and the *maitrī* rite are said to be most excellent when performed during the night.
If one performs recitation (*japa*) by day and *homā* by night;
or if one maintains recitation by night and performs *homā* by day, it will be highly effective with many medicinal substances."
One should perform homa before the recitation and again perform homa after the recitation is finished; if one can do so, this is the most excellent method.
As previously stated, one should first offer the *piṇḍa* (ball-food) as a homa offering;

regardless of whether it is before or after, one should always rely on this method for recitation and homa. Alternatively, if within a particular rite success is achieved by performing only homa, one should know that it is still necessary to recite the mantra. If one acts in this manner, the vidyās will be pleased and the signs of spiritual efficacy will be easily accomplished.
"The practitioner should not give rise to anger;
should not seek sensual pleasures;
and should not disparage themselves."
Not being indolent or weary;
not giving rise to fear;
and not seeking with excessive diligence.

Do not give rise to contempt or arrogance. When reciting, do not speak of other matters; even if the body is utterly exhausted, do not let it slacken. Restrain all evil impulses and do not think of worldly conversation. Do not abandon the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity), and even if you see extraordinary signs, you should not regard them as strange. During the time of recitation, do not discriminate among various appearances.

"When the recitation is completed, one should recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family or the mantra of the Mother of the Family; by reciting these mantras, one shall obtain protection and remain unopposed to the laws of the Family."

Having completed the recitation according to the root ritual, even if one exceeds the prescribed number, there is no cause for fear; rather, one should arouse a sincere mind and offer this supplication:
"I have fulfilled the required number of recitations according to the root ritual. I pray that you, O Venerable One, will accept this as my witness and grant me instruction within my dreams."

"When reciting with right mindfulness, if one should cough, become drowsy, yawn, or forget a syllable of the mantra, one should immediately rise, go to water, and perform the ritual of *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling purification). Even if one has counted the beads and is short by only one round, upon encountering such an affliction, once the *prokṣaṇa* is completed, one should begin reciting from the beginning again;
if there was an interruption caused by an obstacle, one must likewise recite from the very start for each instance."
When you have nearly finished counting the beads with your mind, perform one prostration; when it is complete and you begin again,
perform another prostration before the painted image or before the stūpa.
Or, while at one's seat or wherever one recites, for every single circuit of the *mālā*, one should gaze upon the countenance of the Honored One and perform a prostration.
Having finished the recitation, one should settle the mind in pure contemplation, either visualizing the mantra or its presiding deity.

"During the three periods of recitation, one should simply maintain sincere mental attention from the beginning to the middle to the end; the number of recitations should follow the established pattern without increase or decrease.
One should bathe at the three periods, smear the ground at the three periods, and present various offerings such as flowers and fragrant water while removing withered blossoms."
"One should possess the three robes (*tricīvara*).
Furthermore, one should wash the inner robe (*antarvāsaka*) three times each day, drying it, perfuming it, and sprinkling it with water for purification.

During each of these periods, one may perform one of these acts as permitted. One should keep separate garments for sleeping and for bathing; during these two occasions, one changes the inner robe and washes it once daily. When the robe is dry, its perfuming and sprinkling are permitted."
"Offer the *bhadraghaṭa* and other vessels, washing and cleaning them at the three times of day; once withered flowers have been removed, replace them with fresh ones.

At the three times, constantly recite Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and perform the rites of painting mandalas and honoring the *caityas*. First, recite the *sevā-mantra*; once this is completed, if you have not yet attained the desired result, you must not neglect these practices. Whether it be once, twice, or even for a single session, you should maintain the recitation without interruption."

"If one is afflicted by demonic obstacles, illness, or goiters, the body and mind will lack sincerity and become constantly negligent; the body and mind will be exhausted, one will deviate from the proper seasons and fail to follow the ritual rules, or at times fail to bathe, and thus the recitations and *homa* performed will not count toward the required number.
However, if one restrains the mind and practices according to the Dharma while reciting, those counts should be recorded as valid."

"When performing homa, when reciting mantras, and when invoking deities—within these three matters, the number of mantra recitations must each be completed according to the ritual rules. Even if one intends to complete the count, should there be an obstacle arising from falling short by even one, one must begin counting from the beginning again. If one acts without following the ritual rules, nothing will be accomplished."

"If one constructs a maṇḍala according to the ritual, or performs recitation with the addition of mantras during the two occasions of solar or lunar eclipses, one's merit will increase and there is no doubt that accomplishment will be attained before long."
"If one practices at the eight great sacred stūpas, or at the sites where past Buddhas and Bodhisattvas performed their practices—which are most supreme;
or during the fifteenth day of the first month, which is also a most excellent time;
or if one receives the mantra from a preceptor and first performs the preliminary service (*pūjā*), then by reciting and upholding it, one will quickly achieve success before long."
Alternatively, if one sees the Lord of Mantras in a dream and receives instructions from him, one will also achieve accomplishment swiftly according to those rules.

Furthermore, if the practitioner increases their offerings and honors the exalted deity of the site, or applies even greater sincerity during the specific time, the Lord of Mantras will be pleased and grant accomplishment—even if the required number of recitations has not yet been completed—solely because of this excellence.

One should know that although the siddhi of this dharma is swift, it will not endure for long; for this reason, that which is attained after first completing the ritual service is said to be firm and stable.

During the initial period of service, one should perform extensive offerings; furthermore, on the days of solar and lunar eclipses, as well as on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar month, one should additionally present offerings to the assembly of various ṛṣis and devas.

"As other schools teach, on the aforementioned days, one should perform various virtuous deeds such as the observance of fasting (upavāsa) and so forth; on that day, one should further offer oblations to the mantra-lord of the root-vidyā."

Place a vase filled with scented water and insert hanging flower branches; or take an *argha* vessel and consecrate it by reciting the Amṛtakuṇḍalī mantra, sprinkling it upon one’s own crown to eliminate demonic obstacles.
On that day, one must also increase offerings such as various foods and drinks, anointing the *maṇḍala*, performing *homa*, lighting lamps, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding those rites where it is taught that natural signs will appear through mere recitation—if the previously displayed images, śarīra-stūpas, and the like suddenly shake or emit light and flames, one should know that accomplishment will be swiftly attained before long.
"What are the signs when success is attained?
They are as follows:
the body becomes light, and the suffering of illness is forever eliminated;..."
Their superior wisdom increases and their minds become fearless;
the majestic radiance of their bodies manifests as courageous and robust strength;
and in dreams at night they constantly see pure and true things, their minds remaining ever peaceful and secure.
One does not give rise to weariness while reciting and contemplating or when performing activities;
a wondrous fragrance emanates from the body;
or one practices courageous giving and reveres those who are venerable and virtuous.
One should develop deep reverence for the Lord of Mantras.
When signs such as those described above appear at the time of accomplishment, one should know that these are the characteristics of success.

Having first completed the preliminary service according to the ritual rules, one should make offerings to the deity, adding further oblations and performing homa. Once the preliminary service has been completed according to the prescribed number of recitations, one must then perform the recitation for the attainment of *siddhi*. Furthermore, one should first make a prayer and seek an awakening through a dream.

"When performing the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should not move from the place where the recitation for *siddhi* is to be performed. If one must depart due to various obstacles, upon returning to one's residence, one must again perform the preliminary service according to the rules, and only then proceed with the recitation for *siddhi*."

If one does not rely on the aforementioned recitation, one should perform a rite of purification: recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family one thousand times, or otherwise recite the root-holding mantra one hundred thousand times. If one departs from this, one must again perform the preliminary service as previously described.
"If, while reciting with right mindfulness, one suddenly errs and recites another mantra, having recognized the error, one should sincerely repent for the transgression:
'Due to negligence, this error has occurred; may the Honored One forgive this fault.'"
Then, having prostrated with the crown of the head, one must again recite it from the beginning.

If, due to mental laxity, one recites the root mantra in an impure place, one should immediately recognize this and undergo purification. Upon returning to the place of recitation, one should recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family seven times; for half a month, one shall not eat on one day [of each fortnight].
Next, one shall consume the five pure substances after reciting the mantra of the five pure substances one hundred and eight times before partaking of them.
By wearing these five purifiers for half a month, one shall attain purity even while consuming impure food, and the power of the mantras will increase.
The Five Purifier Mantra of the Buddha Family is as follows:
*Namo bhagavate uṣṇīṣāya maitreśvarāya śāntikarāya svāhā.* The Five Purifier Mantra of the Lotus Family is as follows:
“Namo ratnatrayāya | Namo ’ryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya | Oṃ jaya jaya svāhā. This is the five-purification mantra of the Vajra Family.

“Namo ratnatrayāya | Namo śakrabalavardhanaye | Mahāyakṣasenāpataye | Oṃ | Śikhi śikhi | Ṭini marīce | Prave | Prabhāsavari | Dṛḍhe dṛḍhavati | Prabhāvati | Svāhā. Take yellow cow’s milk, curd, ghee, dung, and urine; recite the mantra over each separately one hundred and eight times, then place them together in one location and again recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while placing them in a *pārasa* vessel.

Alternatively, using the leaves of various milk-exuding trees or an *argha* vessel, one should take a bundle of *kuśa* grass and recite the mantra over it one hundred and eight times. Then, facing east and squatting down, one should drink three *akṣas* (approximate measures) at once; this is repeated three times, with the dosage of the medicine increasing by one *akṣa* each time.
While taking [the medicine], one should not engage in conversation.

During the time of recitation, if an image appears or a voice speaks, one should first exercise discernment; immediately recite the mantra and perform the mudrā of the Lord of the Family (kuladevatā). If it is the work of a māra, they will naturally withdraw.
Or, if the speech that emerges differs from the original rite, one should know it to be the work of a māra.
If one utters speech that encourages the commission of evil deeds, this too is the work of Māra.
If one sees an evil dream, one must first recite the mantra of the Mother of the Family (Kulamātṛ) one hundred and eight times;
if one does not first recite the mantra of the Mother of the Family, one must not perform any further recitation.
When reciting, one must not cease even if the count falls short;
there is no fault if it increases.
One must follow the sequence of recitation as described above; if one deviates from this method while seeking *siddhi*, it cannot be attained.

Chapter 21: Increasing Majesty The Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-one: Increasing Majesty Furthermore, I shall now explain how to increase divine majesty and cause [the deities] to rejoice, so that the mantras one maintains will be swiftly accomplished.

First, having bathed the body and head with perfumed water, perform various offerings during the auspicious time of day. Then, take one hundred and eight *sumana* flowers; for each flower, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, seven times, or three times, reciting it according to the number of syllables in the mantra before offering them to the deity.
Next, offer scented unguents, incense, and fragrant substances;
furthermore, offer food and drink as previously described, adding sugar and curd.
Furthermore, perform the homa by burning one hundred and eight pieces of wood, each not exceeding the prescribed measure;
next, perform the homa one hundred and eight times using milk curd mixed with honey;
then, perform the homa one hundred and eight times using ghee and curd mixed with cooked non-glutinous rice.
These three homas should be performed for twenty-one days, or seven days, or five days, or three mornings.
Once these three are completed, one should take milk porridge mixed with cow’s ghee and perform another homa one hundred and eight times.
When that is finished, one should take an arghya vessel, recite the mantra over it one hundred and eight times, pour a small amount of water into it, and perform the homa.
"By performing these rites, the mantras increase in power; that is to say, the power of other mantras is severed, while one's own mantras gain enhancement;
or mantras may be damaged or benefited;
or mantras may be intercepted by a *pāśa* and fail to function."
Or the mantra may be bound by fetters;
or the mantras may be disordered and intermingled;
or syllables of the mantra may be missing.
Alternatively, if there is an increase in the number of mantra syllables, all such afflictions as mentioned above will be entirely eliminated, and one will attain increased majesty.

From among the medicinal herbs described in the various *homā* rites, take any one of them and perform the *homā* with the mantra for one day and night; through this, one will joyfully attain increased majesty.

"Furthermore, take various fragrances and mix them to form a fragrant paste, fashioning the form of the deity. Offer *mālatī* flowers and burn resinous incense or incense from hard wood. Recite the mantra one hundred and eight times during the three periods of the day; the Lord of Mantras will be pleased, and [the practitioner] shall attain increased majesty."

Fashion an image of the Honored One and place it upon a lotus leaf, or a plantain leaf, or a leaf from a milk-tree, or various grass leaves. Offer it not only by day but also by night. When the ritual is completed, dispatch the deity according to the rite and place it in a great river in the sequence described above.
By following this rule, the practitioner’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) will be pleased and swiftly bestow siddhi.

Chapter 22: The Consecration of the Deity from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. Furthermore, once the preliminary services have been completed, if one wishes for the mantra to increase in majesty and power, it should be consecrated.

Take a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or the like, or a new earthenware jar, and fill it with scented water; place within it the five precious gems, flowers, leaves, fruits, incense, the five kinds of grain seeds, and various types of ointments or powdered solid incense.

Tie fresh, colored silk around the neck of the flask, insert branches from various drooping trees or milky sap trees, recite the mantra of the Lord of the Family or the mantra of the Mother of the Family one hundred and eight times, and then sprinkle it upon the crown of the head of the Mantra-Lord.
One should fashion its form out of gold, or from aloeswood or sandalwood, place it upon a pedestal, and perform the consecration.

Once the consecration is completed, one should further present offerings such as flowers and incense, or various necklaces and ritual implements to make offerings to it, while also performing homa and increasing the recitation of mantras.
In this way, the practitioner can cause the deity to increase in power and swiftly attain *siddhi*.

When performing the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) and reciting mantras, one should perform an empowerment for the deity: taking an *argha* vessel marked with the signs of the deity, one should confer the empowerment upon it;
or, when one has finished bathing oneself, one should again visualize the Lord of Mantras and confer the empowerment three or seven times.
During the period of prior service, one should not neglect or forget [the practice], sometimes using milk, sometimes using clarified butter (*sarpis*), or sometimes using honey;

filling a flask with these and placing seven precious gems within it, one should hold it according to the ritual rules and offer it by pouring over the crown of the *iṣṭadevatā*. Thus, whatever difficult objective one prays for will be swiftly fulfilled.
Chapter 23: The Chapter on Entreaty (*Adhyeṣaṇā*) from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. Furthermore, the rules for the extensive procedure of entreaty are explained:

on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of either the waxing or waning moon, or during an eclipse of the sun or moon, one should abstain from food for one day, or for three days, or for seven days; having bathed to become pure, one should don fresh, clean garments.

Those who seek to pray apart from this morning session should perform the prayer during the bright fortnight by reciting the *śāntika* mantra; subsequently, at dusk, they should bathe with various perfumed waters while reciting the mantra to purify themselves and remove all impurities, then sprinkle water on the five places and make offerings to the presiding deity of the root mantra according to the ritual rules.
Again, offer argha water while reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times; sprinkle it with unopened *jāti* flowers and offer it along with sandalwood-scented perfumed water.
Furthermore, extensively present food known as *uṇḍerī*, adding curd to the meal and making an offering of a garland fashioned from *mālatī* flowers.
First, take cow’s ghee and perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings;

next, use *sākṣasā* wood for one hundred and eight *homa* offerings. Have a young girl weave a cord using white cotton thread or cloth thread, making seven knots with each recitation of the mantra. Then, recite the mantra seven times more and tie it upon the left elbow. Lie down on your right side and contemplate the Lord of Mantras.
Having attained mastery over movement and rest, one dwells as one pleases; having arranged a seat of *kuśa* grass and scattered flowers upon it, one visualizes the form of the Honored One.
Within that dream, one sees the Lord of one’s own family (*kula*), or sees the Lord of Mantras (*mantranātha*).
If one sees a vidyārāja, one should know that this is a sign of accomplishment;
or if one sees the Triple Gem;
or if one sees various bodhisattvas.
One may see the fourfold assembly;
or see signs of siddhi from making offerings;
or see oneself reciting and upholding mantras while performing various rites and so forth.
Or one may see oneself wearing pure white garments;
or see others coming to pay respectful homage and make offerings—know that the supreme siddhi is then close at hand.
Or one may see oneself ascending a mountain peak.
Some see themselves riding elephants;
some see themselves crossing great rivers and seas;
some see themselves ascending fruit trees.
Some see them riding lions;
some riding oxen, deer, horses, or other such animals;
and some riding flying geese, peacocks, or all manner of winged birds.
One may see a beautiful woman adorned with necklaces and holding a flower vase;
or one may see oneself walking along a path surrounded by fragrant flowers and canopies;
or one may see receiving elephants, horses, chariots, precious objects, and so forth—seeing such signs are the signs of *siddhi*.

Alternatively, dreaming of obtaining flowers, fruits, roots, cow-ghee, milk, curd, rice-pollen, or similar items are signs of the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the medicinal substances to be perfected.

"During the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), if one dreams of being shown the medicinal substance for accomplishment or obtains a rosary, one who attains such a sign should know that they must immediately perform the recitation ritual."
Or one may see oneself being perfumed;
or see oneself bathing and becoming pure;
or see oneself wearing necklaces and ornaments. Having seen these signs, one should perform recitation, and *siddhi* will be swiftly attained.

"To perform the rite of recitation, take one hundred and eight *jāti* flowers and, using the *mūlā-devī* mantra together with the root mantra, recite them in unison one hundred and eight times as an offering;
furthermore, recite the mantra for white sandalwood one hundred times. Having thus made this petition, sleep at will, and the Lord of the Root Mantra shall manifest signs of his presence."

Furthermore, take *uśīra* root, grind it, and fashion an image of the Mantra Lord. Prepare a vessel by mixing *ulmuka* ant-earth with cow’s milk and fill it completely; place the image within the milk. Alternatively, mix clarified butter (*sarpis*), milk, and honey, and place them in the vessel. Set the image therein and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, making offerings at the three periods of the day. By making such offerings, the Honored One will be pleased and signs of success will swiftly appear.

Furthermore, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, or on the day of a solar or lunar eclipse, one should observe the fast by abstaining from food and perform extensive offerings.
