Using each of the seven resinous incenses and the five solid incenses individually, one should recite the mantra once and perform one *homa* offering for each. Once the count reaches one thousand two hundred times, the signs of the fulfillment of one’s prayers will swiftly appear before you.
If one performs the ritual of supplication according to the rules, accomplishment will be swiftly attained; seeing these signs, one should have no doubt.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Receiving Mantras. *Susiddhikara Tantra*, Chapter Twenty-Four: Receiving Mantras. "Furthermore, the method for receiving mantras shall be explained in detail."

Kneeling with both knees on the ground, first perform extensive acts of giving before the Venerable Ācārya. Holding exquisite flowers in your hands, generate a heart of earnest devotion and receive the mantra orally from the Ācārya three times. If it is too voluminous to be received through oral recitation, you should write it down using paper and ox-gall ink; having received it, recite it as you please.

“Once one has first entered the maṇḍala, if at a later time they wish to receive the mantra, they should perform extensive offerings to the venerable ācārya on an auspicious day and receive it as before; by receiving the mantra in this correct manner, it will be swiftly accomplished. Even if one has not previously performed the rite of service (*sevā*), one may still achieve accomplishment simply by reciting it.”

Furthermore, using a new vessel free from defects, place flowers, leaves, the seven treasures, and the five grains therein, each according to the ritual rules, but do not add water; with a heart of utmost sincerity, perform extensive offerings.

The ācārya first takes paper leaves and writes down the names of the various mantra-lords, placing them inside a flask; he then performs the adornment and offerings according to the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
While performing this rite, he shall observe fasting and precepts for either one day or three days.

At twilight, take cow bezoar and write out the names of the various mantras, placing them inside a flask; offer it with ointments, flowers, lamps, and food, and perform one hundred and eight homa offerings using the root mantra, while diligently and extensively supplicating the noble assembly to listen attentively.

When three days have passed, one should first cause the disciple to bathe until the body is pure and fragrant. Placing an auspicious *kuśa* grass ring upon the hand, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over it, consecrate the flask with the mantra, and fumigate it with incense. Bowing down with a devoted heart, one should cause the disciple to take a leaf and then prostrate once more;
by receiving [the teaching] in this manner, the recipient will swiftly attain *siddhi*. If one recites other mantras instead, the *siddhi* of the mantra received will be lost.

If, out of joy toward the disciple, one bestows the *siddhi-mantra* that one personally maintains, the disciple should receive it according to the ritual rules and in accordance with the Dharma; because they have previously recited and held it, the disciple shall attain *siddhi* before long.
"First, at the abode of the Lord of Mantras, offer a petition and request that he bestow this mantra upon this disciple, vowing to grant his protection and swiftly confer *siddhi*.
Holding incense and flowers in one's hands, recite it one hundred and eight or one thousand times, then call the disciple forward and transmit it to them."
He should further say:
"At this time, I now bestow [this disciple] upon you, the original Lord of Illumination; I pray that you will take note and grant me *siddhi*.
The disciple should then say:
"I have now received the Illustrious Lord; from this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I vow never to forget him.

As stated above, when a master and disciple receive the mantra-dharma in this manner, they shall attain accomplishment (*siddhi*). Those who receive it otherwise shall not obtain *siddhi*. Thus, one who receives the mantra for attaining *siddhi* in this way will certainly achieve accomplishment therein, without a doubt.
"Just as with mantras, where one may attain *siddhi* without prior service, so it is with the methods for receiving medicinal substances and other such items for *siddhi*.

Alternatively, there may be someone who, having first performed the service and subsequently engaged in recitation and retention (*dhāraṇī*), transmits the method to another according to the rules; the recipient, though not having performed prior service, shall attain accomplishment simply by performing recitation and retention."

"Those who receive mantras, for the sake of attaining *siddhi*, should first extensively offer at the abode of their preceptor flowers, fruits, various roots, renowned garments and fine robes, gold, silver, *maṇi* gems, various miscellaneous precious objects, diverse grains and wheat, ghee, honey, milk, and curd, male and female servants, various bedding, exquisite leather sandals, ornaments for the body, already perfected medicinal herbs, elephants, horses, oxen, calves, and other vehicles—even their own bodies—offering them as servants to be employed. Having served for a long time without fearing toil, they should offer with palms joined in devotion, with reverence and care; by practicing such giving, one quickly attains *siddhi*."
As extensively explained above regarding these various items, one must first offer them to the Ācārya before receiving the sublime phrases of the mantra.

Chapter Twenty-five: Fulfilling the Mantra *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-five: Fulfilling the Mantra Furthermore, if the practitioner of recitation sees the body of the Mantra Lord in a dream, they should know that if the limbs are added, the syllables of the mantra have been added;
if the limbs are diminished, they should know that the syllables of the mantra are deficient. Having thoroughly examined these signs, one should perform the rite of fulfillment.
If one perceives that the mantra differs from that which was received and upheld—
whether by having more or fewer syllables— and doubt arises in the mind, one should perform the rite of fulfillment according to the dharma.

First, write down the erroneous mantras using paper and ox-gall on a thin surface. Having performed the ritual offerings and protections for the Mantra King and his mantras according to the dharma, place them upon the seat of the Lord of Mantras. Then, taking firewood and following the original rite, one should perform homa using only clarified butter (ghṛta) to provide assistance in seeking the Mantra King.
Spread mats of *māo* grass and first pay homage to the Honored Master of the Rites Department;
next, pay homage to the Mother of the Rites Department;
then pay homage to all Buddhas, making this invocation:
"May all Buddhas and the assembly of noble ones grant their assistance and protection.
Having made this request, he lies down upon a bed of *kuśa* grass with his head facing east.

In his dream, the deity manifests a sign: upon the paper written with bezoar, there are additions and omissions; the deity then uses bezoar to annotate the text so that the number of characters is complete, even correcting the strokes and dots until they are perfectly established. He finds that the mantra is unerring—though it may simply be said to be "unerring"—or the deity instructs him directly within the dream until the practice is perfected.
When performing this rite, one should perform protective rites (*rakṣā*) in order to eliminate māras.

Chapter Twenty-Six: Increasing Power. From the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Six: Increasing Power. "Furthermore, if one wishes to increase one's majestic power (*prabhāva*), one should perform *homā*."
Alternatively, one may perform the rite separately using either ghee and honey or milk;
or one may perform the homa by mixing sesame seeds with ghee;
or one may perform the homa by mixing resinous incense with ghee.
Alternatively, one may perform homa with lotus flowers mixed with ghee;
or at times, use *sajjārasa* alone. Or, dwelling among the mountains, one may constantly consume the five pure substances (*pañcāmṛta*) and abstain from other food.

Taking one hundred thousand petals of the flower belonging to one's own *kula*, one should offer each one to the deity while reciting the mantra. With excellent unguents, incense, flowers, lamps, food, and so forth, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times for each offering. Performing this three times a day for three days constitutes such an offering that it increases one’s spiritual power.
Alternatively, one may burn hard wood as a lamp for three periods each day over the course of seven days; this will cause the mantra’s power to increase.
Or, at times, making offerings of *kāmika* food will likewise increase its power.
The rules for recitation, homa, and offering as described above can likewise increase their power.
Chapter 27: Homa. In the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Seven on Homa: "Furthermore, the extensive explanation of the rules for homa shall enable the practitioner to swiftly attain siddhi."
In front of the honored image, construct a homa hearth, one cubit square with sides of equal length and a depth of half a cubit; if a circular hearth is made, its dimensions shall be the same.

"If the place for recitation is within a private chamber, one should go outside; there, facing the image of the Honored One, one should construct a hearth and perform the rites according to the dharma, in accordance with the specific activity."

Place items such as milk-wood and fragrant flowers on the right side, and arrange the four *homa* vessels on the left. Using the *sarvakarmika-mantra*, sprinkle all the materials. Sitting upon a seat of *kuśa* grass, concentrate the mind in meditative absorption and hold the *argha* vessel while invoking the Vidyārāja. Pour a small amount of the *argha* water into the fire pit, and then offer one flower with the recitation of the mantra to the Lord of Mantras.
To remove defilements, one should recite the Kīlikīlī mantra and perform the hand gestures;
for protection, one should sprinkle water with the Mañjuśrī-mañjughoṣa (Muṇḍarī) mantra to purify the area and kindle the fire with wood soaked in milk.
Once the fire has been kindled, first invite the Fire Deity (Agni), saying:

"I now respectfully invite the foremost of fire deities, the immortal among gods, who is honored by those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya); please descend to this place and accept this homa offering."
Next, recite the mantra for summoning the Fire Deity as above.

Having summoned the Fire Deity, first purify with *argha* water three times; then take pure five-grains, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), curd (*dadhi*), and other substances, and while reciting the mantra, perform the homa offering three times to worship the Fire Deity.
The mantra is the same as that for the fire deity’s food offering; with single-minded concentration, visualize the welcoming and sending off of the fire deity and place him upon his original seat.
Thereafter, recite the *Kilikili* mantra and perform the hand gesture (*mudrā*) to purify the fire once again.
All homa rites should be performed in this manner.

Next, invite the principal deity and first recite the deity’s mantra once; then, remaining seated upon your own seat, perform the offerings according to the ritual rules, praying that the Honored One graciously accept the food of the homa.
"The wood for the homa ritual consists of:
palāśa wood, udumbara wood, plakṣa wood, nyagrodha wood, khadira wood, arka wood, vikaṅkata wood, aśvattha wood, kāśmarī wood, śamī wood, apāmārga wood, and aśvatthīna wood."

"Regarding these twelve kinds of wood, take branches measuring two finger-widths in length and one joint in width, all of which must be moist; those freshly harvested may be used for all *homa* rites.

Select branches that are straight and observe that they are uniform from top to bottom. Place them in scented water and wash them thoroughly. With the fine end pointing outward and the coarse end toward oneself, dip both ends in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and cast them into the fire-pit."

When performing each of the rites, such as the śāntika and others, one should first offer a ball of food (piṇḍa) according to the specific procedure of that rite and perform homa; this ritual pattern applies universally to all.
"When preparing food each day, first set aside one portion of the meal and place it before the Honored One; this should be taken for use at the time of *homa*.
When performing recitation (*japa*), place it between both hands in the space between the knees; it should be done likewise during *homa*."

Take a piece of agalloch wood four finger-widths long and as thick as the index finger; smear it with *sugandhaka* resin and perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings. This rite is profound and subtle, enhancing the majesty of the mantra.
"When performing it in this manner, it is universally applicable to all sections of the Tantras. One may perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings using *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter;
or at times, one may perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings using only *sajjarasa*. Both methods are capable of augmenting the majestic power (*prabhāva*) of the mantra."

"To accomplish the mantra-dharma, one performs various homas: first, one invites the Lord of the Family (*kuleśvara*), then invites the Principal Deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), and thereafter performs the homa according to the ritual rules.

To accomplish the mantra-dharma, one performs various homas: first, one uses the mantra of the Family Mother (*kula-mātṛ*) to protect the Principal Deity and then protects oneself, and thereafter performs the homa according to the ritual rules.

To accomplish the mantra-dharma, one performs various homas; when the rite is concluded, in order to augment the power of the mantra, one should recite the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*) of the Family."

In order to accomplish the various mantra rites, one performs homa; at the beginning, one must always use the large ladle for pouring and offering, and when the rite is about to conclude, one likewise uses the large ladle, while during the intervening period, one should use the small ladle.
To accomplish the mantra rites, if the ritual is concluded, one employs the Family Heart Mantra (kula-hṛdaya-mantra) to offer water from the arghya vessel as an oblation.
"As it is taught in the *maṇḍala* ritual, the sequence of the *homa* rites should also be performed in this manner.
First, perform the *abhicāruka* rite;
next, perform the *puṣṭika* rite."
Next, perform the śāntika rite.
Once the homa is completed, take pure water consecrated with the root mantra and sprinkle it from a distance around the hearth three times.

"When the homa is completed, once again address the Fire Deity to receive further offerings; perform the ritual service according to the dharma, then dismiss and send him back while fulfilling his vows. Just as in the rite of invocation, replace the word for 'descending' with the word for 'returning'."
Take the remaining grains, ghee, honey, curd, and so forth, and mix them together in one place; perform *homa* by reciting the mantra for the fire deity three times;
then recite the root mantra according to its specific number of syllables;
finally, perform offerings and provide protection for the deity, protect yourself, and perform the ritual dismissal according to the dharma.
28. Chapter on Requisite Articles, the Twenty-eighth of the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, the various branches of accomplishment shall be explained in detail.
That is to say, in order to accomplish all mantras, one should first prepare various miscellaneous items and subsequently perform the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*).
If one has already performed the preliminary service, one should next engage in recitation, namely:
various types of ointment incense (*vilepana*) and various types of burning incense (*dhūpa*).
"The five kinds of solid incense are:
aloeswood, white sandalwood, red sandalwood, *sāla* wood, and celestial wood (*devadāru*).
The seven resinous incenses are:"
Gandharasa incense, sārjarasa incense, guggulu incense, spṛkkā incense, turuṣka incense, śallakī incense, and śrīveṣṭaka incense.
White mustard seeds, poison, salt, black mustard, sesame, oil, cow’s ghee, a copper vessel, and a copper tray.
“The five grains are:
barley, wheat, rice, mung beans, and sesame.”
"The five treasures are:
gold, silver, pearls, conch shells, and red pearls.
The five medicines are:"
The *khaṇḍakārikā* medicine, the *vṛhatī* medicine, the *saha* medicine, the *sahadevā* medicine, and the *śitānīlikā* medicine with honey.
“The Five-Colored Thread” states:
blue, yellow, red, white, and black.

“The youth [prepares] the thread, a vajra-lamp, a wick-lamp, a clay lamp-stand, the five kinds of colored pigments, a *khadira* wood peg, branches of milky sap trees, a stand of *kṛmuka* wood, a large ladle, a small ladle, ox-gallstone (*gorocanā*), forged steel, red sandalwood, a purification-thread, a bathing robe, a black antelope skin, *pāṭala* flowers, *śāli* rice flowers, wooden sandals, *cāṅgerī* grass, *mahādarbha* grass, and *saptaparṇa* incense—these are for the flower basket.”

One should prepare in advance all the various items mentioned above, such as those required for food and drink—namely ghee, honey, granulated sugar, rock sugar, and so forth—as well as a rosary; thereafter, one should perform the preliminary service and engage in extensive recitation.

Chapter Twenty-nine: On the Characteristics of Accomplishing Various Objects. *Susiddhikara Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-nine: On the Characteristics of Accomplishing Various Objects. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the objects of accomplishment, which are based upon the *siddhi* of the mantras of these three families. They are as follows:
the *cintāmaṇi*, the auspicious vase (*bhadraghaṭa*), raining jewels, hidden treasure (*nidhi*), the wheel, yellow orpiment, and the sword."

These seven substances are the most supreme among the superior; they can bring about the accomplishment of all various *siddhis*, increase merit and virtue, and even lead to the full realization of the Dharma of the Dharma-King—how much more so regarding other worldly matters?
The mantras of the three families—the Buddha Family, the Lotus Family, and the Vajra Family—all possess such supreme accomplishments.
Whichever of these three families one practices and upholds, one will fully attain the five supernormal powers as the highest *siddhi*.

"Regarding the 'seven items': if one wishes to accomplish the Cintāmaṇi, once the ritual efficacy has been achieved, one should fashion a golden pedestal measuring one cubit in length, or alternatively, one may use silver to make it finely adorned. One should place a maṇi-jewel atop the pedestal; this jewel should be made of red crystal, radiant and free of blemishes, or fine crystal, perfectly rounded according to the rite. Having prepared this treasure, one should recite the mantra at night while drawing the pattern of the pedestal."

"If one wishes to accomplish the rite for raining down jewels, once the efficacy of the rite has been established, by merely maintaining a sincere heart, one will be able to cause gold, silver, and various kinds of miscellaneous jewels to rain down within a radius of five *yojanas*."

"If one wishes to accomplish the dharma of hidden treasures (*nidhi*), once the efficacy of the rite has been realized, one should simply, with a sincere heart, cause the treasure to arise at whatever place is intended. It shall provide gold, silver, and various jewels to relieve the poor; though used for all manner of expenses, the treasury will never be exhausted."

"If one wishes to accomplish the Wheel-Rishi rite, one should fashion a wheel from tempered iron, measuring two finger-widths in diameter and one span (vitasti) in circumference; the wheel should be provided with six spokes and a sharp, well-finished rim. By performing the ritual in this manner, one will swiftly attain *siddhi*."

"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of yellow orpiment, one should take 'radiant orpiment'—its color and light like those of the rising sun, or like the golden light of molten gold; this is considered the finest quality."

"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the sword, one should take a fine blade of bīḍāla-iron measuring two cubits in length, as wide as four fingers when measured by the little finger, free from all defects, and blue-black in color like the throat of a śikhaṇḍin bird."

"If one wishes to accomplish the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa rite, one should fashion a Buddha-uṣṇīṣa out of gold, like a painted seal, and place it upon a pedestal; the frame of that pedestal should be made of *sphaṭika* (crystal) gem."
"If one wishes to accomplish the Lotus Dharma, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus from gold, measuring two finger-widths or one span (vitasti);
or it may be made of silver; or of refined copper; or of white sandalwood."

"If one wishes to accomplish the Vajra rite, one should fashion a vajra from high-quality blade-iron sixteen finger-widths in length, with three prongs at each end; or it may be made of red sandalwood;
or it may be made of the Three Jewels, namely:
gold, silver, or refined copper."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of realgar, one should take realgar that is the color of molten gold, which breaks into pieces and emits light; such realgar can accomplish this supreme matter."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of ox-gallstone (*gorocanā*), one should take the gallstone of a yellow cow as the best.
If one wishes to accomplish the *karikā* medicine, one should take that medicine which is the color of a *dīnāra* flower as the finest."
"If one wishes to accomplish the *sru-ta-anjana* medicine, that which resembles earthworm dung is the best.
If one wishes to accomplish white cotton cloth, take fine and soft material, remove all hair and down, and dye it with saffron."

"If one wishes to accomplish the protective cord (*rakṣāsūtra*), take fine threads of white cotton and twist them into three strands; then, combine these three strands into a single rope and have a young girl spin it together. All must be twisted to the right, or the threads must be entirely combined in that manner."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of flower garlands, one should take *jāti* flowers to make a garland.
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of cow-dung ash, one should take clean cow dung from a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), burn it to make white ash, and mix it with *kakkola* (camphor) incense."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the wooden sandal, one should take śrīparṇī wood to fashion the sandal and place a cover upon it.
If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the parasol, it should be made from peacock feathers, with its handle fashioned from fresh, high-quality bamboo."
"If you wish to accomplish bows, arrows, spears, lances, single-bladed swords, clubs, and various other weapons for use according to worldly custom, you may fashion them as you please.

"If you wish to accomplish worldly items such as saddled horses, chariots, cattle, sheep, and all manner of birds and beasts, or any other objects that people commonly regard as superior, you may fashion them according to your inclination, or produce them in accordance with the original ritual method."

"If one wishes to accomplish the Vetāla, one should take the corpse of one born of a noble family, who died suddenly in the prime of youth from illness, whose body is free of scars, which has not yet begun to bloat or decompose, and whose sense faculties are intact; having taken such a corpse, one should perform the accomplishment."
Whatever rites one performs—whether superior, middling, or inferior—the objects to be taken are likewise so; one should perform these rites only when the mind is free from fear.
Chapter 30: Chapter on Taking Objects from the Susiddhikara Sūtra. "Furthermore, I shall now explain the method for taking objects.
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the waxing and waning moon, at the time of a solar eclipse, or on days when the earth trembles—one should take those objects before noon;
or, having attained a state of mental alertness during recitation, one should take the various objects;
or, having bathed for purification, abstaining from food and observing the fast while seeking a state of virtuous alertness, one should take the various objects.
Regarding the requisites mentioned, one should go to wherever such items are available and acquire them at a high price, even if they do not match the value;
or, at times when one perceives an increase in one's own power and is able to endure various conditions such as hunger and cold, one should acquire the requisites at that time.

Regarding the various items to be taken, each should be selected according to its inherent quality—superior, middling, or inferior—and one should take only those that are excellent; having obtained them in accordance with the Dharma, one should apply diligent effort to perform the rite of accomplishment.

Chapter 31: The Chapter on Purification Furthermore, I shall now explain the ritual methods for purifying various objects. Those that should be washed are cleansed with the five purifiers; those that should not be washed are sprinkled with the five purifiers.
Observe the proportions of the various substances: grind the five purifying agents into powder;
grind realgar with milk into powder;
grind cinnabar with cow’s urine into powder.
"Powdered ox-gall mixed with *sū* should be blended with colored pigments and milk;
however, the *āñjana* medicine should be prepared as a powder alone.
Objects such as knives and wheels are washed with water mixed with cow dung; other items mentioned that require washing should first be washed with cow urine."
Next, wash with sesame-water;
next, wash with scented water.

Whatever other items are commonly used in the world should likewise be washed with water, or after washing with scented water, they should be consecrated by sprinkling them with water empowered by the various ritual mantras.
Next, purify by sprinkling water with the Family Heart Mantra;
next, purify by sprinkling water with the Family Mother Mantra.
Those things that ought to be washed should first be cleansed with the five pure substances, followed by washing with sesame-water.
Next, they shall be washed with scented water; whatever requires purification should be treated in this manner. **Chapter Thirty-Two:

On the Quantities of Materials** *The Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-Two: On the Quantities of Materials* "Furthermore, to explain in detail the quantities of materials for accomplishment: the materials for accomplishment refer to bodily ornaments, various weapons, and diverse garments according to worldly custom. Regarding the measures used, one should prepare fine powders to perform the rite of accomplishment."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of realgar:
five *liang* is the superior method, three *liang* is the middling method, and one *liang* is the inferior method.
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of ox-gallstone:"
One *liang* is the superior method; half a *liang* is the middling method; one *fen* is the inferior method.
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of realgar (*manaḥśilā*), two *liang* is the superior method; one *liang* is the middling method; half a *liang* is the inferior method."
"If one wishes to accomplish the *añjana* rite:
three parts constitute the superior method, two parts the middling method, and one part the inferior method.
"If one wishes to accomplish the *ghṛta* (clarified butter) rite:"
Seven *liang* constitute the superior method; five *liang*, the middling method; and three *liang*, the inferior method.
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of ashes:
five *liang* constitute the superior method; three *liang*, the middling method; and two *liang*, the inferior method."
"If one wishes to accomplish the rite of saffron:
its measure is comparable to that of realgar.
Regarding the various medicinal pills for accomplishment taught in the *Antardhāna* rites:"
Regarding the number [of pills], twenty-one pills constitute the superior method, fifteen pills the middling method, and seven pills the inferior method.

Within these fundamental methods, if the quantities of the various substances are small, one should increase their numbers; otherwise, one may follow the total quantity or adhere strictly to the original method.

Alternatively, one may follow what is esteemed by the world regarding the quantity and number [of recitations], taking into account the power of one’s contemplation and recitation as well as the number of companions; one should be fully prepared, and through the vast state of the blessings and intimacy of the *iṣṭadevatā*, any accomplishment whatsoever may be achieved.
The methods for *siddhi* are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior; the quantities of various substances are likewise so.

Chapter Thirty-Three: The Consecration Mandala. From the Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-Three: The Consecration Mandala. "Furthermore, I shall explain in detail the secret and wondrous rites for accomplishing all substances, so that *siddhi* may be swiftly attained."

If one wishes to begin the practice of the *sādhana*, one should first prepare all the requisites for *siddhi*; empower the mantra of the tutelary deity and perform self-consecration through the *homa* rite, and construct a consecration maṇḍala, making offerings according to the ritual rules.

Having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should then commence the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*). If one constructs a great consecration maṇḍala, one will be able to accomplish all matters; as previously explained, the methods for the King of Mantras (*vidyārāja*), the maṇḍala, the purification of the site, and so forth, should all be conducted in this manner.

That maṇḍala is square with four corners and four gates; its dimensions are eight cubits, or seven, or five. Only the western gate is opened. The boundary paths are decorated in five colors according to the ritual rules, matching the proportions of the central terrace; those on the next outer layer are reduced by half, and the subsequent layers follow the same principle.

"To the west of this, four cubits away, construct another maṇḍala measuring five, four, or three cubits, opening only the eastern gate; or it may be made at half the size of the location for the consecration of the fundamental great maṇḍala."
In general, it is taught that for the layout of a maṇḍala, having the ground slope toward the north is auspicious;
however, when the maṇḍala ground slopes toward the north, it is said to be the most excellent.
"Alternatively, one may paint it using a single color; outside the four corners, one should fashion a three-cubit *vajra*;
within the central platform, one should paint an eight-petaled lotus according to the ritual rules. All maṇḍalas should be treated in this same manner."
Around the perimeter outside the lotus petals, draw auspicious and wondrous seals;
within the four gates, draw vajras;
furthermore, at each corner, draw a bhadraghaṭa (auspicious vase); do likewise for the outer abhiṣeka maṇḍala.

"Those who wish to perform the consecration must have four types [of vases]. The locations where the vases are placed should all guard the corners of the boundary. According to the mantras and vidyās being recited, one should draw the seal (mudrā) of the principal deity within the pedestal and place a vase there;

according to the class of the mantra being used, one should draw the seal of the Lord of that Family—namely, those of the Buddha-Crown, Lotus, or Vajra families. It should be known that this rite is most secret."
"If one does not know the names or the families (*kula*) of the mantras one possesses, nor has mastered them, one should place a single flask named 'Discerning All Affairs' (*sarvakarmaprasādhana*);
or place a flask for accomplishing aims and benefits (*siddhārtha*);
or place a single flask named 'All Mantras' (*sarvamantra*)."
"Next, on the outer eastern side, paint the seal of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa.
On its right side is the seal of the Family Mother (Kulīśvarī), and on its left side is the seal of the Family Heart (Kulahr̥daya);
next to the right is the seal of Śakti, and next to the left is the seal of the Tooth."
Next, to the right of Ānanda, and next to the left of Subhūti,
the seals of all other mantras and vidyās are to be arranged on the left and right, extending even to the two corners.
Next, on the northern side, draw the seal of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
On the right is the mudrā of the Mother of the Family; on the left is the mudrā of the Heart of the Family.
Next on the right is the mudrā of Lokeśvara; next on the left is the mudrā of Tārā.
Next on the right is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Amoghasiddhi; next on the left is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The various other mantras, vidyās, and mudrās are to be arranged on the left and right, extending even to the two corners.
Next, on the southern side, draw the Vajra-mudrā; on its right side, the Kula-mātṛ-mudrā, and on its left side, the Kula-hṛdaya-mudrā;
next, on the right, the Vajra-muṣṭi-mudrā, and on the left, the Vajrabhakṣa-mudrā.
Next, on the right, place the Vajra mudrā; next, on the left, place the Vajradaṇḍa mudrā.
Arrange the mudrās of all other mantras and vidyās on the left and right, extending even to the two corners.

"Next, on the south side of the western gate, paint the seal of Brahmā and the Vidyārāja Brahmaśrī along with their retinues; continuing thus, until the north side of the southern corner gate, paint the seal of the deity Rudra and the seal of his consort, along with their retinues;
and so on, until the third maṇḍala gate of the north corner, where the deities of the eight directions are painted, each with their respective retinues, filling their assigned positions."
"Outside the gate of the second maṇḍala, paint Nanda the Nāga King on the right side and Upananda the Nāga King on the left side;
outside the gate of the third maṇḍala, paint Sunanda the Nāga King on the right side and Upasunanda the Nāga King on the left side."
Outside the maṇḍala, draw the seal of the amṛta-flask.
"One who performs the ritual worship of the maṇḍala in this manner should perform three kinds of homa according to the dharma."
One should perform the *abhicāruka* rite for the purpose of expelling *vināyakas*;
one should perform the *puṣṭika* rite for the sake of one's own benefit;
and one should perform the *śāntika* rite for the purpose of pacifying all calamities.

"One should perform the *ābhicāruka* rites using the mantras for accomplishing various tasks belonging to one's own respective family; alternatively, one may use the Amṛtaghaṭa mantra, which is applicable to all three families.
One should perform the *pauṣṭika* rites using the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) of one's own respective family;
and one should perform the *śāntika* rites using the mother-mantra (*mātṛkā*) of one's own respective family."
"Within the maṇḍala, all the noble deities assembled there should each perform three kinds of homa using their respective root mantras;
or they may perform homa using the mantra that accomplishes all matters."

"At the site of the homa, one should perform it to the east of the southern gate of the maṇḍala according to the homa ritual. Regarding substances such as ghee and others, one should offer them one hundred times for each of the three types of mantras—or increase that number—in order to augment the power of the various mantras; thus, one should perform these three kinds of homa.

Next, one should offer seven times for each of the mantras of the three families, though the lords of the three families should have their offerings increased in number. Alternatively, one may simply offer one hundred times for each of the three families; if one cannot distinguish [the specific requirements], offering seven or even three times will suffice."
"The mantra-holders he carries should be placed within the interior of the maṇḍala below the principal deity; outside the maṇḍala,
Hārītī is separately installed on the eastern side,
Śūlinī on the southern side, and Aikāśīrṣa on the western side."
To the north, one should place Kuṭa-kṣeli and offer them according to their preferences.
Having performed the ritual offerings to the mantras and the homa as prescribed, one should empower the previously placed water jar used for its intended purpose by reciting its respective mantra;
likewise, one should empower the jar placed before the deity by using that same mantra.
The vases within the pavilion should be consecrated using the mantras of the Vidyārājas;
likewise, the vase installed by Kuṇḍalī at the entrance must also be consecrated with his mantra.
Regarding the vases placed at the two corners on the eastern side of the terrace maṇḍala: for the northeast corner, use the Family Heart Mantra;
for the southeast corner, use the Family Mother Mantra;
and for the northwest corner, use the Mantra Capable of Accomplishing All.
For the southwest corner, one should use all mantras.

Having thus empowered this superior vase and having made offerings, one should next circumambulate it to the right; as previously described for the method of empowerment, one should likewise install the auspicious vase (śrī-kalaśa) in this manner.
That is to say:

grains, medicinal herbs, flowers, fruits, branches and leaves of fragrant trees, flower garlands, and jewels are placed within the vase, which is then wrapped around its neck with new silk and brocade.
All consecration rites should be performed in this manner.

One should then have a companion consecrate the practitioner on the crown of the head; these companions must all maintain the recitation of mantras and be pure according to the Dharma, or one may request the Ācārya to bestow the consecration upon them.
In order to dispel all obstacles to one's practice, one should first perform the consecration using the Krodha-ṭaṇḍala jar;
fourth, one should perform the consecration using the jar containing the specific mantra to be practiced, while the remaining two jars may be used as one pleases.
When this is completed, one should utilize cow bezoar, unguents, incense, mustard seeds, thread bracelets, and garments.
Having performed the consecration, one should again perform a *homa* offering for the sake of pacifying all obstacles, and then immediately dismiss [the deities].

Alternatively, in a pure location, one may construct a small maṇḍala using only a single color, ensuring it is perfectly square and measuring two cubits in size. Therein, one should place the great mudrās of the three families; on the western side, the spear mudrā (*śakti-mudrā*) should be placed as before. By conferring empowerment according to the ritual with a pure flask, one will be freed from all obstacles, the tutelary deity will be pleased, and one will swiftly attain this most supreme secret siddhi before long.

34. Chapter on Light Substances: Susiddhikara Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-Four. "Furthermore, once the ritual consecration (*abhiṣeka*) has been performed according to the Dharma, one should perform *homā* for twenty-one days, seven days, or one month, or as corresponds to the specific accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Alternatively, one should perform *homā* three times daily using ghee, honey, and curd mixed with sesame seeds, as prescribed in the root text;
or one may offer milk porridge or curd-rice according to the root text."
"Three times each day, one should fumigate the accomplished object with incense and sprinkle it with scented water;
empower and gaze upon the object with mantras;
and place a *śrī-kaṭaka* (auspicious ring) upon a finger, pressing it against the object."
Sprinkle ox-gall water or white mustard seeds upon the object, and on auspicious festival days, present various offerings to that object.
If the rite is performed during the waxing moon, take the fifteenth day; if during the waning moon, take the fourteenth day. By performing the ritual in this manner, the object will be made radiant.

In all cases, one should employ the mantra of the Family Mother (*kuleśvarī*). Furthermore, one should add offerings such as various flowers and garlands, anoint the hands with incense, place a ring of *kuśa* grass, and press it upon the object to be accomplished. One should recite the mantra throughout the night, performing one hundred and eight recitations during each of the three watches of the night. In this manner, the object of accomplishment shall be made manifest; from beginning to end, one should proceed in this way.
If one possesses these dharmas, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
The mantra for the Illumination of the Buddha Family is:
"Oṃ tija seṃ vidhi siddhyadhaya huṃ phaṭ. The mantra for the Illumination of the Lotus Family is:
“Oṃ abhi abhi ni-pāya mahā-śrīye svāhā. The mantra for the manifestation of light in the Vajra family is: “Oṃ jvala jvalaya bandhuri svāhā.
For the rites of all three families, one should use red karavīra flowers; having empowered them with the mantra, one should sprinkle them over the object.
Alternatively, one may use mañjarī flowers or white mustard seeds; at the beginning, the end, and the middle, one should likewise scatter and sprinkle them over the object.
If there is agitation within the realm or the appearance of different signs, it shall likewise be dispersed;
even when on the verge of accomplishment, if it is thus dispersed, it will instead become radiant and manifest.

If one wishes to accomplish substances such as clarified butter (*sarpis*), one should use mantra-empowered scented water to sprinkle those objects, whereby they become radiant and manifest. Using such methods to make objects radiant, one should not interrupt the practice even if success is not immediately achieved; alternatively, one may construct a maṇḍala to bring about this radiance.
"As before, prepare a maṇḍala on purified ground using five colors, measuring four cubits in size and having a single gate.
In the eastern side of the inner court, first place the wheel seal (*cakra-mudrā*);
in the northeast corner, place the bowl seal (*pātra-mudrā*)."
Place the *kāṣāya* seal in the southeast corner.
Next, place the lotus seal on the northern side;
place the *daṇḍa* staff seal in the northwest corner.
In the northeast corner, place the seal of the *kamaṇḍalu* flask.
Next, on the southern side, place the seal of the *vajra*;
in the southeast corner, place the seal of the *gadā*.
In the southwest corner, place the seal of the kalaśa flask.
On the western side, place the seal of the vajrāṅkuśa and the seal of the vajramuṣṭi;
in the southwest corner, place the seal of kīlikila.
In the northwest corner, place the seal of Śumbha.
Furthermore, on the eastern side, place the wheel; on its right side, place the seal of the Mother of the Buddha Family (Buddhakulī Mātṛ).
Again, on the northern side, place the lotus seal; on its right side, place the seal of the Mother of the Pañcarakṣā Family.
Next, place the Vajra mudrā on the southern side, and to its right, place the mudrā of the Mother Maṃjugī;
then, outside the gate of the maṇḍala, place the mudrā of Caṇḍa-mahāroṣaṇa, who can crush all hostile armies, as previously described, and perform offerings according to the preceding ritual.

Furthermore, on the northern side, place the seals of the Six-Armed One, Hayagrīva, Tārā, and Canda, as well as all the retinues belonging to their respective families, arranging them in sequence; the forms of these should all be white.

Furthermore, on the eastern side, place the seals of the Tathāgata Śakti, Tejorāśi, Aparājita Vidyārāja, and Aparājita Vidyārājñī; then, on the southern side, arrange in sequence all the retinues within that family.
Finally, on the western side, install the various seals of the three families as you see fit.

"Next, place the great deities of the eight directions, such as Kuvira and others, in the outer enclosure; in the remaining empty spaces, place at will the mantra-lords who accomplish all matters within the three families."

Next, place the hand-seal (*mudrā*) of the presiding deity of the respective family within the central platform; place the object to be accomplished therein according to what is prescribed in its specific root-text, and install that presiding deity upon the central platform.
To the east of the object, place the root mantra and the mudrā held by the practitioner;

to the west of the object, install the homa fire-pit; next, to the west, the reciter sits down, and each person invokes [the deity] according to their own root mantra and the prescribed ritual, as previously described.

Having completed the sequential offerings, one should consecrate the object by performing homa with the vidyās of the three families in succession; thereafter, perform the consecration by means of homa using the root mantra.
"Among all radiant dharmas, homa is supreme.
Whenever one first performs homa, one should first recite the *kulamātṛ* mantra over scented water and sprinkle it upon the objects; when the homa is completed, one should likewise sprinkle them."
Alternatively, one may use the heart-mantra of Mañjughoṣa;
or, using the four-syllable mantra of the Vidyārāja, perform the homa for all three families to bring about radiance.
Whichever mantra is employed for the homa, first recite that mantra, and next recite the words of supplication.
Furthermore, one recites the mantra in the middle, and again recites the words of petition;
subsequently, one also recites the mantra, placing the words of petition once more.
In this manner, within the mantra, the words of petition are placed in three locations: the upper, middle, and lower sections.

Finally, append the syllables *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is what is called: *jvālāmukha jvala jvalaya siddhi-sādhanī tejas-tejini tejo-dharāṇi dīpya dīpya dīpyamāne jvāle dīpya vardhaya mā vilamba āviśa rakṣa saṃnidhāna kuru hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
"By means of such phrases of invocation, one should illuminate the object; it is not an impediment to reciting them variously in repetitions at the beginning, middle, and end.
Once the homa is completed, one should next perform the illumination by reciting while scattering white karavīra flowers over the object;
alternatively, one may use red karavīra flowers, white mustard seeds, or sumana flowers to perform the illumination."
"First, apply scented ointment to the hands and press it upon the object;
next, scatter white mustard seeds while reciting the mantra over various flowers;
then, fumigate it with burning incense."
Thereafter, one should sprinkle with scented water while reciting.
One should understand the sequence to be as follows:

during the three periods of the first, middle, and last watches of the night, one sprinkles while reciting the mantra of the scented water belonging to the primary treasury-lord; next, having finished sprinkling while reciting the primary *dhāraṇī* mantra, one performs the *homa* and recitation as before until sunrise. One who possesses this method will swiftly attain accomplishment.

“Thus, by illuminating various objects as well as one’s own body, one will certainly and swiftly achieve accomplishment regarding those objects; even if the objects are few, one shall obtain great efficacy. One who possesses this rite will see those objects increase and attain purity. Therefore, one should perform the rite of illumination; this is called the secret method for accomplishing all things.”
"On all festival days, one should perform such rites of illumination; on other days, perform illumination as the occasion requires.

When the required number of recitations has been completed and one wishes to perform the rite of accomplishment (*sādhana*), one should first perform the rite of illumination in full during the first watch of the night, and only then achieve success."
Susiddhikara Sūtra, Vol. Lower. On the twenty-third day of the eighth month in the twenty-fifth year of Ōei, by Ejun of the Daibenzōin.
